title: Male Hypogonadism (Testosterone Deficiency): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (J Clin Endocrinol Metab)
snippet: Diagnosis of male hypogonadism requires persistent low morning fasting total testosterone (<300 ng/dL [10.4 nmol/L] on two separate occasions drawn between 8 AM and 10 AM) accompanied by unequivocal signs and symptoms: diminished libido, erectile dysfunction, decreased spontaneous erections, loss of axillary/pubic hair, and osteopenia. Serum LH and FSH differentiate primary (hypergonadotropic, testicular failure) from secondary (hypogonadotropic, hypothalamic-pituitary pathology). The TRAVERSE trial (NEJM 2023) demonstrated noninferiority of testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) regarding major adverse cardiac events in men with confirmed hypogonadism and pre-existing CVD. TRT is contraindicated in active prostate cancer, PSA > 4.0 ng/mL, severe untreated sleep apnea, or baseline hematocrit > 50%. Guideline Protocol: Weight loss (5-10% weight loss increases endogenous testosterone in obese men); progressive resistance strength training; structured management of obstructive sleep apnea. Thresholds: Target mid-normal morning total testosterone (400-700 ng/dL); withhold or titrate down if hematocrit exceeds 54% to prevent erythrocytosis-induced thrombosis.

title: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Fertil Steril)
snippet: Rotterdam diagnostic criteria require 2 out of 3 features: oligo- or anovulation, clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism (Ferriman-Gallwey hirsutism score ≥ 4-6, elevated free/total testosterone), and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound (≥20 follicles per ovary or ovarian volume ≥10 mL), after excluding thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, and non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Insulin resistance drives excess ovarian theca cell androgen production. Combined oral contraceptives (COCs) are first-line for irregular menses and hyperandrogenism; metformin improves insulin sensitivity and metabolic parameters; letrozole is first-line for ovulation induction in infertility (surpassing clomiphene in the PPCOS II trial; NEJM 2014). Guideline Protocol: 5-10% body weight reduction restores regular ovulatory cycles in over 50% of overweight patients; low-glycemic index dietary regimen; regular aerobic and resistance exercise. Thresholds: Unscheduled amenorrhea > 90 days requires progestin-induced withdrawal bleed or ultrasound to rule out endometrial hyperplasia.

title: Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Am J Gastroenterol)
snippet: Peptic ulcer disease involves mucosal breaks ≥ 5 mm in the stomach or duodenum extending into the muscularis propria, primarily driven by Helicobacter pylori infection or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) provides definitive diagnosis and endoscopic Forrest classification for bleeding risk. H. pylori eradication with 14-day bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI + bismuth subcitrate + metronidazole + tetracycline) achieves >85-90% cure rates despite clarithromycin resistance, reducing ulcer recurrence from >60% to <5%. Eradication must be confirmed via urea breath test or stool antigen ≥ 4 weeks post-treatment and ≥ 2 weeks off PPI therapy. NSAID ulcers require PPI therapy and switching to celecoxib or acetaminophen. Guideline Protocol: Complete cessation of tobacco and NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen); avoidance of heavy alcohol ingestion; structured stress reduction. Thresholds: Active ulcer with visible bleeding vessel (Forrest Ia/Ib/IIa) mandates endoscopic dual therapy (hemoclip + epinephrine) plus high-dose IV PPI infusion for 72 hours.

title: Chronic Hepatitis B Infection: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Hepatology)
snippet: Chronic hepatitis B (persistence of HBsAg > 6 months) causes immune-mediated necroinflammation, progressing to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Treatment indications depend on serum HBV DNA levels, ALT elevations, and stage of liver fibrosis (transient elastography / FibroScan). Nucleos(t)ide analogues with high genetic barrier to resistance (entecavir 0.5 mg daily, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate [TDF] 300 mg daily, or tenofovir alafenamide [TAF] 25 mg daily) suppress viral replication to undetectable levels in >95% of adherent patients, reversing fibrosis and dramatically reducing HCC incidence. HCC surveillance with abdominal ultrasound ± alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) every 6 months is mandatory for all cirrhotic patients, Asian men >40, Asian women >50, and African Americans >20. Guideline Protocol: Complete abstinence from alcohol; vaccination against Hepatitis A; weight management to avoid concurrent MAFLD/steatohepatitis; family screening for HBsAg and anti-HBs. Thresholds: HBV DNA > 2,000 IU/mL with ALT > 2x ULN or significant fibrosis (F2 or greater) mandates antiviral therapy; any cirrhosis with detectable HBV DNA requires immediate treatment.

title: Gastroparesis: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Am J Gastroenterol)
snippet: Gastroparesis is a chronic neuromuscular gastric disorder characterized by delayed gastric emptying without mechanical mechanical obstruction, most commonly idiopathic (50%) or diabetic (30%). Gold-standard diagnosis requires 4-hour solid-phase gastric emptying scintigraphy (GES) showing > 10% gastric retention at 4 hours or > 60% at 2 hours. Management begins with dietary modifications (small, frequent, low-fat, low-insoluble-fiber meals). In diabetes, strict glycemic control is paramount because acute hyperglycemia (>200 mg/dL) slows gastric peristalsis. Prokinetic therapy includes metoclopramide (FDA-approved, limited to <12 weeks when possible due to tardive dyskinesia risk) or erythromycin; oral dopamine antagonist domperidone is utilized under special programs. Refractory cases may benefit from gastric peroral endoscopic myotomy (G-POEM). Guideline Protocol: Consume 4-6 small meals daily; choose homogenized, pureed, or liquid nutrients; chew thoroughly; avoid high-fiber foods (oranges, broccoli) that form bezoars; remain upright for 2 hours post-meal. Thresholds: Gastric retention > 10% at 4 hours on standardized solid meal scintigraphy confirms delayed gastric emptying.

title: Achalasia: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Am J Gastroenterol)
snippet: Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by loss of myenteric plexus inhibitory ganglion cells, causing incomplete lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation and absent peristalsis. Patients present with progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food, chest pain, and weight loss. High-resolution manometry (HRM) is the gold standard diagnostic tool, categorizing disease via Chicago Classification: Type I (classic), Type II (panesophageal pressurization; >90% treatment response), and Type III (spastic). Diagnosis requires Integrated Relaxation Pressure (IRP > 15 mmHg) and 100% aperistalsis. Definitive therapies disrupt LES smooth muscle: Pneumatic balloon dilation (PD), laparoscopic Heller myotomy (LHM with partial fundoplication), or peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM; European achalasia trial demonstrated >85-90% success rates at 2-5 years, Eckardt score ≤ 3). Guideline Protocol: Eat slowly; chew food to a liquid consistency; drink warm water with meals; elevate head of bed 30 degrees to prevent nocturnal pulmonary aspiration. Thresholds: Integrated relaxation pressure (IRP) > 15 mmHg on high-resolution manometry with 100% aperistalsis confirms diagnosis; post-treatment Eckardt score ≤ 3 indicates clinical remission.

title: Microscopic Colitis: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Gastroenterology)
snippet: Microscopic colitis encompasses lymphocytic colitis (≥20 intraepithelial lymphocytes per 100 surface epithelial cells) and collagenous colitis (subepithelial collagen band thickness ≥ 10 µm), presenting with chronic, non-bloody, watery diarrhea (often 5-15 bowel movements/day), fecal urgency, nocturnal diarrhea, and fecal incontinence. Macroscopic colonoscopy appearance is typically normal, making systematic mucosal biopsies throughout the ascending, transverse, and descending colon mandatory. First-line medical therapy is oral budesonide (9 mg/day for 6-8 weeks; Cochrane Meta-analysis RR for clinical remission 3.18, 95% CI 2.04-4.97). Discontinuation of potential offending triggers (NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs, statins) is recommended. Low-dose budesonide (3-6 mg/day) maintains remission in frequent relapsers. Guideline Protocol: Identify and eliminate dietary triggers (caffeine, artificial sweeteners like sorbitol, dairy if lactase deficient); stop non-essential NSAIDs and PPIs; pelvic floor muscle training for fecal urgency. Thresholds: Clinical remission defined as < 3 stools per day and < 1 watery stool per day on a standardized diary.

title: Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Hepatology)
snippet: Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic immune-mediated hepatic necroinflammation characterized by hypergammaglobulinemia (elevated IgG), circulating autoantibodies (Type 1: ANA, ASMA; Type 2: anti-LKM1), and interface hepatitis with plasma cell infiltrates on liver biopsy. Untreated, 5-year survival is <50% in severe disease. Standard induction therapy consists of oral prednisone (30-60 mg/day tapered) or budesonide (9 mg/day in non-cirrhotic patients) combined with azathioprine (1-2 mg/kg/day). Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) and NUDT15 genotype/phenotype testing prior to azathioprine initiation prevents life-threatening myelosuppression. Treatment aims for complete biochemical remission (normalization of both serum transaminases and IgG levels), which must be maintained for ≥ 2 years before attempting cautiously supervised withdrawal. Guideline Protocol: Complete abstinence from alcohol; vaccination against hepatitis A and B; baseline DEXA scan and calcium/vitamin D supplementation while on systemic corticosteroids. Thresholds: Complete biochemical response requires normalization of AST, ALT, and total serum IgG below upper limit of normal.

solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Complete biochemical response requires normalization of AST, ALT, and total serum IgG below upper limit of normal.

title: Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Hepatology)
snippet: Primary biliary cholangitis is a chronic autoimmune cholestatic liver disease predominantly affecting women (9:1 ratio), characterized by progressive immune destruction of intrahepatic interlobular bile ducts. Hallmark diagnosis requires ≥2 of 3 criteria: sustained elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP > 1.5x ULN), presence of antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA titer ≥ 1:40, found in >95% of patients), and compatible liver biopsy findings (florid duct lesions). First-line therapy is oral ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA 13-15 mg/kg/day), which delays disease progression, prolongs transplant-free survival, and normalizes life expectancy in complete biochemical responders (Paris II criteria: ALP and AST ≤ 1.5x ULN with normal bilirubin at 1 year). Incomplete responders are escalated to second-line obeticholic acid or PPAR agonists (bezafibrate/elafibranor). Guideline Protocol: Skin care protocols for chronic pruritus (mild cool baths, emollients); fat-soluble vitamin supplementation (Vitamins A, D, E, K); regular weight-bearing exercise to prevent osteoporosis. Thresholds: Alkaline phosphatase > 1.67x ULN or elevated total bilirubin after 12 months of UDCA therapy indicates incomplete response and need for second-line therapy.

patient_plain_language: Primary biliary cholangitis is an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks and damages the tiny drainage tubes (bile ducts) inside your liver. When bile gets trapped, it leaks into the bloodstream, causing deep itching, fatigue, and eventual liver scarring.

solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Alkaline phosphatase > 1.67x ULN or elevated total bilirubin after 12 months of UDCA therapy indicates incomplete response and need for second-line therapy.

title: Acute Pancreatitis: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Am J Gastroenterol)
snippet: Diagnosis requires at least 2 of 3 Atlanta criteria: characteristic epigastric pain radiating to the back, serum lipase or amylase > 3x the upper limit of normal, and characteristic cross-sectional imaging findings (contrast-enhanced CT or MRI). Gallstones (40-50%) and alcohol (30%) are leading etiologies. Landmark WATERFALL trial (NEJM 2022) demonstrated that aggressive fluid resuscitation significantly increased fluid overload (20.5% vs 6.3%) without improving clinical outcomes compared to moderate resuscitation (Lactated Ringer's 1.5 mL/kg/hr after 10 mL/kg bolus if hypovolemic). Prophylactic antibiotics are strictly not recommended. Early oral refeeding with a low-fat solid or liquid diet as soon as ileus has resolved and pain improves shortens hospital stay and reduces infectious complications. Guideline Protocol: Complete abstinence from alcohol and tobacco; cholecystectomy during index admission for mild biliary pancreatitis to prevent recurrent life-threatening attacks; low-fat dietary intake. Thresholds: Rising BUN (>20 mg/dL or any increase at 24 hours) or hematocrit > 44% signals hemoconcentration and increased risk of pancreatic necrosis.

solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Frequent vital signs, urine output (>0.5 mL/kg/hr), hematocrit, and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) checks in the first 24-48 hours; repeat ultrasound or MRCP if etiology unclear.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Rising BUN (>20 mg/dL or any increase at 24 hours) or hematocrit > 44% signals hemoconcentration and increased risk of pancreatic necrosis.

title: Hemorrhoidal Disease and Anal Fissure: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Dis Colon Rectum)
snippet: Hemorrhoids are vascular cushions in the anal canal; enlargement and distal displacement result in bleeding, prolapse, and thrombosis. Internal hemorrhoids present with painless bright red rectal bleeding on toilet paper or in bowl; external hemorrhoids cause hygiene issues or acute severe pain when thrombosed. Anal fissures are longitudinal mucosal tears distal to the dentate line causing sharp knife-like pain during defecation and bright rectal streaks. Cochrane meta-analysis confirms dietary fiber supplementation (25-35 g/day) and water intake reduce bleeding by 50%. First-line medical therapy for chronic fissures is topical calcium channel blockers (diltiazem 2% ointment) or topical nitroglycerin 0.4% ointment for 6-8 weeks (heals 65-75% by relaxing internal anal sphincter hypertonicity). Office procedures (rubber band ligation) treat persistent Grade I-III internal hemorrhoids. Guideline Protocol: Daily dietary fiber intake of 25-35 grams (soluble psyllium supplement); 2 liters water daily; avoid straining or sitting on toilet > 3-5 minutes; warm sitz baths for 10-15 minutes twice daily. Thresholds: Acutely thrombosed external hemorrhoid presenting within 72 hours of symptom onset benefits from simple office surgical excision under local anesthesia.

patient_plain_language: Hemorrhoids are swollen, inflamed blood vessel cushions in your lower rectum, while an anal fissure is a small crack or tear in the delicate skin of the anus. Hard stools and straining stretch these tissues, causing bright red bleeding and sharp stinging pain with bowel movements.

solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Acutely thrombosed external hemorrhoid presenting within 72 hours of symptom onset benefits from simple office surgical excision under local anesthesia.

title: Acute Diverticulitis: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Gastroenterology)
snippet: Acute diverticulitis represents inflammation and micro-perforation of a colonic diverticulum, predominantly in the sigmoid and descending colon. Contrast-enhanced abdominal pelvic CT is the imaging gold standard (sensitivity/specificity >95%), differentiating uncomplicated (localized colonic wall thickening and pericolic fat stranding) from complicated disease (abscess, macroperforation/peritonitis, fistula, or stricture). Randomized clinical trials (AVOD and DIABOLO) demonstrated that systemic antibiotics do not improve recovery time, complication rates, or recurrence in immunocompetent patients with mild, uncomplicated diverticulitis, supporting conservative outpatient observation without antibiotics. Colonoscopy is recommended 6-8 weeks post-resolution of complicated or first-episode diverticulitis to rule out misdiagnosed colorectal carcinoma (present in 2-4%). Guideline Protocol: Clear liquid diet for 2-3 days during acute painful phase, advancing to regular diet as tolerated; high-fiber diet long term; avoidance of NSAIDs; regular physical activity. Thresholds: Pelvic abscess ≥ 3-4 cm on CT warrants percutaneous catheter drainage; generalized peritonitis (Hinchey III/IV) requires emergent operative intervention.

patient_plain_language: Diverticulitis occurs when small pouches in your colon wall become inflamed or irritated. This typically causes sharp aching pain in the lower left side of your belly, mild fever, and nausea.

solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Outpatient clinical check at 48-72 hours; diagnostic colonoscopy 6-8 weeks after complete symptom resolution.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Pelvic abscess ≥ 3-4 cm on CT warrants percutaneous catheter drainage; generalized peritonitis (Hinchey III/IV) requires emergent operative intervention.

title: Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Am J Gastroenterol)
snippet: SIBO is defined as excessive colonic-type bacterial colonization in the small intestine (≥ 10³ colony-forming units/mL on duodenal aspirate culture), or positive non-invasive breath testing (increase in breath hydrogen ≥ 20 ppm above baseline within 90 minutes or breath methane ≥ 10 ppm at any time [intestinal methanogen overgrowth, IMO] using glucose or lactulose substrate). Patients experience chronic postprandial bloating, flatulence, watery diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, and in severe cases, fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption (A, D, E) and B12 deficiency from bacterial deconjugation of bile acids. Rifaximin (550 mg three times daily for 14 days) is the evidence-based first-line non-absorbable antibiotic, producing symptom response in >60-70% of hydrogen-predominant SIBO. Methane-positive IMO requires dual therapy (rifaximin + neomycin or metronidazole). Guideline Protocol: Temporary low-FODMAP diet to decrease rapidly fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols; spacing meals 4-5 hours apart to promote migrating motor complex (MMC) cleansing waves. Thresholds: Hydrogen rise ≥ 20 ppm within 90 minutes or methane ≥ 10 ppm establishes positive breath test.

patient_plain_language: SIBO occurs when bacteria that normally belong in the large intestine migrate backwards and colonize the small intestine in high numbers. When you eat carbohydrates, these bacteria ferment the food prematurely, creating large amounts of hydrogen or methane gas that cause severe bloating, pain, and diarrhea.

doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Does my treatment plan include a 14-day course of rifaximin, and will my insurance require prior authorization?

solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Clinical symptom review at 2-4 weeks post-antibiotic treatment; repeat breath testing only if symptoms fail to resolve or rapidly recur; periodic serum B12 and vitamin D levels.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Hydrogen rise ≥ 20 ppm within 90 minutes or methane ≥ 10 ppm establishes positive breath test.

title: Barrett's Esophagus: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Am J Gastroenterol)
snippet: Barrett's esophagus (BE) is the metaplastic replacement of normal squamous esophageal epithelium by specialized columnar epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia), extending ≥ 1 cm proximal to the gastroesophageal junction, resulting from chronic GERD. BE is the sole established precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma. Screening with high-definition endoscopy is recommended in men with chronic GERD symptoms (>5 years) and ≥2 risk factors (age >50, Caucasian, central obesity, history of smoking, first-degree relative with BE/cancer). All patients require once-daily PPI maintenance therapy. Endoscopic surveillance follows the Seattle biopsy protocol (4-quadrant biopsies every 2 cm): non-dysplastic BE requires repeat EGD every 3-5 years; confirmed low-grade or high-grade dysplasia warrants endoscopic eradication therapy (radiofrequency ablation [RFA] ± endoscopic mucosal resection [EMR]). Guideline Protocol: Smoking cessation; weight loss to decrease intra-abdominal pressure; avoid lying flat within 3 hours of meals; elevate head of bed 6 inches. Thresholds: Length ≥ 1 cm with histological intestinal metaplasia confirms BE; any dysplasia must be independently confirmed by an expert gastrointestinal pathologist.

patient_plain_language: Barrett's esophagus happens when years of acid reflux irritate the bottom of your swallowing tube. To protect itself from stomach acid, the lining transforms its delicate cells into tougher, intestinal-type cells. Because these changed cells carry a small risk of turning cancerous over time, doctors monitor them with regular cameras.

solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Endoscopic surveillance every 3-5 years for non-dysplastic BE; every 6-12 months for confirmed low-grade dysplasia without ablation; immediate ablation for confirmed high-grade dysplasia.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Length ≥ 1 cm with histological intestinal metaplasia confirms BE; any dysplasia must be independently confirmed by an expert gastrointestinal pathologist.

title: Clostridioides difficile Infection (CDI): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Clin Infect Dis)
snippet: C. difficile infection is toxin-mediated colitis typically precipitated by broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure (clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins) disrupting colon microbiota. Diagnosis requires ≥ 3 unformed liquid stools in 24 hours plus laboratory confirmation: multi-step testing with NAAT/PCR and toxin EIA or cell cytotoxicity assay. The 2021 IDSA guidelines designate fidaxomicin (200 mg orally twice daily for 10 days) as the preferred first-line agent over oral vancomycin (125 mg orally four times daily for 10 days), demonstrating sustained clinical cure and significantly lower recurrence rates (15% vs 25%, p=0.005). Metronidazole is no longer recommended for non-severe CDI. Recurrent CDI is treated with tapered vancomycin, fidaxomicin, or fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT / live biotherapeutic products, e.g., fecal microbiota spores, live-brpk / Rebyota / Vowst). Guideline Protocol: Strict hand hygiene with soap and water (alcohol-based hand rubs do NOT kill C. diff bacterial spores); contact isolation precautions; immediate discontinuation of inciting broad-spectrum antibiotics. Thresholds: Severe CDI defined by WBC ≥ 15,000 cells/µL or serum creatinine > 1.5 mg/dL; fulminant CDI defined by hypotension, shock, ileus, or megacolon.

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Strict hand hygiene with soap and water (alcohol-based hand rubs do NOT kill C. diff bacterial spores); contact isolation precautions; immediate discontinuation of inciting broad-spectrum antibiotics.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Clinical symptom resolution (stool frequency and consistency); follow-up 'test of cure' stool testing is strictly contraindicated because spores persist after cure.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Severe CDI defined by WBC ≥ 15,000 cells/µL or serum creatinine > 1.5 mg/dL; fulminant CDI defined by hypotension, shock, ileus, or megacolon.

title: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Stroke)
snippet: A TIA is defined neurobiologically as a transient episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia, without acute tissue infarction on diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI). ABCD2 score (Age ≥60, BP ≥140/90, Clinical features [unilateral weakness, speech impairment], Duration, Diabetes) stratifies 90-day stroke risk. Landmark POINT and CHANCE randomized trials demonstrated that high-risk TIA (ABCD2 ≥ 4) or minor stroke requires dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT: aspirin 81 mg + clopidogrel 75 mg daily after loading doses) initiated within 24 hours and continued for 21 days (POINT trial: major ischemic events reduced by 25%, HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.59-0.95; CHANCE trial: HR 0.68), followed by single antiplatelet monotherapy long-term to minimize major bleeding risk. Guideline Protocol: Emergent diagnostic evaluation within 24 hours: brain MRI with DWI, vascular imaging (CTA/MRA of head and neck), 12-lead ECG, telemetry/Holter to rule out atrial fibrillation; Mediterranean diet and blood pressure < 130/80 mmHg. Thresholds: ABCD2 score ≥ 4 indicates high early stroke recurrence risk, mandating hospitalization and 21-day DAPT.

patient_plain_language: A TIA (transient ischemic attack), sometimes called a 'warning stroke' or 'mini-stroke', occurs when blood flow to a part of your brain is briefly blocked. The symptoms disappear within minutes to hours, but it is a critical warning sign that a major, permanent stroke could happen soon unless treated immediately.

solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: ABCD2 score ≥ 4 indicates high early stroke recurrence risk, mandating hospitalization and 21-day DAPT.

title: Myasthenia Gravis: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Neurology)
snippet: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder caused by pathogenic autoantibodies directed against acetylcholine receptors (AChR-Ab, 85%), muscle-specific kinase (MuSK), or LRP4, manifesting as fluctuating, fatigable skeletal muscle weakness with diurnal variation (worse in the evening or after exertion). Ptosis and diplopia occur in >85%; bulbar and respiratory involvement produce dysarthria, dysphagia, and dyspnea. First-line symptomatic treatment is oral pyridostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, 30-60 mg every 4-6 hours). Corticosteroids (prednisone) combined with steroid-sparing agents (azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil) induce immunosuppression. Landmark MGTX trial (NEJM 2016) proved extended transsternal thymectomy provides long-term clinical benefit in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG under age 65. Guideline Protocol: Rest periods prior to meals to facilitate safe swallowing; avoid extreme heat/hot baths; strictly avoid neuromuscular-blocking medications (fluoroquinolones, macrolides, aminoglycosides, beta-blockers, magnesium). Thresholds: Forced vital capacity (FVC) < 15-20 mL/kg or NIF worse than -20 to -30 cmH2O indicates impending myasthenic crisis requiring ICU transfer.

patient_plain_language: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune condition where your body's antibodies block communication between your nerves and muscles. This causes muscles to tire out unusually fast with use, leading to drooping eyelids, double vision, and weakness when chewing or lifting your arms.

doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Do I have an up-to-date wallet card listing common prescription antibiotics and drugs that are strictly forbidden in myasthenia?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: At what degree of swallowing difficulty or breathing fatigue should I go directly to the emergency department for intravenous IVIG or plasma exchange?

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Rest periods prior to meals to facilitate safe swallowing; avoid extreme heat/hot baths; strictly avoid neuromuscular-blocking medications (fluoroquinolones, macrolides, aminoglycosides, beta-blockers, magnesium).
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis (QMG) or MG Activities of Daily Living (MG-ADL) score tracking; pulmonary function testing (forced vital capacity [FVC] and negative inspiratory force [NIF]) during flares; chest CT to screen for thymoma.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Forced vital capacity (FVC) < 15-20 mL/kg or NIF worse than -20 to -30 cmH2O indicates impending myasthenic crisis requiring ICU transfer.

title: Trigeminal Neuralgia: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Eur J Neurol)
snippet: Trigeminal neuralgia is characterized by sudden, unilateral, brief, electric shock-like paroxysmal pain limited to the distribution of one or more branches of the fifth cranial nerve (most frequently V2 maxillary and V3 mandibular), triggered by innocuous sensory tactile stimuli (washing, shaving, talking, brushing teeth, light breeze). Classical trigeminal neuralgia is caused by neurovascular compression of the trigeminal nerve root entry zone (most often by the superior cerebellar artery), detectable on high-resolution 3D constructive interference in steady state (CISS/FIESTA) MRI. Carbamazepine (200-1,200 mg/day; Cochrane review NNT=1.7) and oxcarbazepine (600-1,800 mg/day) are the gold-standard first-line pharmacotherapies. Microvascular decompression (MVD / Janetta procedure) provides long-term pain freedom in >70-80% of refractory classical cases. Guideline Protocol: Identify and minimize trigger mechanisms (use soft toothbrushes, protect face from cold wind with scarves, chew on unaffected side); pre-medication HLA-B*1502 genetic screening in patients of Asian descent to avoid Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Thresholds: Carbamazepine titrated to pain relief while monitoring for serum sodium < 130 mEq/L or elevated transaminases.

patient_plain_language: Trigeminal neuralgia, sometimes referred to as 'tic douloureux', is a severe nerve pain disorder caused by an irritated nerve in your face. Simple daily actions like brushing your teeth, chewing, or feeling a gentle breeze against your cheek can trigger excruciating, lightning-bolt shocks across your jaw or cheek.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Did my specialized brain MRI show a blood vessel pressing directly against my trigeminal nerve root?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Are my blood counts and sodium levels being checked regularly while taking carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: If medications no longer control my pain attacks or cause severe drowsiness, would I be a candidate for surgical microvascular decompression?

solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Carbamazepine titrated to pain relief while monitoring for serum sodium < 130 mEq/L or elevated transaminases.

title: Essential Tremor: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Neurology)
snippet: Essential tremor is the most common movement disorder, characterized by an 8-12 Hz bilateral action or kinetic tremor prominently affecting the hands and forearms during voluntary movement (drinking from a cup, handwriting, using utensils), with or without head ('no-no' or 'yes-yes') or voice tremor, in the absence of other neurological signs (rigidity, bradykinesia, resting tremor). Family history is present in >50% (autosomal dominant transmission). Level A first-line therapies include propranolol (60-240 mg/day, reducing tremor amplitude by ~50%) and primidone (50-250 mg/day). Topiramate, gabapentin, and atenolol serve as Level B alternatives. For medically refractory disabling tremor, magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound (MRgFUS) thalamotomy or deep brain stimulation (DBS) targeting the ventral intermediate nucleus (VIM) of the thalamus produces >70% long-term tremor reduction. Guideline Protocol: Elimination of tremor-aggravating stimulants (excess caffeine, energy drinks, pseudoephedrine); use of weighted utensils, heavy mugs, and wrist weights; occupational therapy for writing ergonomics. Thresholds: Propranolol contraindicated in severe asthma or sinus bradycardia (resting HR < 55 bpm).

patient_plain_language: Essential tremor is a nervous system disorder that causes rhythmic shaking of your hands when you try to use them for everyday tasks like holding a coffee cup, eating soup, or writing. It is an 'action tremor' (worse when moving) rather than a resting tremor.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Does my clinical exam rule out Parkinson's disease (confirming this is an action tremor without resting rigidity)?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Does my pulse rate or history of asthma allow me to safely take propranolol for my hand tremors?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: If medications don't control the shaking enough to eat or write, am I a candidate for non-invasive focused ultrasound or deep brain stimulation?

red_flags: Sudden asymmetric onset accompanied by facial droop, limb weakness, or rapid cognitive decline indicating alternative central pathology

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Elimination of tremor-aggravating stimulants (excess caffeine, energy drinks, pseudoephedrine); use of weighted utensils, heavy mugs, and wrist weights; occupational therapy for writing ergonomics.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Fahn-Tolosa-Marin Tremor Rating Scale assessment annually; heart rate and blood pressure checks before and after propranolol titration.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Propranolol contraindicated in severe asthma or sinus bradycardia (resting HR < 55 bpm).

title: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Neurosurgery)
snippet: Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus is characterized by the classic clinical triad of gait disturbance ('magnetic', shuffling, wide-based, apraxic gait; typically the earliest and most responsive symptom), cognitive decline (subcortical dementia, psychomotor slowing), and urinary urgency/incontinence ('wobbly, wacky, and wet'). Brain MRI demonstrates ventriculomegaly disproportionate to sulcal enlargement (Evans' index > 0.30) with tight high-convexity sulci and enlarged Sylvian fissures (DESH pattern: disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid-space hydrocephalus). Diagnostic confirmation requires a high-volume lumbar puncture tap test (removal of 30-50 mL CSF) showing quantitative improvement in timed 10-meter walk velocity and step count. Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunting provides dramatic and sustained functional improvement in >75% of carefully selected patients (SINPHONI trials). Guideline Protocol: Physical therapy for gait training and fall prevention; structured home safety modifications (grab bars, removing throw rugs); scheduled toileting regimens. Thresholds: Evans' index > 0.30 on brain MRI plus ≥20% improvement in timed walk test post-LP confirms shunt-responsive NPH.
key_takeaway: Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus is characterized by the classic clinical triad of gait disturbance ('magnetic', shuffling, wide-based, apraxic gait; typically the earliest and most responsive symptom), cognitive...
patient_plain_language: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a treatable brain condition where excess spinal fluid slowly builds up in the fluid cavities (ventricles) of your brain. This extra fluid presses on nearby brain circuits, causing a classic trio of symptoms: a shuffling 'feet stuck to the floor' walk, mild memory confusion, and urinary urgency.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What is my Evans' index on brain imaging and did my MRI show the classic enlarged ventricles?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Can we schedule a high-volume lumbar puncture tap test to see if draining temporary spinal fluid improves my walking speed?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: If my walking speed improves after the spinal tap, are we ready to consult neurosurgery for a ventriculoperitoneal shunt?

red_flags: Sudden severe headache, persistent vomiting, fever, or lethargy after shunt surgery indicating shunt malfunction or infection

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Physical therapy for gait training and fall prevention; structured home safety modifications (grab bars, removing throw rugs); scheduled toileting regimens.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Quantitative timed 10-meter walk test and cognitive testing before and 2-4 hours after lumbar puncture; post-shunt clinical evaluation and non-contrast head CT at 1, 3, and 12 months.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Evans' index > 0.30 on brain MRI plus ≥20% improvement in timed walk test post-LP confirms shunt-responsive NPH.

title: Cluster Headache: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Headache)
snippet: Cluster headache is the most severe trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia, characterized by strictly unilateral, excruciating, piercing, or boring retro-orbital/temporal pain lasting 15-180 minutes, occurring from once every other day up to 8 times daily during cluster periods (often lasting 6-12 weeks). Attacks are accompanied by ipsilateral cranial autonomic symptoms (conjunctival injection, lacrimation, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, eyelid edema, forehead sweating, or miosis/ptosis) and severe motor agitation/restlessness (pacing). First-line acute abortive therapy mandates 100% normobaric oxygen via non-rebreather mask (12-15 L/min for 15-20 min; aborts >75% of attacks within 15 min; Cochrane review) or subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg. First-line preventive therapy is oral verapamil (high-dose: 240-960 mg/day), requiring baseline and serial ECG monitoring for PR prolongation and heart block. Galcanezumab (300 mg SQ monthly) is FDA-approved for episodic cluster prevention. Guideline Protocol: Strict avoidance of all alcohol during active cluster bouts (alcohol reliably triggers an attack within 45 minutes); maintain regular sleep-wake rhythms; avoid daytime napping. Thresholds: PR interval > 0.20 seconds or heart rate < 50 bpm on verapamil mandates dose reduction or cardiology consultation.

patient_plain_language: Cluster headaches are excruciating, one-sided headaches centered around or behind one eye that strike in clusters lasting weeks to months. Often nicknamed 'suicide headaches' due to their extreme intensity, they cause the eye to water and turn red, with intense restlessness that makes sitting still impossible.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Do I have a home medical oxygen tank with a high-flow non-rebreather mask (12 to 15 liters per minute) for fast attack relief?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Are we performing serial ECG tracings as we increase my verapamil dose to ensure my heart rate and electrical conduction stay safe?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Would I benefit from a short steroid taper or galcanezumab injections to break my current cluster cycle?

red_flags: Sudden maximal-intensity headache ('thunderclap' headache reaching peak in <1 minute) requiring urgent exclusion of subarachnoid hemorrhage

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Strict avoidance of all alcohol during active cluster bouts (alcohol reliably triggers an attack within 45 minutes); maintain regular sleep-wake rhythms; avoid daytime napping.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: ECG at baseline and after every 80 mg dose increase of verapamil above 240 mg/day (to detect PR interval prolongation and AV block); headache attack log.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: PR interval > 0.20 seconds or heart rate < 50 bpm on verapamil mandates dose reduction or cardiology consultation.

title: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Eur J Neurol)
snippet: ALS is a progressive, fatal neurodegenerative disease characterized by simultaneous degeneration of upper motor neurons (corticospinal: spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign) and lower motor neurons (anterior horn cells: muscle weakness, atrophy, fasciculations) across bulbar, cervical, thoracic, and lumbosacral regions. Gold standard diagnosis follows the Awaji/Gold Coast criteria supported by electromyography (EMG). Multidisciplinary specialized care extends survival and improves quality of life. Riluzole (50 mg orally twice daily) extends median tracheostomy-free survival by 2-3 months by modulating glutamatergic neurotransmission. Edaravone (IV/oral free radical scavenger) slows functional decline in early disease. Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation (NIV / BiPAP) significantly prolongs survival and slows respiratory decline when initiated once forced vital capacity (FVC) drops below 80% or sniff nasal inspiratory pressure (SNIP) < 40 cmH2O. Guideline Protocol: Multidisciplinary clinic visits (neurologist, pulmonologist, speech therapist, occupational therapist, registered dietitian); high-calorie, nutrient-dense diet to prevent hypermetabolic weight loss; early discussion of advance care planning. Thresholds: FVC < 80% of predicted, orthopnea, or daytime hypercapnia mandates immediate initiation of noninvasive ventilation (BiPAP).
key_takeaway: ALS is a progressive, fatal neurodegenerative disease characterized by simultaneous degeneration of upper motor neurons (corticospinal: spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign) and lower motor neurons (anterior horn cel...
patient_plain_language: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), also known as Lou Gehrig's disease, is a condition where the nerve cells in your brain and spinal cord that control voluntary muscles slowly break down. Over time, muscles become weak and thin, affecting walking, speaking, swallowing, and breathing.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What is my current forced vital capacity (FVC) sitting and lying down, and what is my ALSFRS-R functional score?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Are my liver enzymes normal on riluzole, and are we monitoring my swallowing safety to prevent aspiration pneumonia?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: When should we order a noninvasive breathing machine (BiPAP) to support my lungs and help me sleep comfortably?

red_flags: Severe respiratory insufficiency with morning headaches (CO2 retention), inability to clear throat secretions, or acute aspiration choking events

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Multidisciplinary clinic visits (neurologist, pulmonologist, speech therapist, occupational therapist, registered dietitian); high-calorie, nutrient-dense diet to prevent hypermetabolic weight loss; early discussion of advance care planning.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R) and upright/supine spirometry (FVC) every 3 months; liver function tests every month for the first 3 months on riluzole.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: FVC < 80% of predicted, orthopnea, or daytime hypercapnia mandates immediate initiation of noninvasive ventilation (BiPAP).

title: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor Cerebri): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (JAMA)
snippet: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) predominantly affects women of childbearing age with obesity (BMI > 30), characterized by elevated intracranial pressure (>250 mmH2O on lumbar puncture in adults) in the absence of ventriculomegaly, mass lesion, or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Classic symptoms include daily throbbing headaches, transient visual obscurations (dimming of vision lasting seconds with postural changes), pulsatile tinnitus ('whooshing' sound in ears), and horizontal diplopia (cranial nerve VI palsy). The hallmark physical sign is bilateral papilledema, which risks permanent optic atrophy and blindness. The landmark IIHTT trial proved that weight reduction combined with acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, titrated up to 1-4 g/day) significantly improved Humphrey visual field mean deviation, reduced papilledema grade, and improved quality of life compared to placebo. Guideline Protocol: Structured lifestyle weight management program targeting 5-15% sustained body weight reduction (often induces disease remission); sodium-restricted diet; discontinuation of offending medications (tetracyclines, retinoids/Accutane, excess vitamin A). Thresholds: CSF opening pressure > 250 mmH2O confirms elevated ICP; worsening visual field loss (mean deviation worsening by >2 dB) warrants surgical intervention (optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunt).

patient_plain_language: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension, or pseudotumor cerebri, occurs when fluid pressure builds up inside your skull without an actual tumor. This high pressure squeezes your optic nerves, leading to daily headaches, a rhythmic whooshing heartbeat sound in your ears, and brief dimming or blurring of vision.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What was my cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure on spinal tap, and what is the severity grade of my papilledema?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Are my serum electrolytes and potassium levels being monitored while I am taking acetazolamide (Diamox)?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Are my automated visual field tests showing that my peripheral vision is completely stable, or is there any sign of vision loss?

red_flags: Rapid progressive constriction of peripheral vision, loss of central visual acuity, or persistent double vision (impending optic nerve compromise)

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Structured lifestyle weight management program targeting 5-15% sustained body weight reduction (often induces disease remission); sodium-restricted diet; discontinuation of offending medications (tetracyclines, retinoids/Accutane, excess vitamin A).
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Humphrey automated visual field testing and optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the retinal nerve fiber layer every 1-3 months; comprehensive dilated funduscopic exam.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: CSF opening pressure > 250 mmH2O confirms elevated ICP; worsening visual field loss (mean deviation worsening by >2 dB) warrants surgical intervention (optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunt).

title: Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS / Willis-Ekbom Disease): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Neurology)
snippet: Diagnostic criteria (IRLSSG) require: (1) an irresistible urge to move the legs usually accompanied by uncomfortable paresthesias, (2) symptoms begin or worsen during periods of rest or inactivity, (3) symptoms are partially or totally relieved by movement (walking, stretching), and (4) symptoms occur exclusively or predominantly in the evening or night. Central nervous system iron deficiency in the substantia nigra impairs dopamine neurotransmission. Serum ferritin should be evaluated; oral iron supplementation is indicated if ferritin < 75 mcg/L or transferrin saturation < 20%, and IV ferric carboxymaltose is superior for refractory iron deficiency. First-line pharmacotherapy has shifted to alpha-2-delta calcium channel ligands (gabapentin enacarbil, pregabalin) over dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole) because dopamine agonists cause severe clinical augmentation (earlier symptom onset, increased intensity, spread to arms) in up to 50-70% of long-term users. Guideline Protocol: Avoidance of exacerbating triggers: caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, sedating antihistamines (diphenhydramine), dopamine antagonists, and SSRIs/SNRIs; moderate regular exercise; warm evening baths. Thresholds: Serum ferritin < 75 mcg/L or transferrin saturation < 20% mandates therapeutic iron repletion.

patient_plain_language: Restless legs syndrome is a neurological sensory condition that causes an overwhelming, creepy-crawly urge to move your legs when you try to rest, sit still, or fall asleep. Moving or walking provides temporary relief, but the sensations return as soon as you lie down again.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What was my fasting ferritin and transferrin saturation level to see if low brain iron stores are causing my symptoms?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Why are alpha-2-delta medications like gabapentin generally preferred today over older dopamine drugs that can make symptoms worse over time?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Am I taking any over-the-counter nighttime sleep aids like Benadryl that could actually be making my restless legs flare up?

red_flags: Sudden severe impulse control disorders (compulsive gambling, binge eating, hypersexuality) if taking dopamine agonist medications

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Avoidance of exacerbating triggers: caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, sedating antihistamines (diphenhydramine), dopamine antagonists, and SSRIs/SNRIs; moderate regular exercise; warm evening baths.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Morning fasting iron panel (ferritin and transferrin saturation) every 6-12 months; International RLS Severity Scale (IRLS) symptom monitoring.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Serum ferritin < 75 mcg/L or transferrin saturation < 20% mandates therapeutic iron repletion.

title: Bell's Palsy (Idiopathic Facial Paralysis): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg)
snippet: Bell's palsy is an acute, unilateral peripheral lower motor neuron facial nerve (CN VII) paresis or paralysis, causing weakness of both upper and lower facial muscles (inability to furrow forehead, close eye, or smile), peaking within 72 hours, thought to result from HSV-1 reactivation causing nerve edema inside the fallopian canal. It is distinguished from central stroke where forehead movement is preserved due to bilateral cortical innervation. Cochrane systematic reviews and landmark RCTs confirm that oral corticosteroids (prednisone 60-80 mg/day for 7-10 days initiated within 72 hours of symptom onset) significantly increase complete recovery rates from ~70% to >85% (RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.05-1.26; NNT=10). Adding antiviral therapy (valacyclovir 1 g TID) provides modest incremental benefit in severe complete paralysis (House-Brackmann grade V-VI). Aggressive corneal protection is paramount to prevent exposure keratitis. Guideline Protocol: Aggressive daytime artificial tears every 1-2 hours; lubricating ophthalmic ointment at night; tape the eyelid safely shut at night with moisture chamber to prevent corneal ulceration. Thresholds: Initiation of high-dose oral corticosteroids within 72 hours of symptom onset is the critical therapeutic window.
key_takeaway: Bell's palsy is an acute, unilateral peripheral lower motor neuron facial nerve (CN VII) paresis or paralysis, causing weakness of both upper and lower facial muscles (inability to furrow forehead, close eye, or smile), ...
patient_plain_language: Bell's palsy is a sudden, temporary weakness or paralysis of the muscles on one side of your face caused by inflammation of the main facial nerve. Unlike a stroke, Bell's palsy causes your entire half of the face to droop, including your eyebrow and forehead, making it difficult to close your eye or smile.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Does my physical exam confirm that my forehead is paralyzed, ruling out a central brain stroke?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Have I started oral steroid pills within the critical 72-hour window to give my facial nerve the best chance of 100% recovery?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: What exact eye drops, lubricating night ointments, and protective tape should I use to protect my eye from drying out and scratching?

red_flags: Inability to close the eye leading to severe eye pain, foreign body sensation, redness, or cloudy cornea (impending corneal ulceration)

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Aggressive daytime artificial tears every 1-2 hours; lubricating ophthalmic ointment at night; tape the eyelid safely shut at night with moisture chamber to prevent corneal ulceration.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: House-Brackmann facial nerve grading at baseline and follow-up at 1, 3, and 6 months; ophthalmology referral if eye closure is incomplete.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Initiation of high-dose oral corticosteroids within 72 hours of symptom onset is the critical therapeutic window.

title: Nephrolithiasis (Kidney Stones): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (J Urol)
snippet: Nephrolithiasis affects ~10% of individuals, with calcium oxalate (75-80%) and uric acid (10%) being the most prevalent compositions. Acute presentation involves severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with microscopic or gross hematuria. Low-dose non-contrast abdominopelvic CT is the imaging gold standard. Stones < 5 mm have an ~75-80% spontaneous passage rate, while stones ≥ 7-10 mm frequently require urologic intervention (ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy or shock wave lithotripsy). Prevention requires 24-hour urine collection. High fluid intake to achieve > 2.5 L daily urine output halves recurrence risk (Cochrane RR 0.45). Normal dietary calcium (1,000-1,200 mg/day) reduces stone formation by binding dietary oxalate in the gut, whereas calcium restriction paradoxically increases stones. Thiazide diuretics reduce hypercalciuria; potassium citrate alkalinizes urine to dissolve uric acid stones and bind calcium. Guideline Protocol: Fluid intake to maintain > 2.5 liters urine output/day (urine color clear/pale); dietary sodium restriction (<2,300 mg/day; high sodium increases urinary calcium excretion); limit animal protein; do not restrict dietary calcium. Thresholds: Stones > 10 mm, persistent pain, severe hydronephrosis, or fever with infected obstructed stone require urgent urologic intervention.

patient_plain_language: Kidney stones are hard mineral crystal deposits that form inside your kidneys when your urine becomes overly concentrated. When a stone moves down the narrow drainage tube toward your bladder, it causes intense, cramping back and flank pain, nausea, and blood in your urine.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What is the measured size and exact location of my stone on the CT scan, and was my filtered stone sent for mineral analysis?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Should we complete a 24-hour urine collection to identify the chemical imbalance causing my stones and prevent future ones?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: How much water do I need to drink every day to ensure my urine volume is consistently above 2.5 liters?

red_flags: Fever and shaking chills accompanying flank pain (infected obstructed kidney / urosepsis emergency requiring urgent decompression)

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Fluid intake to maintain > 2.5 liters urine output/day (urine color clear/pale); dietary sodium restriction (<2,300 mg/day; high sodium increases urinary calcium excretion); limit animal protein; do not restrict dietary calcium.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: 24-hour urine metabolic profile (volume, calcium, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, sodium, pH) 6-8 weeks post-resolution; repeat annually; stone composition analysis.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Stones > 10 mm, persistent pain, severe hydronephrosis, or fever with infected obstructed stone require urgent urologic intervention.

title: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (N Engl J Med)
snippet: ADPKD is the most common hereditary kidney disorder (1:400 to 1:1,000 live births), caused by germline mutations in PKD1 (80%) or PKD2 (15%), resulting in progressive bilateral fluid-filled renal cyst expansion, destruction of renal parenchyma, and end-stage kidney disease in >50% by age 60. Hypertension develops early and requires aggressive control (target BP < 110/75 mmHg in young patients with preserved eGFR; HALT-PKD trial). Total kidney volume (TKV) measured by MRI and classified via the Mayo Imaging Classification (Classes 1C-1E) stratifies rapid progressors. The selective vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist tolvaptan (TEMPO 3:4 and REPRISE trials) significantly slowed TKV growth and reduced the rate of eGFR decline by ~1.0-1.2 mL/min/1.73m² per year, and is indicated for patients with rapidly progressive disease. Guideline Protocol: High fluid intake (≥ 3 liters/day water to suppress endogenous vasopressin production); strict dietary sodium restriction (<2,000 mg/day); avoid contact sports risking cyst rupture. Thresholds: Mayo Imaging Classification 1C, 1D, or 1E (predicted eGFR loss > 3 mL/min/1.73m²/year) qualifies for tolvaptan therapy.
key_takeaway: ADPKD is the most common hereditary kidney disorder (1:400 to 1:1,000 live births), caused by germline mutations in PKD1 (80%) or PKD2 (15%), resulting in progressive bilateral fluid-filled renal cyst expansion, destruct...
patient_plain_language: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is a genetic condition where thousands of fluid-filled sacs (cysts) slowly grow and multiply inside your kidneys over decades. As the cysts enlarge, your kidneys grow to several times their normal size, crowding out healthy kidney tissue and causing high blood pressure.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What is my total kidney volume (TKV) and Mayo imaging classification on MRI?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Do I have a family history of brain aneurysms that warrants a screening MRA scan of my brain arteries?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Am I a candidate for tolvaptan (Jynarque) to slow the growth of kidney cysts and preserve my kidney function?

red_flags: Sudden severe flank pain with gross dark hematuria and fever (infected renal cyst), or sudden explosive 'worst headache of life' (ruptured intracranial aneurysm)

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: High fluid intake (≥ 3 liters/day water to suppress endogenous vasopressin production); strict dietary sodium restriction (<2,000 mg/day); avoid contact sports risking cyst rupture.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: eGFR and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio every 3-6 months; monthly liver function tests for the first 18 months on tolvaptan (due to idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity risk); baseline brain MRA screening for intracranial berry aneurysms in patients with high-risk family history.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Mayo Imaging Classification 1C, 1D, or 1E (predicted eGFR loss > 3 mL/min/1.73m²/year) qualifies for tolvaptan therapy.

title: Nephrotic Syndrome: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Kidney Int)
snippet: Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by heavy proteinuria (> 3.5 g/24 hr or spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio [uPCR] > 3.0 g/g), hypoalbuminemia (serum albumin < 3.0 g/dL), generalized peripheral and periorbital edema, and hyperlipidemia. Major primary adult etiologies include membranous nephropathy (anti-PLA2R positive in 70-80%), focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), and minimal change disease (MCD). Renal biopsy provides definitive histological confirmation. MCD responds dramatically to high-dose oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day, achieving remission in >80%). Membranous nephropathy risk stratification dictates therapy: rituximab (CD20-depleting B-cell therapy, MENTOR trial; NEJM 2019) is superior to cyclosporine for inducing sustained complete/partial remission with favorable safety profile. Severe hypoalbuminemia (<2.0-2.5 g/dL) carries high venous thromboembolism risk (DVT/PE/renal vein thrombosis), requiring prophylactic anticoagulation. Guideline Protocol: Dietary sodium restriction (<2,000 mg/day) to control refractory edema; moderate dietary protein intake (0.8 g/kg/day; high-protein diets increase glomerular hyperfiltration and worsen proteinuria); pneumococcal and influenza vaccinations. Thresholds: Proteinuria > 3.5 g/24 hr with albumin < 3.0 g/dL establishes nephrotic state; serum albumin < 2.0-2.5 g/dL in membranous nephropathy triggers prophylactic anticoagulation evaluation.
key_takeaway: Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by heavy proteinuria (> 3.5 g/24 hr or spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio [uPCR] > 3.0 g/g), hypoalbuminemia (serum albumin < 3.0 g/dL), generalized peripheral and periorbital edem...
patient_plain_language: Nephrotic syndrome is a kidney condition where the tiny filtering units in your kidneys (glomeruli) become damaged and leaky. Instead of keeping essential proteins in your blood, they spill large amounts of protein into your urine, causing your body to retain fluid and swell, particularly around your eyes, ankles, and legs.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What is my current 24-hour urine protein or urine protein-to-creatinine ratio and blood albumin level?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Because my blood albumin is very low, do I need blood thinners to protect me from dangerous blood clots in my legs or lungs?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Will I need a kidney biopsy or an anti-PLA2R antibody blood test to determine the exact type of kidney disease causing my protein leak?

red_flags: Sudden unilateral calf swelling and tenderness (DVT), sudden shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain (pulmonary embolism), or flank pain with gross hematuria (renal vein thrombosis)

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Dietary sodium restriction (<2,000 mg/day) to control refractory edema; moderate dietary protein intake (0.8 g/kg/day; high-protein diets increase glomerular hyperfiltration and worsen proteinuria); pneumococcal and influenza vaccinations.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (uPCR), serum albumin, creatinine, eGFR, and lipid panel every 1-3 months; anti-PLA2R antibody titers every 3 months for membranous nephropathy.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Proteinuria > 3.5 g/24 hr with albumin < 3.0 g/dL establishes nephrotic state; serum albumin < 2.0-2.5 g/dL in membranous nephropathy triggers prophylactic anticoagulation evaluation.

title: IgA Nephropathy (Berger's Disease): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (The Lancet)
snippet: IgA nephropathy is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide, caused by galactose-deficient IgA1 deposition in the glomerular mesangium, inducing mesangial proliferation, matrix expansion, and glomerulosclerosis. Classic presentation is episodic synpharyngitic gross hematuria (coca-cola colored urine 24-48 hours after an upper respiratory infection) or asymptomatic microscopic hematuria with persistent proteinuria. Definitive diagnosis requires kidney biopsy scored via the Oxford Classification (MEST-C score). Foundational supportive therapy for all patients with proteinuria > 0.5 g/day mandates maximally tolerated ACE inhibitors or ARBs, combined with SGLT2 inhibitors (DAPA-CKD trial; 71% reduction in kidney failure composite). For persistent proteinuria ≥ 0.75-1.0 g/day despite supportive therapy, targeted-release enteric budesonide (Nefecon 16 mg daily) provides significant eGFR preservation and proteinuria reduction. Guideline Protocol: Strict dietary sodium restriction (<2,000 mg/day); smoking cessation; aggressive systolic blood pressure target < 120 mmHg (KDIGO 2021). Thresholds: Persistent proteinuria ≥ 0.75-1.0 g/day despite ≥ 3 months of optimized supportive therapy indicates high risk of progressive kidney failure, qualifying for immunosuppressive or targeted therapies.
key_takeaway: IgA nephropathy is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide, caused by galactose-deficient IgA1 deposition in the glomerular mesangium, inducing mesangial proliferation, matrix expansion, and glomeruloscleros...
patient_plain_language: IgA nephropathy is an immune disorder where abnormal antibodies called IgA get trapped in the microscopic filters of your kidneys. This triggers chronic inflammation and scarring, often noticed when your urine turns brown or tea-colored during or right after a throat infection.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What is my current urine protein-to-creatinine ratio and eGFR kidney filtration rate?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Am I on the maximum safe dose of a blood pressure protector (ACE inhibitor or ARB) plus an SGLT2 inhibitor to shield my kidneys?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: If my urine protein remains over 1 gram per day, would I benefit from a targeted gut steroid capsule (budesonide/Tarpeyo)?

red_flags: Rapid deterioration of kidney function (creatinine doubling over weeks), rapid drop in urine output, or severe uncontrolled high blood pressure

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Strict dietary sodium restriction (<2,000 mg/day); smoking cessation; aggressive systolic blood pressure target < 120 mmHg (KDIGO 2021).
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (uPCR), microscopic urinalysis, serum creatinine, and eGFR every 3-6 months; annual cardiovascular risk assessment.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Persistent proteinuria ≥ 0.75-1.0 g/day despite ≥ 3 months of optimized supportive therapy indicates high risk of progressive kidney failure, qualifying for immunosuppressive or targeted therapies.

title: Overactive Bladder (OAB): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (J Urol)
snippet: Overactive bladder is a clinical syndrome characterized by urinary urgency (compelling desire to pass urine which is difficult to defer), usually accompanied by frequency (≥8 micturitions/24 hr) and nocturia (≥2 voids/night), with or without urgency urinary incontinence (OAB wet vs OAB dry), in the absence of UTI or other pathology. Initial management focuses on behavioral therapies (bladder training, timed voiding, fluid management, pelvic floor muscle therapy). Second-line therapy consists of oral antimuscarinics (solifenacin, oxybutynin; cautioned in elderly due to anticholinergic cognitive burden and dementia risk) or beta-3 adrenergic agonists (mirabegron 25-50 mg daily, vibegron 75 mg daily; relax detrusor without anticholinergic side effects). Third-line modalities for refractory cases include intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA (100 units), sacral neuromodulation (InterStim), or percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS). Guideline Protocol: Pelvic floor muscle training (Kegel exercises) with biofeedback; bladder retraining with progressive voiding intervals; fluid intake moderation (avoid excess fluids after 6 PM); eliminate dietary bladder irritants (caffeine, artificial sweeteners, carbonated beverages, spicy foods). Thresholds: Post-void residual (PVR) > 150-200 mL warrants caution when prescribing antimuscarinics to prevent acute urinary retention.

patient_plain_language: Overactive bladder is a condition where your bladder muscles squeeze and spasm before your bladder is actually full, creating a sudden, urgent need to run to the bathroom that can be hard to hold back. It often causes frequent daytime trips and waking up multiple times each night.

title: Stress Urinary Incontinence: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Obstet Gynecol)
snippet: Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) is involuntary leakage of urine upon physical exertion, sneezing, coughing, laughing, or lifting, occurring when intra-abdominal pressure exceeds urethral closure pressure in the setting of pelvic floor muscle laxity or intrinsic sphincter deficiency. First-line therapy is supervised pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT / Kegels; Cochrane systematic review confirms PFMT yields >5-fold higher cure/improvement rates vs control, RR 5.34). Vaginal pessaries or urethral inserts provide non-surgical mechanical urethral support. For patients desiring definitive surgical correction, the synthetic midurethral sling (retropubic or transobturator tape) remains the gold standard procedure with >85-90% subjective cure rates at 5 years. Burch colposuspension or autologous fascial slings serve as non-mesh alternatives. Guideline Protocol: Supervised pelvic floor physical therapy (at least 3 sets of 10-15 contractions held 6-8 seconds daily for at least 12 weeks); weight reduction in overweight/obese women (5-10% weight loss reduces incontinence episodes by 50%); treatment of chronic constipation. Thresholds: Positive cough stress test during physical exam with bladder comfortably full confirms stress incontinence.

patient_plain_language: Stress urinary incontinence happens when the muscles and tissues supporting your bladder and urethra weaken. Sudden physical pressure on your abdomen—such as coughing, sneezing, laughing, jumping, or exercising—causes accidental urine leakage.

title: Interstitial Cystitis (Bladder Pain Syndrome): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (J Urol)
snippet: Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) is defined as an unpleasant sensation (pain, pressure, discomfort) perceived to be related to the urinary bladder, associated with lower urinary tract symptoms of more than 6 weeks duration, in the absence of infection or other identifiable causes. Pain typically intensifies as the bladder fills and temporarily relieves following voiding. Cystoscopy may reveal glomerulations (petechial hemorrhages on hydrodistention) or Hunner lesions (circumscribed reddish mucosal lesions with radiating vessels; present in 10-15%). Stepwise management: Step 1 involves patient education, fluid regulation, and elimination of dietary triggers (caffeine, citrus, alcohol, artificial sweeteners). Step 2 incorporates specialized pelvic floor physical therapy (targeting muscle spasms and trigger points; strictly avoiding strengthening Kegels) and oral medications (amitriptyline 25-75 mg, cimetidine, hydroxyzine, or pentosan polysulfate sodium). Hunner lesions respond to endoscopic fulguration. Guideline Protocol: Dietary modification using an elimination diet to identify bladder irritants (coffee, tea, tomatoes, spicy foods, acidic fruit); gentle myofascial physical therapy (avoid Kegel exercises which exacerbate hypertonic pelvic floor spasms); application of heat/cold to pelvic area. Thresholds: Cystoscopic identification of Hunner lesions dictates direct endoscopic electrocautery or triamcinolone injection.

patient_plain_language: Interstitial cystitis, or bladder pain syndrome, is a chronic inflammatory condition where you feel aching, pressure, or burning pain in your bladder that worsens as your bladder fills with urine. People often feel the urge to urinate dozens of times a day to relieve the aching pressure.

disease: Chronic Prostatitis / Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome (CP/CPPS)
title: Chronic Prostatitis / Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome (CP/CPPS): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Eur Urol)
keywords: chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome (cp/cpps)
snippet: NIH Category III chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CP/CPPS) is characterized by chronic pelvic, perineal, scrotal, penile, or suprapubic pain persisting for at least 3 months within the previous 6 months, in the absence of uropathogenic bacteria on standard cultures. It is frequently accompanied by painful ejaculation, voiding dysfunction, and severe negative cognitive and emotional impact. Management utilizes the multi-modal UPOINT clinical phenotyping system (Urinary, Psychosocial, Organ-specific, Infection, Neurological/systemic, Tenderness of muscles), directing tailored therapy rather than empiric repeated antibiotic courses: alpha-blockers (tamsulosin 0.4 mg) for urinary obstruction; anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDs); neuromodulating medications (pregabalin, duloxetine); specialized myofascial pelvic floor physical therapy for pelvic floor hypertonicity; and cognitive-behavioral therapy. Guideline Protocol: Myofascial pelvic floor trigger-point release physical therapy; avoid prolonged sitting and bicycling (use split saddles); warm sitz baths; stress reduction and mindfulness-based pelvic relaxation. Thresholds: Repeated negative urine cultures establish non-bacterial CP/CPPS (NIH Category III), mandating cessation of repetitive antibiotic therapies.

patient_plain_language: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome in men causes ongoing aching pain, pressure, or discomfort in the pelvic floor, groin, or testicles, often made worse by sitting or after ejaculation. It is usually not an active bacterial infection, but rather a combination of tense pelvic floor muscles and irritated pelvic nerves.

title: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) with LUTS: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (J Urol)
snippet: Benign prostatic hyperplasia involves non-malignant adenomatous stromal and epithelial proliferation of the prostate transition zone, causing bladder outlet obstruction and lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS: weak stream, hesitancy, intermittency, straining, post-void dribbling, frequency, nocturia). Symptom severity is quantified via the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS). Medical therapy: Alpha-1 adrenergic antagonists (tamsulosin 0.4 mg, alfuzosin 10 mg) rapidly relax prostate smooth muscle, improving IPSS by 4-6 points within 2-4 days. 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (5-ARIs: finasteride 5 mg, dutasteride 0.5 mg) shrink prostate volume by ~20-25% and reduce the long-term risk of acute urinary retention and BPH-related surgery (MTOPS and CombAT trials), indicated when prostate volume > 30 cc or PSA > 1.5 ng/mL. Tadalafil 5 mg daily is approved for concomitant erectile dysfunction. Guideline Protocol: Limit fluid intake in the 2 hours before bed; reduce caffeine and alcohol consumption; avoid OTC decongestants (pseudoephedrine) and first-generation antihistamines which can trigger urinary retention; practice double-voiding. Thresholds: PVR > 250-300 mL, recurrent urinary tract infections, bladder calculi, or refractory urinary retention warrants surgical intervention (TURP, HoLEP, water vapor thermal therapy/Rezum, or prostatic urethral lift/UroLift).

patient_plain_language: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is an age-related, non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate gland in men. Because the prostate wraps around the tube that carries urine from your bladder, its growth squeezes the pipe, causing a weak or stopped stream, nighttime bathroom trips, and straining.

title: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Kidney Int Suppl)
snippet: KDIGO diagnostic criteria define AKI by any of: increase in serum creatinine by ≥ 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours; increase in serum creatinine to ≥ 1.5 times baseline within 7 days; or urine volume < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours. Etiologies are categorized into prerenal (hypovolemia, heart failure, sepsis, NSAIDs/ACEi causing decreased renal perfusion; fractional excretion of sodium FeNa < 1%, BUN:creatinine ratio > 20:1); intrinsic renal (acute tubular necrosis [ATN] from ischemia or nephrotoxins, acute interstitial nephritis [AIN], glomerulonephritis; FeNa > 2%, muddy brown granular casts); and postrenal obstructive (nephrolithiasis, BPH, neurogenic bladder; hydronephrosis on renal ultrasound). Core management mandates prompt hemodynamic resuscitation with balanced crystalloids (SMART trial; NEJM 2018), discontinuation of all nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, IV iodinated contrast), relief of obstruction, and dose-adjustment of all renally cleared drugs. Guideline Protocol: Strict fluid balance tracking (intake vs output); avoidance of all nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, OTC herbal supplements, contrast dye); protocolized electrolyte dietary restrictions (low potassium, low phosphorus) during oliguric phase. Thresholds: Absolute indications for urgent renal replacement therapy (dialysis): refractory hyperkalemia (K+ > 6.5 mEq/L with ECG changes), refractory metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.15), refractory pulmonary edema, or uremic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy).

patient_plain_language: Acute kidney injury is a sudden, sharp decline in kidney function that occurs over hours or days. When the kidneys suddenly struggle to filter the blood—often due to severe dehydration, an infection, or certain medications—waste products and excess fluids rapidly build up in the body.

title: Ankylosing Spondylitis (Axial Spondyloarthritis): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Ann Rheum Dis)
snippet: Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) is a chronic inflammatory rheumatic disease predominantly affecting the axial skeleton and sacroiliac joints, strongly associated with HLA-B27 (>85%). It presents as chronic inflammatory back pain (onset <45 years, insidious onset, improvement with exercise but not with rest, morning stiffness >30 minutes, waking during the second half of the night). Sacroiliitis on MRI (active bone marrow edema) or pelvic radiographs (modified New York criteria) confirms diagnosis. First-line pharmacotherapy is continuous treatment with full-dose NSAIDs (naproxen, celecoxib). For patients with persistently high disease activity (ASDAS ≥ 2.1) despite ≥ 2 NSAIDs, biological DMARDs targeting TNF (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab) or IL-17A (secukinumab, ixekizumab), or JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib, tofacitinib) provide significant symptom relief, suppress spinal inflammation, and improve function. Guideline Protocol: Lifelong daily structured spinal extension physiotherapy and home exercise program; pulmonary deep-breathing exercises to maintain chest wall expansion; strict smoking cessation (smoking accelerates syndesmophyte formation and spinal fusion). Thresholds: ASDAS ≥ 2.1 indicates high disease activity, qualifying for biologic therapy (TNF inhibitor or IL-17 inhibitor).

patient_plain_language: Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic autoimmune form of arthritis that targets your spine and pelvic joints. Unlike ordinary mechanical back pain, the stiffness and ache feel worse after resting or sleeping and actually improve when you get up and move around. Over years, it can cause the spinal bones to fuse together.

title: Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Nat Rev Rheumatol)
snippet: Psoriatic arthritis affects ~20-30% of patients with cutaneous psoriasis, presenting across six clinical domains: peripheral arthritis (often asymmetric, involving DIP joints), enthesitis (inflammation at tendon insertions, e.g., Achilles, plantar fascia), dactylitis ('sausage digits'), axial disease, skin psoriasis, and nail dystrophy (pitting, onycholysis; strongly correlates with DIP arthritis). CASPAR criteria require inflammatory articular disease plus ≥ 3 points from personal/family psoriasis, nail dystrophy, negative RF, current/past dactylitis, and juxta-articular new bone formation. Conventional synthetic DMARDs (methotrexate 15-25 mg/week) treat peripheral arthritis. GRAPPA guidelines recommend targeted biologics—TNF inhibitors, IL-17A inhibitors (secukinumab), IL-23 inhibitors (guselkumab, risankizumab), or JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib)—to inhibit structural joint damage and clear skin lesions simultaneously. Guideline Protocol: Low-impact joint conditioning (swimming, cycling); physical therapy and orthotics for foot enthesitis; weight management (obesity impairs biologic response); smoking cessation. Thresholds: Erosive changes on hand/foot radiographs or active dactylitis/enthesitis warrants early escalation to targeted biologic/targeted synthetic DMARDs.

Beyond red, scaly skin patches, it can cause swollen fingers or toes that look like little sausages, painful heels where tendons attach to bone, and stiff, aching joints.
