title: Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Ann Rheum Dis)
snippet: Systemic sclerosis is a complex autoimmune disease characterized by microvascular obliteration, immune dysregulation, and progressive widespread fibrosis of skin and internal organs. Divided into limited cutaneous (lcSSc: CREST syndrome; anti-centromere positive in 60-80%) and diffuse cutaneous (dcSSc: anti-Scl-70/topoisomerase I or anti-RNA polymerase III positive; rapid proximal skin thickening and early visceral organ failure). Scleroderma renal crisis (SRC) presents with acute malignant hypertension and oliguric renal failure, strongly linked to anti-RNA polymerase III and high-dose corticosteroid use (>15 mg/day prednisone is contraindicated); immediate ACE inhibitor therapy (captopril) is lifesaving. Interstitial lung disease (SSc-ILD) is the leading cause of death; mycophenolate mofetil (SLS II trial; Lancet Respir Med 2016) and nintedanib (SENSCIS trial; NEJM 2019) preserve FVC and slow lung fibrosis. Guideline Protocol: Strict avoidance of cold exposure; keep core body and extremities warm (heated gloves/socks); elevate head of bed 6 inches to manage refractory GERD; skin moisturization and stretching. Thresholds: Drop in FVC ≥ 10% or FVC 5-9% with DLCO drop ≥ 15% indicates progressive SSc-ILD requiring initiation or intensification of antifibrotic/immunosuppressive therapy.

patient_plain_language: Systemic sclerosis, or scleroderma, is a rare autoimmune disorder where the body produces too much collagen protein, causing the skin to become tight, thick, and firm. In addition to fingers turning white and painful in the cold (Raynaud's), it can cause acid reflux and stiffen lung tissues.

solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Drop in FVC ≥ 10% or FVC 5-9% with DLCO drop ≥ 15% indicates progressive SSc-ILD requiring initiation or intensification of antifibrotic/immunosuppressive therapy.

title: Sjögren's Syndrome: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Ann Rheum Dis)
snippet: Sjögren's syndrome is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands, predominantly the lacrimal and salivary glands, resulting in severe keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes) and xerostomia (dry mouth). ACR-EULAR criteria require a score ≥ 4 based on: labial salivary gland biopsy with focal lymphocytic sialadenitis (focus score ≥ 1/4 mm²), positive anti-SSA/Ro antibodies, ocular staining score ≥ 5, Schirmer's test ≤ 5 mm/5 min, and unstimulated whole saliva flow rate ≤ 0.1 mL/min. Symptomatic secretagogue therapy (pilocarpine 5 mg QID or cevimeline 30 mg TID) stimulates M3 muscarinic receptors to increase saliva and tear secretion. Topical ophthalmic cyclosporine (0.05%) or lifitegrast (5%) treats ocular surface inflammation. Hydroxychloroquine (200-400 mg/day) reduces inflammatory arthralgias and systemic fatigue. Patients have a ~15-20 fold increased lifetime risk of non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma (predominantly MALT lymphoma). Guideline Protocol: Frequent water sipping; sugar-free xylitol gum/lozenges; preservative-free artificial tears; home cool mist humidifiers; meticulous oral hygiene (flossing, fluoridated prescription toothpaste, biannual dental exams). Thresholds: Unstimulated salivary flow ≤ 0.1 mL/min or Schirmer's ≤ 5 mm/5 min objective cutoffs; development of monoclonal paraprotein, cryoglobulins, or low C4 warrants lymphoma workup.

patient_plain_language: Sjögren's syndrome is an autoimmune condition where your immune system attacks your body's moisture-producing glands. The primary symptoms are severely dry, gritty eyes and a dry mouth that makes chewing dry crackers, speaking for long periods, or swallowing difficult.

title: Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Ann Rheum Dis)
snippet: Polymyalgia rheumatica is an inflammatory disorder occurring almost exclusively in individuals > 50 years (mean age 73), presenting with sudden-onset, severe bilateral aching and morning stiffness (>45 minutes) in the shoulder girdle, pelvic girdle, and neck, accompanied by elevated inflammatory markers (ESR > 40 mm/hr, CRP > 10 mg/L). Musculoskeletal ultrasound characteristically demonstrates bilateral subacromial/subdeltoid bursitis, trochanteric bursitis, or biceps tenosynovitis. Hallmark diagnostic feature is a rapid, dramatic clinical response (>70% improvement within 48-72 hours) to moderate-dose oral corticosteroids (prednisone 12.5-25 mg/day). Tapering is performed slowly over 12-24 months. For frequent relapsers or high steroid-toxicity risk, the IL-6 receptor antagonist sarilumab is FDA-approved (SAPHYR trial; NEJM 2023: 28% sustained remission on sarilumab vs 10% on placebo, p=0.02). Approximately 15-20% of PMR patients develop concurrent Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA). Guideline Protocol: Bone-protection measures: calcium (1,000-1,200 mg/day), vitamin D (800-1,000 IU/day), baseline DEXA scan, and bisphosphonate therapy if high fracture risk; gentle progressive range-of-motion physical therapy. Thresholds: Rapid symptomatic relief (>70% improvement in pain/stiffness) within 72 hours of starting 15 mg prednisone strongly supports PMR diagnosis.
key_takeaway: Polymyalgia rheumatica is an inflammatory disorder occurring almost exclusively in individuals > 50 years (mean age 73), presenting with sudden-onset, severe bilateral aching and morning stiffness (>45 minutes) in the sh...
patient_plain_language: Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is an inflammatory condition affecting older adults that causes severe stiffness and aching across both shoulders, hips, thighs, and neck, particularly upon waking in the morning. Getting out of bed or lifting your arms to put on a jacket can feel almost impossible, but it responds quickly to low-dose steroid medication.

doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Are my bones being protected against osteoporosis with calcium, vitamin D, and a bone density scan while taking prednisone?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: What is our gradual monthly tapering schedule for prednisone, and what symptoms indicate that we are tapering too quickly?

solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: ESR and CRP at baseline, 1 month, and before each planned prednisone dose reduction; vigilant screening for symptoms of giant cell arteritis (headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, vision loss) at every visit.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Rapid symptomatic relief (>70% improvement in pain/stiffness) within 72 hours of starting 15 mg prednisone strongly supports PMR diagnosis.

title: Dermatomyositis / Polymyositis: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (N Engl J Med)
snippet: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies are characterized by symmetric, progressive proximal skeletal muscle weakness (difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a chair, lifting objects overhead) and markedly elevated serum creatine kinase (CK, often 5-50x ULN). Dermatomyositis features pathognomonic cutaneous signs: heliotrope rash (violaceous periorbital erythema and edema) and Gottron's papules (scaly violaceous plaques over MCP and PIP joints), plus shawl sign, V-sign, and mechanic's hands (anti-synthetase syndrome). Myositis-specific antibodies (anti-Mi-2, anti-Jo-1, anti-TIF1-gamma, anti-NXP2, anti-MDA5) define clinical phenotypes and cancer risk. Anti-TIF1-gamma and anti-NXP2 carry high risk of age-associated underlying malignancy (ovarian, breast, lung, GI), mandating comprehensive cancer screening. First-line therapy is high-dose oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day) plus steroid-sparing immunosuppressants (methotrexate, azathioprine). The landmark ProDERM phase 3 trial established IVIG (2 g/kg monthly) as safe and significantly superior to placebo (79% response vs 44%, p<0.001). Guideline Protocol: Strict sun protection (broad-spectrum SPF 50+, protective clothing; UV light directly exacerbates cutaneous dermatomyositis); physical therapy with gentle active-assisted range of motion during acute phase, progressing to resistance training during remission; speech therapy for dysphagia. Thresholds: Anti-TIF1-gamma or anti-NXP2 positive antibodies require intensive age-appropriate and CT body cancer screening.
key_takeaway: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies are characterized by symmetric, progressive proximal skeletal muscle weakness (difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a chair, lifting objects overhead) and markedly elevated serum cre...
patient_plain_language: Dermatomyositis is an autoimmune condition where your immune system causes inflammation in both your muscles and skin. It causes progressive muscle weakness in your thighs and shoulders—making it hard to stand up from a low chair or brush your hair—along with distinct purple-red rashes over your eyelids and knuckles.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What is my current blood creatine kinase (CK) muscle enzyme level, and what did my myositis autoantibody panel reveal?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Has a comprehensive screening for underlying cancer been scheduled, as recommended for adults diagnosed with dermatomyositis?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Did my lung CT scan and breathing tests show any signs of inflammatory lung disease?

red_flags: Severe choking and difficulty swallowing (pharyngeal muscle paralysis / high aspiration risk), or rapid shortness of breath over days to weeks (anti-MDA5 rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease)

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Strict sun protection (broad-spectrum SPF 50+, protective clothing; UV light directly exacerbates cutaneous dermatomyositis); physical therapy with gentle active-assisted range of motion during acute phase, progressing to resistance training during remission; speech therapy for dysphagia.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Serum CK, aldolase, and Manual Muscle Testing (MMT-8) every 4-8 weeks; pulmonary function tests (FVC, DLCO) and high-resolution chest CT to detect rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (especially if anti-MDA5 positive); comprehensive age-appropriate cancer screening.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Anti-TIF1-gamma or anti-NXP2 positive antibodies require intensive age-appropriate and CT body cancer screening.

title: Rotator Cuff Tendinopathy and Tears: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (J Am Acad Orthop Surg)
snippet: Rotator cuff disorders encompass tendinopathy, partial-thickness tears, and full-thickness tears primarily involving the supraspinatus tendon. Patients present with anterolateral shoulder pain exacerbated by overhead activity, pain radiating to the deltoid insertion, and nocturnal pain when lying on the affected side. Physical exam reveals painful arc (60-120 degrees), positive Hawkins-Kennedy/Neer impingement signs, and weakness on empty-can (Jobe's) or external rotation tests. MRI of the shoulder is the imaging gold standard. Cochrane reviews and randomized clinical trials confirm that structured, supervised physical therapy focusing on rotator cuff strengthening and scapular stabilizing exercises is as effective as surgical acromioplasty or repair for non-traumatic, degenerative rotator cuff tears at 1, 2, and 5-year follow-up. Acute full-thickness traumatic tears in young, active patients benefit from prompt surgical repair within 3 months to prevent muscle retraction and fatty infiltration. Guideline Protocol: Structured active rotator cuff and periscapular strengthening physical therapy (at least 12 weeks); avoid repetitive overhead lifting and heavy carrying during acute inflammatory phase; sleep positioning with pillow support under arm. Thresholds: Failure of conservative therapy after 3-6 months in symptomatic full-thickness tears or acute traumatic full-thickness tears warrants orthopedic surgical evaluation.

patient_plain_language: The rotator cuff is a team of four muscles and tendons that keep your shoulder ball centered in its socket. Wear-and-tear or injury can fray or tear these tendons, causing aching pain on the outside of your shoulder, especially when reaching up overhead or trying to sleep on that side.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Did my shoulder MRI show tendinitis, a partial-thickness tear, or a complete full-thickness tendon tear?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Can I try a dedicated 12-week physical therapy strengthening program before considering surgery, based on AAOS guidelines?

solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Failure of conservative therapy after 3-6 months in symptomatic full-thickness tears or acute traumatic full-thickness tears warrants orthopedic surgical evaluation.

title: Plantar Fasciitis: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (J Orthop Sports Phys Ther)
snippet: Plantar fasciitis is a degenerative non-inflammatory fasciosis of the thick plantar aponeurosis origin at the medial calcaneal tuberosity. Pathognomonic clinical presentation is sharp, stabbing heel pain with the first steps in the morning upon getting out of bed, or after prolonged periods of sitting (post-static dyskinesia), which temporarily eases after walking a few minutes, but worsens by the end of the day. Risk factors include obesity (BMI > 30), limited ankle dorsiflexion (<0 degrees), pes planus or pes cavus, and prolonged occupational weight-bearing. Evidence-based first-line conservative management resolves >90% of cases within 6-12 months: plantar fascia-specific stretching exercises, gastrocnemius/soleus calf stretching, prefabricated or custom arch orthoses (NNT=5), night splints maintaining neutral dorsiflexion, and cushioned supportive footwear. Corticosteroid injections provide short-term relief (<4-6 weeks) but carry risks of plantar fascia rupture and calcaneal fat pad atrophy. Guideline Protocol: Plantar fascia-specific stretching (pulling toes back toward shin for 30 seconds, 3 times before taking first morning step); calf muscle eccentric stretching; wear supportive shoes with arch support at all times (never walk barefoot, even indoors); night splints; ice bottle rolling. Thresholds: Symptoms persisting > 6 months despite compliant conservative therapy classify as chronic recalcitrant plantar fasciitis, qualifying for extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT).

patient_plain_language: Plantar fasciitis is an irritation and thickening of the strong, shock-absorbing band of tissue that supports the arch of your foot. It causes sharp, stabbing heel pain during your very first morning steps out of bed, which feels like stepping on a nail before it gradually loosens up.

doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Why should I try night splints, custom orthotics, and stretching before considering cortisone shots that could weaken the heel fat pad?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: If morning heel pain persists after 6 months of stretching, would non-invasive extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) be appropriate?

solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Clinical reassessment of morning pain visual analogue scale (VAS) and Foot Function Index at 6 and 12 weeks of conservative stretching; imaging only if symptoms persist beyond 3 months.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Symptoms persisting > 6 months despite compliant conservative therapy classify as chronic recalcitrant plantar fasciitis, qualifying for extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT).

title: Adhesive Capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (J Orthop Sports Phys Ther)
snippet: Adhesive capsulitis is characterized by progressive, painful loss of both active and passive glenohumeral range of motion in all planes, predominantly external rotation (>50% reduction or <30 degrees) and abduction, caused by capsular contracture and synovial inflammation. Strongly associated with diabetes mellitus (prevalence up to 20%), thyroid disorders, and periods of prolonged shoulder immobilization. Follows a three-phase continuum: Freezing (painful stage, 2-9 months), Frozen (stiff stage, 4-12 months), and Thawing (recovery stage, 12-42 months). Cochrane systematic reviews and randomized trials demonstrate that an early intra-articular glenohumeral corticosteroid injection (e.g., triamcinolone 40 mg with ultrasound guidance) combined with gentle, pain-free stretching physical therapy significantly accelerates pain relief and functional motion recovery compared to physical therapy alone (standardized mean difference -0.65). Aggressive forceful manipulation is contraindicated in the inflammatory freezing stage. Guideline Protocol: Gentle, pain-free range-of-motion stretching exercises (pendulum exercises, pulley stretches, finger-ladder climbing); strict avoidance of aggressive, forceful stretching that exacerbates capsular synovitis; heat application prior to exercises. Thresholds: Passive external rotation deficit > 50% compared to the unaffected contralateral side confirms adhesive capsulitis.
key_takeaway: Adhesive capsulitis is characterized by progressive, painful loss of both active and passive glenohumeral range of motion in all planes, predominantly external rotation (>50% reduction or <30 degrees) and abduction, caus...
patient_plain_language: Adhesive capsulitis, commonly called 'frozen shoulder', happens when the strong capsule of connective tissue surrounding your shoulder joint becomes inflamed, thickens, and tightens up. The joint loses its lubrication and shrinks, making it difficult to reach your arm behind your back or overhead.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What is my measured passive external rotation angle compared to my good shoulder?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Would an ultrasound-guided cortisone injection into the shoulder capsule help shorten the painful 'freezing' phase?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: How can I ensure my physical therapist uses gentle stretching rather than aggressive forced movements that could inflame the capsule further?

red_flags: Sudden total loss of shoulder movement accompanied by high fever, severe redness, or chills (ruling out septic arthritis of the shoulder)

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Gentle, pain-free range-of-motion stretching exercises (pendulum exercises, pulley stretches, finger-ladder climbing); strict avoidance of aggressive, forceful stretching that exacerbates capsular synovitis; heat application prior to exercises.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Goniometric measurement of passive external rotation, abduction, and internal rotation every 4-6 weeks; optimize glycemic control in diabetic patients (HbA1c).
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Passive external rotation deficit > 50% compared to the unaffected contralateral side confirms adhesive capsulitis.

title: Lumbar Spinal Stenosis: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Spine J)
snippet: Lumbar spinal stenosis involves narrowing of the central spinal canal, lateral recess, or neural foramina by degenerative bone and soft tissue changes (facet arthropathy, ligamentum flavum hypertrophy, disc bulging). Pathognomonic symptom is neurogenic claudication: bilateral or unilateral aching, heaviness, weakness, cramping, or numbness in the buttocks, thighs, or calves brought on by walking or prolonged standing, and characteristically relieved by sitting or lumbar flexion ('shopping cart sign'—forward leaning increases spinal canal cross-sectional area by up to 20%). It is distinguished from vascular claudication, which is provoked by bicycling (flexed posture) and relieved simply by standing still. Lumbosacral spine MRI confirms anatomical stenosis. Conservative management includes flexion-based physical therapy, NSAIDs, and epidural steroid injections. The landmark SPORT trial demonstrated that surgical decompression (laminectomy) produces significant and sustained improvement in pain and function in symptomatic patients failing conservative therapy. Guideline Protocol: Flexion-based core stabilization exercises; stationary bicycling or elliptical training (maintains lumbar spine flexion); use of assistive walking aids or rolling carts to reduce upright lordosis; structured weight loss. Thresholds: Progressive motor weakness (foot drop) or inability to walk > 50-100 meters despite 3-6 months of conservative management indicates surgical decompression.
key_takeaway: Lumbar spinal stenosis involves narrowing of the central spinal canal, lateral recess, or neural foramina by degenerative bone and soft tissue changes (facet arthropathy, ligamentum flavum hypertrophy, disc bulging). Pat...
patient_plain_language: Lumbar spinal stenosis is an age-related narrowing of the bone canal in your lower back that houses your nerves. Standing or walking upright pinches these nerves, causing aching heaviness, cramping, and fatigue in your legs and buttocks that goes away when you sit down or lean forward over a grocery cart.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Does my lower back MRI show central canal stenosis, lateral recess narrowing, or slipped vertebrae (spondylolisthesis)?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: What is the difference between my nerve-related leg symptoms and poor blood circulation in my leg arteries?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: If walking becomes severely limited despite physical therapy and steroid injections, what does a minimally invasive decompression surgery involve?

red_flags: Loss of bowel or bladder control, numbness in the groin/buttocks saddle area, or sudden foot drop (Cauda Equina Syndrome Emergency)

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Flexion-based core stabilization exercises; stationary bicycling or elliptical training (maintains lumbar spine flexion); use of assistive walking aids or rolling carts to reduce upright lordosis; structured weight loss.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Walking distance tolerance assessment and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) every 6-12 weeks; clinical surveillance for cauda equina syndrome.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Progressive motor weakness (foot drop) or inability to walk > 50-100 meters despite 3-6 months of conservative management indicates surgical decompression.

title: Herpes Zoster (Shingles): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (N Engl J Med)
snippet: Herpes zoster results from reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in dorsal root or cranial nerve ganglia. Classic presentation involves prodromal dermatomal pain, burning, or allodynia followed by a unilateral, dermatomal eruption of grouped, painful, erythematous maculopapules that rapidly evolve into clear vesicles. Antiviral therapy (valacyclovir 1,000 mg TID or famciclovir 500 mg TID for 7 days) initiated within 72 hours of rash onset accelerates lesion healing, reduces acute viral shedding, and decreases the severity and duration of postherpetic neuralgia (PHN: pain persisting > 90 days after rash onset). Landmark ZOE-50 and ZOE-70 randomized trials established that the 2-dose recombinant adjuvanted zoster vaccine (Shingrix) provides >97% protective efficacy against shingles and >91% protection against PHN in adults ≥ 50 years, with sustained immunity > 10 years. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (involving CN V1) risks permanent corneal blindness. Guideline Protocol: Keep the rash clean and dry; cover lesions with non-adherent sterile dressings to prevent transmission to varicella-naive or immunocompromised individuals; avoid scratching; cool compresses. Thresholds: Initiation of oral antivirals within 72 hours of vesicle eruption is the critical evidence-based window.

patient_plain_language: Shingles is a painful blistering rash caused by the chickenpox virus waking up after sleeping quietly in your nerve roots for decades. It typically forms a sensitive band of red blisters on just one side of your chest, back, or face, accompanied by burning nerve pain.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Has it been less than 72 hours since the first blisters appeared so I can start antiviral pills immediately?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Does my rash involve my forehead, eye, or the tip of my nose requiring an emergency eye doctor exam?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Once this episode clears, when should I receive the 2-dose Shingrix vaccine to prevent shingles from ever returning?

red_flags: Blisters on the tip of the nose or around the eye (Hutchinson's sign indicating risk of blindness), or neck stiffness and high fever (zoster meningitis)

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Keep the rash clean and dry; cover lesions with non-adherent sterile dressings to prevent transmission to varicella-naive or immunocompromised individuals; avoid scratching; cool compresses.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Clinical review at 7-10 days to ensure crusting; emergent ophthalmology evaluation if vesicles involve the tip or side of the nose (Hutchinson's sign) indicating ophthalmic division (V1) involvement; monitor for postherpetic neuralgia at 30, 60, and 90 days.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Initiation of oral antivirals within 72 hours of vesicle eruption is the critical evidence-based window.

title: Infectious Mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr Virus): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (N Engl J Med)
snippet: Infectious mononucleosis is caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV / HHV-4), transmitted via infected saliva ('kissing disease'), peaking in adolescents and young adults aged 15-24 years. Classic clinical triad: fever, exudative pharyngitis, and prominent symmetric posterior cervical and generalized lymphadenopathy, frequently accompanied by marked fatigue, palatal petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, and transient periorbital edema (Hoagland sign). Laboratory confirmation relies on heterophile antibody testing (Monospot test; sensitivity ~85%, can be false-negative in first week) and peripheral blood smear showing lymphocytosis (>50%) with >10% atypical activated CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes. EBV-specific serologies (viral capsid antigen [VCA] IgM/IgG, EBNA) confirm atypical cases. Administration of aminopenicillins (amoxicillin, ampicillin) induces a characteristic pruritic maculopapular rash in >90% of patients. Splenic rupture occurs in 0.1-0.5% (typically between days 4 and 21 of illness). Guideline Protocol: Strict cessation of all contact sports, strenuous exercise, and heavy lifting for at least 3-4 weeks from symptom onset (or until splenomegaly fully resolves) to prevent traumatic splenic rupture; generous hydration; rest. Thresholds: Absolute restriction from contact sports for minimum 21 days from symptom onset; systemic corticosteroids are indicated only for impending airway obstruction from severe tonsillar hypertrophy.

patient_plain_language: Infectious mononucleosis ('mono') is a viral infection caused by the Epstein-Barr virus, spread through saliva. It causes severe sore throat with swollen neck glands, fever, and extreme fatigue that can last for weeks, along with temporary enlargement of your spleen.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Did my Monospot test and blood smear show atypical lymphocytes?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Why must I avoid taking amoxicillin or penicillin-type antibiotics during this illness to prevent a full-body rash?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: What is the exact date when I can safely return to sports or the gym without risking rupture of my enlarged spleen?

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Strict cessation of all contact sports, strenuous exercise, and heavy lifting for at least 3-4 weeks from symptom onset (or until splenomegaly fully resolves) to prevent traumatic splenic rupture; generous hydration; rest.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Clinical reassessment at 2-3 weeks; abdominal palpation or ultrasound to evaluate spleen size before clearing athletes to return to contact sports.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Absolute restriction from contact sports for minimum 21 days from symptom onset; systemic corticosteroids are indicated only for impending airway obstruction from severe tonsillar hypertrophy.

title: Influenza Infection (Flu): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Clin Infect Dis)
snippet: Influenza is an acute respiratory infection caused by influenza A and B orthomyxoviruses, presenting abruptly with high fever (38-40°C), rigors, myalgias, prominent headache, dry cough, sore throat, and profound prostration. Rapid molecular assays (RT-PCR) are the preferred diagnostic test with high sensitivity/specificity (>95%). Neuraminidase inhibitors (oral oseltamivir 75 mg BID for 5 days) or the cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor baloxavir marboxil (single oral dose) shorten symptom duration by ~1-1.5 days and reduce lower respiratory tract complications, otitis media, and hospitalizations when initiated within 48 hours of symptom onset. In hospitalized, severely ill, or high-risk patients (age ≥65, children <2, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, immunosuppressed, pregnant/postpartum), antiviral therapy is recommended as early as possible, regardless of duration of illness. Guideline Protocol: Bed rest; liberal oral hydration; isolation from vulnerable contacts; annual influenza vaccination (universal recommendation for all persons ≥ 6 months of age). Thresholds: Antiviral therapy should be initiated within 48 hours of illness onset for maximal clinical benefit; high-risk and hospitalized patients should be treated even after 48 hours.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Did my molecular rapid flu swab confirm Influenza A or Influenza B?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Am I within the 48-hour window from my first fever to start an antiviral pill like Tamiflu or Xofluza?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: What warning signs indicate that I might be developing a secondary bacterial pneumonia in my lungs?

red_flags: Severe shortness of breath, blood-tinged sputum, chest pain when breathing, oxygen saturation < 92%, confusion, or a fever that breaks and then suddenly returns worse

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Bed rest; liberal oral hydration; isolation from vulnerable contacts; annual influenza vaccination (universal recommendation for all persons ≥ 6 months of age).
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Clinical reassessment at 48-72 hours post-antiviral therapy; pulse oximetry checks; monitor for secondary bacterial pneumonia (biphasic fever, productive purulent sputum).
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Antiviral therapy should be initiated within 48 hours of illness onset for maximal clinical benefit; high-risk and hospitalized patients should be treated even after 48 hours.

title: Malaria (Plasmodium falciparum / vivax): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (The Lancet)
snippet: Malaria is a mosquito-borne protozoan infection caused by Plasmodium species (P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, P. knowlesi), transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes. Classic presentation features paroxysmal fevers, rigors, diaphoresis, headache, hemolytic anemia, and splenomegaly. Gold standard diagnosis requires microscopic examination of Giemsa-stained thick (sensitivity) and thin (species identification and parasitemia quantification) blood smears, repeated every 12-24 hours if initially negative. Uncomplicated P. falciparum is treated with Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT: oral artemether-lumefantrine [Coartem] or atovaquone-proguanil [Malarone]). Severe malaria (parasitemia > 5%, cerebral malaria, severe anemia, acute kidney injury, ARDS, lactic acidosis) requires immediate IV artesunate (2.4 mg/kg IV at 0, 12, and 24 hours), which reduced mortality by 35% in Asia (SEAQUAMAT) and 22% in Africa (AQUAMAT) compared to IV quinine. P. vivax and P. ovale require primaquine or tafenoquine to eradicate dormant liver hypnozoites, mandatory after G6PD deficiency screening. Guideline Protocol: Bed nets treated with long-lasting insecticidal netting (LLINs); indoor residual spraying; insect repellent with DEET (20-50%); chemoprophylaxis adherence for travelers to endemic areas. Thresholds: Parasitemia > 5%, impaired consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale < 11), jaundice with bilirubin > 3 mg/dL, or serum creatinine > 3 mg/dL classifies as Severe Malaria requiring IV artesunate in ICU.
key_takeaway: Malaria is a mosquito-borne protozoan infection caused by Plasmodium species (P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, P. knowlesi), transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes. Classic presentation features paroxy...
patient_plain_language: Malaria is a serious, mosquito-transmitted blood infection caused by microscopic parasites that multiply inside your liver and then burst out into your red blood cells. It causes intense cycling waves of shaking chills followed by high, burning fevers and drenching sweats.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What is my identified Plasmodium species and exact blood parasitemia percentage on my thin smear?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Was my G6PD enzyme level tested before starting primaquine pills to clear the dormant parasites from my liver?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Does my infection show any features of severe malaria requiring intravenous artesunate in the hospital?

red_flags: Altered mental status, confusion, seizures (cerebral malaria), extreme shortness of breath (ARDS), dark brown/black urine ('blackwater fever'), or inability to sit up

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Bed nets treated with long-lasting insecticidal netting (LLINs); indoor residual spraying; insect repellent with DEET (20-50%); chemoprophylaxis adherence for travelers to endemic areas.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Serial blood smears every 12-24 hours until parasitemia clears; G6PD screening prior to 8-aminoquinoline (primaquine/tafenoquine) administration; delayed hemolytic anemia monitoring at 2-4 weeks post-artesunate.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Parasitemia > 5%, impaired consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale < 11), jaundice with bilirubin > 3 mg/dL, or serum creatinine > 3 mg/dL classifies as Severe Malaria requiring IV artesunate in ICU.

title: Dengue Fever: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (N Engl J Med)
snippet: Dengue is an arboviral infection caused by 4 distinct serotypes (DENV-1 to 4) transmitted by diurnal Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. Classic 'breakbone fever' features sudden high fever (up to 40°C), severe retro-orbital headache, diffuse arthralgias/myalgias, and a transient macular rash. Diagnosis is confirmed by serum NS1 antigen or RT-PCR within days 1-5, or IgM serology after day 5. The disease progresses through 3 phases: Febrile (days 1-3), Critical (days 3-7, coinciding with defervescence when capillary permeability peaks), and Recovery. Severe dengue (dengue hemorrhagic fever / dengue shock syndrome) is characterized by severe plasma leakage (defined by hematocrit increase ≥ 20% alongside acute thrombocytopenia < 100,000 cells/µL, or narrow pulse pressure ≤ 20 mmHg), severe bleeding, or severe organ impairment. Management during the critical phase hinges on meticulous, protocolized isotonic IV fluid titration to match microvascular leakage without precipitating pulmonary edema. NSAIDs and aspirin are strictly contraindicated due to antiplatelet effects and bleeding risk. Guideline Protocol: Strict avoidance of all NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin); exclusively use acetaminophen (max 3 g/day) for fever; liberal oral rehydration with electrolyte solutions; mosquito repellent and bed netting. Thresholds: Warning signs: severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, fluid accumulation (pleural effusion/ascites), liver enlargement > 2 cm, or acute rise in hematocrit with rapid drop in platelets.

patient_plain_language: Dengue fever, known as 'breakbone fever' due to the intense pain in your muscles and joints, is a mosquito-spread tropical virus. The most critical window happens right as the high fever breaks (days 3 to 7), when blood vessels can suddenly become leaky.

title: Community-Acquired MRSA Skin Infection: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (N Engl J Med)
snippet: Community-associated methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (CA-MRSA) typically presents as a painful, erythematous, fluctuant skin abscess, furuncle, carbuncle, or purulent cellulitis, often carrying the Panton-Valentine leukocidin (PVL) cytotoxin gene. Landmark randomized trials establish that incision and drainage (I&D) is the primary and essential definitive therapy for cutaneous abscesses. The landmark DAWN trial proved that adding oral antibiotic therapy (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole [TMP-SMX 1-2 DS tablets BID] or clindamycin [300-450 mg TID] for 7-10 days) significantly increased cure rates (82-83% vs 69% placebo, p<0.001) and reduced recurrence rates in drainable abscesses. Oral doxycycline (100 mg BID) is an alternative. For recurrent CA-MRSA furunculosis, a 5-day decolonization protocol (intranasal mupirocin 2% ointment BID plus chlorhexidine 4% body washes daily) significantly reduces reinfection and household transmission. Guideline Protocol: Do not squeeze or self-drain boils at home; keep draining wounds covered with clean, dry dressings; wash towels and bed linens in hot water; avoid sharing personal items (razors, towels); regular hand washing. Thresholds: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (fever > 38°C, tachycardia > 90 bpm, tachypnea), rapid progression, or immunocompromise mandates systemic antimicrobial therapy.

title: Giardiasis: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Cochrane Database Syst Rev)
snippet: Giardiasis is an intestinal protozoan infection caused by Giardia duodenalis (lamblia/intestinalis), acquired via ingestion of fecally contaminated water (backcountry hikers drinking wilderness stream water, municipal water supplies, swimming pools) or food. Ingested cysts excyst in the duodenum into flagellated trophozoites that attach to the enterocyte brush border with a ventral sucking disk, causing blunting of microvilli and malabsorption. Incubation period is 1-2 weeks, presenting with foul-smelling, watery, greasy stools that float (steatorrhea), sulfurous burping/eructations, abdominal cramping, flatulence, and significant weight loss, characteristically without fever or blood/fecal leukocytes. Diagnosis is established via stool stool antigen enzyme immunoassay (EIA) or stool multiplex PCR (sensitivity >95%). First-line therapy is tinidazole (single oral dose of 2 g; cure rate >90-95%) or nitazoxanide (500 mg BID for 3 days), which have superseded 5-7 day metronidazole due to superior tolerability and single-dose compliance. Guideline Protocol: Boil wilderness water for at least 1 full minute (or 3 minutes at high altitude) or use <1-micron pore size water filters; practice strict hand hygiene after diaper changing; avoid swallowing recreational pool or lake water. Thresholds: Stool antigen EIA or PCR positive for Giardia duodenalis confirms diagnosis and directs anti-protozoal therapy.

It causes foul-smelling, greasy diarrhea that floats, lots of gas, and characteristic 'rotten egg' burps.

title: Streptococcal Pharyngitis (Strep Throat): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Clin Infect Dis)
snippet: Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes, GAS) accounts for 20-30% of acute pharyngitis in children and 5-15% in adults. Clinical features are scored via Modified Centor / McIsaac criteria (tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, fever > 38°C, absence of cough, age-based points). Patients meeting ≥ 2-3 points should undergo Rapid Antigen Detection Testing (RADT) or throat throat molecular NAAT; negative RADT in children/adolescents mandates backup throat culture. Antimicrobial therapy is indicated only for confirmed GAS to prevent acute rheumatic fever, reduce symptom duration by ~1-2 days, and prevent suppurative complications (peritonsillar abscess). Penicillin V (500 mg orally BID/TID for 10 days) or amoxicillin (50 mg/kg once daily, max 1,000 mg for 10 days) remains first-line, as GAS remains 100% susceptible to beta-lactams globally. Cephalosporins, clindamycin, or azithromycin serve as penicillin-allergic options. Guideline Protocol: Replace toothbrush after 24-48 hours of antibiotic therapy; salt-water gargles; warm fluids and honey; return to school/work after 12-24 hours of effective antibiotics and when afebrile. Thresholds: Positive rapid strep antigen test or throat culture mandates full 10-day course of penicillin/amoxicillin to prevent acute rheumatic fever.

title: Lyme Disease (Borrelia burgdorferi): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Clin Infect Dis)
snippet: Lyme disease is a tick-borne spirochetal infection caused by Borrelia burgdorferi sensu stricto (in North America), transmitted by Ixodes scapularis and Ixodes pacificus blacklegged ticks attached for ≥ 36-48 hours. Stage 1 (Early localized): Erythema migrans (EM) rash (expanding annular erythematous patch ≥ 5 cm, often with central clearing / 'bull's-eye') appears 7-14 days post-bite. Diagnosis of EM in an endemic area is purely clinical; serology is insensitive (<40%) in early localized disease and should not be ordered. Stage 2 (Early disseminated): Multiple EM lesions, cranial neuropathy (unilateral or bilateral Bell's palsy), lymphocytic meningitis, or Lyme carditis (AV heart block). Stage 3 (Late): Asymmetric, migratory mono/oligoarthritis (prominently knee). Standard two-tier serologic testing (EIA screen followed by Western blot or second EIA) confirms disseminated/late disease. Oral doxycycline (100 mg BID for 10-14 days) is first-line; amoxicillin (500 mg TID for 14 days) or cefuroxime are alternatives. Guideline Protocol: Tick prevention: wear permethrin-treated clothing, apply 20-30% DEET, perform full-body tick checks within 2 hours of outdoor exposure; remove embedded ticks promptly using fine-tipped tweezers pulling straight out without twisting. Thresholds: A single dose of oral doxycycline (200 mg within 72 hours of tick removal) provides effective post-exposure prophylaxis if tick was attached ≥ 36 hours in a high-endemic area.

title: Sepsis and Septic Shock: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Crit Care Med)
snippet: Sepsis-3 consensus defines sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, clinically quantified by an acute increase in SOFA (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) score ≥ 2 points. Septic shock is a subset characterized by profound circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities, defined by persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥ 65 mmHg and serum lactate > 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation, carrying mortality > 40%. The 1-Hour Sepsis Bundle mandates: (1) measure serum lactate level (remeasure if initial > 2 mmol/L), (2) obtain blood cultures prior to antibiotics, (3) administer broad-spectrum IV antimicrobials within 1 hour, (4) rapidly infuse 30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloids (e.g., Plasmalyte or Lactated Ringer's) for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L, and (5) initiate norepinephrine as first-line vasopressor if MAP remains < 65 mmHg during or after fluid loading. Guideline Protocol: Rapid source identification and surgical/percutaneous source control (e.g., abscess drainage, debridement of infected tissue, removal of infected vascular catheters) within 6-12 hours of presentation. Thresholds: Target mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥ 65 mmHg; serum lactate clearance (>20% reduction every 2 hours) serves as dynamic surrogate of tissue perfusion.

Instead of just fighting the germs, the immune system triggers widespread inflammation that can drop your blood pressure dangerously low and damage vital organs.

title: Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Gastroenterology)
snippet: Iron deficiency anemia is the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide, defined by microcytic hypochromic red cell indices (MCV < 80 fL) with low body iron stores: serum ferritin < 30-45 ng/mL (in non-inflammatory states; ferritin < 100 ng/mL in inflammatory states) or transferrin saturation (TSAT) < 20%. In adult men and postmenopausal women, IDA is GI tract blood loss until proven otherwise; bidirectional endoscopy (EGD and colonoscopy) is strongly recommended by AGA guidelines to rule out occult gastrointestinal malignancy (detected in 10-15%). Oral iron supplementation (oral ferrous sulfate 65 mg elemental iron on alternate days) optimizes fractional iron absorption by limiting hepcidin surges. Intravenous iron formulations (ferric carboxymaltose, ferumoxytol, iron sucrose) are indicated for oral intolerance, malabsorption (celiac, IBD, bariatric surgery), third-trimester pregnancy, or heavy ongoing bleeding. Guideline Protocol: Dietary enhancement with heme iron sources (lean red meat, poultry, fish); consume non-heme iron foods alongside ascorbic acid (vitamin C) to boost absorption; avoid drinking black tea or coffee with iron-rich meals (tannins inhibit absorption). Thresholds: Serum ferritin < 30-45 ng/mL is the most sensitive and specific threshold for depleted marrow iron stores.

Without enough iron, you feel exhausted, look pale, become short of breath with stairs, and may crave chewing ice.

title: Vitamin B12 Deficiency (Pernicious / Megaloblastic Anemia): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (N Engl J Med)
snippet: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency causes megaloblastic macrocytic anemia (MCV often > 100-110 fL) with hypersegmented neutrophils, and irreversible neuropsychiatric pathology (subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord: bilateral peripheral neuropathy, loss of vibratory and position sense, spastic ataxia, and cognitive decline). Etiologies include autoimmune pernicious anemia (destruction of gastric parietal cells; anti-intrinsic factor antibodies), malabsorption (terminal ileal disease, Crohn's, bariatric resection), prolonged metformin or PPI use, and strict veganism. Serum B12 < 200 pg/mL confirms deficiency; borderline levels (200-350 pg/mL) require metabolic confirmation via elevated serum methylmalonic acid (MMA) and homocysteine (distinguishing B12 from folate deficiency, where MMA remains normal). Cochrane review shows oral high-dose cyanocobalamin (1,000-2,000 mcg daily) is as effective as intramuscular injections (1,000 mcg weekly then monthly) for hematologic recovery, though IM is preferred for severe neurologic impairment. Guideline Protocol: Dietary incorporation of fortified nutritional yeast, dairy, eggs, or meat; daily oral supplementation for strict vegans; falls prevention physiotherapy for sensory ataxia. Thresholds: Serum B12 < 200 pg/mL or MMA > 0.4 µmol/L confirms biochemical B12 deficiency.

title: Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Blood Adv)
snippet: Primary immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an acquired autoimmune disorder characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia (platelet count < 100 x 10⁹/L) caused by autoantibody-mediated platelet destruction (anti-GPIIb/IIIa) and impaired megakaryocyte thrombopoiesis, in the absence of other cytopenias or underlying disorders. Presentation ranges from asymptomatic bruising/petechiae to mucosal bleeding (epistaxis, gingival bleeding, menorrhagia) and catastrophic intracranial hemorrhage (1-2%). First-line therapy for platelets < 20-30 x 10⁹/L or active bleeding consists of oral corticosteroids: high-dose dexamethasone (40 mg daily for 4 days; achieves faster initial responses and higher sustained remission rates than prednisone) or prednisone (1 mg/kg/day for 1-2 weeks tapered). IVIG (1 g/kg single dose) rapidly raises platelets within 24-48 hours during emergency bleeding. Second-line therapies for persistent/chronic ITP include Thrombopoietin Receptor Agonists (TPO-RAs: romiplostim, eltrombopag, avatrombopag; sustained response >70-80%), rituximab, or laparoscopic splenectomy. Guideline Protocol: Avoid contact sports or high-impact activities while platelet count < 30-50 x 10⁹/L; avoid antiplatelet and anticoagulant medications (aspirin, NSAIDs); use soft-bristle toothbrush. Thresholds: Platelet count < 20-30 x 10⁹/L or significant mucosal bleeding warrants active medical intervention; target platelets > 50 x 10⁹/L for minor procedures and > 100 x 10⁹/L for neurosurgery.

With fewer platelets in your blood, you bruise very easily, develop tiny red pinpoint rash dots (petechiae), and bleed longer from small cuts.

title: Multiple Myeloma: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (The Lancet)
snippet: Multiple myeloma is a clonal plasma cell malignancy characterized by bone marrow plasmacytosis (≥10%) and the presence of CRAB criteria (Hypercalcemia > 11 mg/dL, Renal insufficiency [creatinine > 2 mg/dL or CrCl < 40], Anemia [Hb < 10 g/dL], Bone lytic lesions) or myeloma-defining biomarkers (SLiM: ≥60% clonal marrow plasma cells, serum involved/uninvolved free light chain ratio ≥ 100, >1 focal MRI bone lesion). Workup requires serum/urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (SPEP/UPEP/IFE), serum free light chains (sFLC), and whole-body low-dose CT or PET-CT. Triplet and quadruplet induction regimens incorporating the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab, proteasome inhibitor bortezomib, immunomodulatory drug lenalidomide, and dexamethasone (Dara-VRd or Dara-Rd) produce deep responses and unprecedented progression-free survival (MAIA and GRIFFIN trials). Autologous stem cell transplant (ASCT) remains standard for eligible patients, followed by lenalidomide maintenance. Guideline Protocol: Generous daily hydration (≥ 2-3 liters/day) to prevent renal tubular light-chain cast nephropathy; avoid all NSAIDs; bone protection with zoledronic acid or denosumab plus weight-bearing exercises to reduce pathological fractures. Thresholds: M-protein disappearance plus negative immunofixation and marrow flow cytometry with <1 clonal cell per 100,000 cells defines Minimal Residual Disease (MRD) negativity (10⁻⁵).

When abnormal plasma cells multiply uncontrollably inside your bone marrow, they crowd out healthy blood cells, dissolve weak holes in bones, and produce abnormal proteins that can damage your kidneys.

title: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (The Lancet (ELEVATE-TN))
snippet: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is the most prevalent adult leukemia in Western countries, defined by persistent clonal B-cell lymphocytosis in peripheral blood (≥ 5 x 10⁹/L) co-expressing CD5, CD19, CD20 (dim), and CD23 on flow cytometry. Staged via Rai (0 to IV) or Binet (A to C) systems. Asymptomatic early-stage disease (Rai 0, Binet A) managed with active surveillance ('watch and wait'), as randomized trials showed early chemotherapy does not improve overall survival. Treatment indications (iwCLL criteria): constitutional 'B' symptoms, progressive bone marrow failure, massive splenomegaly, or lymphocyte doubling time < 6 months. Targeted front-line oral therapies targeting Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK inhibitors: acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib) or BCL-2 (venetoclax combined with anti-CD20 antibody obinutuzumab) have completely displaced traditional chemoimmunotherapy (FCR), achieving superior progression-free survival even in high-risk TP53-mutated or del(17p) disease. Guideline Protocol: Universal annual influenza, pneumococcal (PCV20), and recombinant zoster (Shingrix) vaccinations (avoid live-attenuated vaccines due to humoral immune defect); sun protection and annual full-body dermatologic exams (8-fold increased skin cancer risk). Thresholds: Lymphocyte count doubling time < 6 months, platelets < 100 x 10⁹/L, or hemoglobin < 10 g/dL meets iwCLL treatment criteria.

In its early stages, it often causes no symptoms and is found on routine blood tests; many people live normal active lives for years under careful monitoring without ever needing chemotherapy.

title: Polycythemia Vera (PV): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (N Engl J Med)
snippet: Polycythemia vera is a Philadelphia-chromosome-negative myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by autonomous erythrocytosis, driving hyperviscosity and major thrombotic complications (arterial and venous, including Budd-Chiari and portal vein thrombosis). >98% of patients harbor the activating JAK2 V617F or exon 12 driver mutation. Diagnostic criteria require: elevated hemoglobin/hematocrit (>16.5 g/dL / 49% in men; >16.0 g/dL / 48% in women), hypercellular bone marrow with trilineage panmyelosis, JAK2 mutation, and subnormal serum erythropoietin (EPO). Landmark CYTO-PV trial proved that strict hematocrit maintenance < 45% reduced cardiovascular death and major thrombosis fourfold compared to a 45-50% target (HR 3.91, 95% CI 1.45-10.53, p=0.007). All patients receive low-dose aspirin (81-100 mg daily; ECLAP trial). High-risk patients (age ≥60 or prior thrombosis) require cytoreductive therapy (hydroxyurea or ropeginterferon alfa-2b; ruxolitinib in refractory cases). Aquagenic pruritus (itching triggered by warm showers) is a hallmark symptom. Guideline Protocol: Therapeutic phlebotomy (removal of 450-500 mL blood) to maintain hematocrit strictly < 45%; avoidance of iron supplementation (relative iron deficiency is therapeutically desired to slow red cell manufacturing); smoking cessation; manage aquagenic pruritus with lower shower temperatures and antihistamines. Thresholds: Target hematocrit strictly < 45.0% in all patients to prevent fatal thrombotic events.

The extra cells make your blood unusually thick and sluggish, like motor oil in winter, increasing the danger of blood clots.

title: Rosacea: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Cochrane Database Syst Rev)
snippet: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory centrofacial dermatosis characterized by neurovascular dysregulation and innate immune hyperreactivity (cathelicidin LL-37 processing by kallikrein 5, Demodex folliculorum mite hypersensitivity). Phenotypes include: Erythematotelangiectatic (persistent centrofacial erythema, flushing, telangiectasias), Papulopustular (dome-shaped red papules and pustules without comedones, distinguishing it from acne vulgaris), Phymatous (sebaceous hyperplasia, rhinophyma), and Ocular rosacea (blepharitis, conjunctivitis, burning/grittiness; present in >50%). First-line topical therapies for papulopustular rosacea: ivermectin 1% cream (superior to metronidazole; anti-parasitic against Demodex and anti-inflammatory), azelaic acid 15% gel, or metronidazole 0.75-1%. Subantimicrobial-dose oral doxycycline (40 mg modified-release daily; anti-inflammatory without antibacterial resistance) is indicated for moderate-to-severe disease. Persistent facial erythema responds to topical alpha-agonists (brimonidine 0.33%, oxymetazoline 1%) or vascular pulsed-dye laser (PDL). Guideline Protocol: Identify and avoid individual flushing triggers: hot beverages, spicy foods, alcohol (especially red wine), extreme temperatures, emotional stress; daily mineral broad-spectrum sunscreen (zinc oxide/titanium dioxide SPF 30+); gentle soap-free facial cleansers. Thresholds: Presence of inflammatory papules and pustules without comedones confirms papulopustular rosacea.

patient_plain_language: Rosacea is a chronic skin condition causing persistent facial redness, flushing, and small acne-like bumps across your nose, cheeks, and forehead. Unlike teenage acne, there are no blackheads, and flare-ups are often triggered by sun, heat, spicy foods, or hot coffee.

title: Alopecia Areata: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (N Engl J Med)
snippet: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition caused by collapse of immune privilege in anagen hair follicles, mediated by CD8+ NKG2D+ T-cell infiltration and IFN-gamma/IL-15 signaling. Classic presentation is sudden onset of well-circumscribed, smooth, circular patches of non-scarring hair loss on the scalp or beard, showing pathognomonic exclamation-mark hairs and yellow/black dots on dermoscopy (trichoscopy). May progress to alopecia totalis (entire scalp) or alopecia universalis (complete body hair loss). Severity of Alopecia Tool (SALT) scores extent of hair loss. For limited patchy disease (SALT < 20-30%), first-line therapy is intralesional corticosteroid injections (triamcinolone acetonide 2.5-5 mg/mL into the dermis every 4-6 weeks) or potent topical corticosteroids. Landmark BRAVE-AA1 and BRAVE-AA2 phase 3 trials established oral Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors (baricitinib 2-4 mg daily; ritlecitinib 50 mg daily) as breakthrough FDA-approved therapies for severe disease (SALT score ≥ 50), producing significant scalp hair regrowth (SALT score ≤ 20 achieved in ~35-40% of patients vs 3-5% placebo at 36 weeks). Guideline Protocol: Psychosocial counseling and peer support groups (high burden of anxiety and depression); scalp sun protection (broad-spectrum sunscreen SPF 50+, hats/scarves); gentle hair care. Thresholds: SALT score ≥ 50 (≥50% scalp hair loss) or rapidly progressive widespread disease qualifies for systemic oral JAK inhibitor therapy.

This results in smooth, round, coin-shaped bald spots on your scalp or beard without any skin scarring.

title: Hidradenitis Suppurativa: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (The Lancet)
snippet: Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic, painful, inflammatory follicular occlusion disorder predominantly affecting apocrine gland-bearing intertriginous skin (axillae, inguinal, perineal, inframammary regions). Manifests as recurrent painful inflammatory nodules, sterile abscesses, discharging epithelialized sinus tracts (tunnels), and dense bridged scarring. Staged using Hurley classification: Stage I (isolated nodules/abscesses, no sinus tracts), Stage II (recurrent abscesses with sinus tracts and scarring, separated), Stage III (diffuse coalescent tracts and interconnected abscesses across an entire anatomic area). Medical therapy: Topical clindamycin 1% for mild Hurley I; oral combination antibiotics (clindamycin 300 mg BID + rifampin 300 mg BID for 10-12 weeks) for Hurley II flares. Pivotal Phase 3 trials demonstrated that biological therapy targeting TNF (adalimumab 40 mg weekly, PIONEER trials) or IL-17A (secukinumab 300 mg every 2-4 weeks, SUNSHINE/SUNRISE trials) significantly achieves HiSCR (Hidradenitis Suppurativa Clinical Response: ≥50% reduction in inflammatory nodules without abscess increase). Deroofing or wide surgical excision is required for established chronic epithelialized tunnels. Guideline Protocol: Smoking cessation (smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor, present in >80%); structured weight management (friction reduction); wear loose-fitting breathable cotton clothing; antiseptic washes (chlorhexidine or benzoyl peroxide wash); wound care dressings. Thresholds: Moderate-to-severe disease (Hurley Stage II/III or IHS4 > 3) failing oral antibiotics indicates initiation of targeted biological therapy (adalimumab or secukinumab).

title: Vitiligo: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (N Engl J Med)
snippet: Vitiligo is an acquired autoimmune depigmenting disorder characterized by progressive destruction of epidermal melanocytes, mediated by autoreactive CD8+ cytotoxic T cells driven by IFN-gamma and JAK1/JAK2 signaling. Clinically presents as well-demarcated, amelanotic milky-white macules and patches without epidermal atrophy or scale, exhibiting bright blue-white fluorescence under Wood's lamp. Segmental (unilateral, dermatomal) vs Non-segmental (bilateral, symmetric; ~90% of cases). Koebner phenomenon (depigmentation at sites of cutaneous friction/trauma) indicates active disease. The landmark TRuE-V1 and TRuE-V2 randomized phase 3 trials established the topical JAK inhibitor ruxolitinib 1.5% cream (applied twice daily) as the first FDA-approved disease-directed therapy for non-segmental vitiligo in patients ≥ 12 years, achieving ≥75% improvement in Facial Vitiligo Area Scoring Index (F-VASI75) in ~30% of patients at 24 weeks and ~50% at 52 weeks. Narrowband ultraviolet B (NB-UVB) phototherapy (2-3 times/week) synergizes with medical therapy to stimulate melanocyte stem cell migration from hair follicles. Guideline Protocol: Meticulous sun protection of depigmented patches (broad-spectrum SPF 50+; depigmented skin has zero melanin and burns easily, triggering Koebner phenomenon); avoid tight abrasive clothing and repetitive friction; cosmetic camouflage creams. Thresholds: F-VASI75 response (≥75% repigmentation of facial vitiligo) indicates optimal therapeutic milestone.

title: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Am J Psychiatry)
snippet: Obsessive-compulsive disorder is characterized by recurrent, persistent, intrusive, and distressing thoughts, urges, or images (obsessions) and/or repetitive physical behaviors or mental acts (compulsions) that the individual feels driven to perform to reduce anxiety, consuming > 1 hour/day or causing clinically significant distress. Cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) circuit hyperactivity underlies pathophysiology. First-line evidence-based psychotherapeutic treatment is specialized Cognitive Behavioral Therapy incorporating Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP; effect size g=1.39). First-line pharmacotherapy mandates high-dose selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs: fluoxetine 60-80 mg, sertraline 200 mg, escitalopram 20-40 mg, or fluvoxamine 200-300 mg daily), requiring higher doses and longer trial durations (10-12 weeks at maximum tolerated dose) than required for major depressive disorder. Clomipramine (tricyclic with potent serotonin reuptake inhibition) is second-line; augmentation with atypical antipsychotics (aripiprazole 5-10 mg, risperidone 1-2 mg) improves refractory cases. Guideline Protocol: Structured Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) behavioral therapy homework (facing feared triggers hierarchically while voluntarily refraining from ritualistic compulsions); family accommodation reduction. Thresholds: Y-BOCS score reduction ≥ 35% defines full clinical response; Y-BOCS ≤ 12 indicates clinical remission.

To quiet the intense anxiety, you feel an overwhelming urge to perform repetitive routines, checks, or mental rituals (compulsions), which only temporarily relieves the anxiety before the cycle repeats.

title: Panic Disorder: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Cochrane Database Syst Rev)
snippet: Panic disorder is characterized by recurrent, unexpected panic attacks—abrupt surges of intense fear or intense discomfort reaching a peak within minutes, accompanied by ≥ 4 somatic and cognitive symptoms (palpitations, sweating, trembling, dyspnea, choking sensation, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills/heat sensations, paresthesias, derealization/depersonalization, fear of losing control, fear of dying)—followed by ≥ 1 month of persistent concern about additional attacks or maladaptive behavioral changes (avoidance). First-line treatment consists of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT with interoceptive exposure to panic-related sensations) or SSRIs/SNRIs (sertraline, paroxetine, citalopram, venlafaxine). SSRIs should be initiated at half standard starting doses (e.g., sertraline 25 mg) because panic disorder patients exhibit heightened sensitivity to initial jitteriness/anxiety. Benzodiazepines provide rapid acute relief but carry risks of physical dependence, tolerance, cognitive blunting, and increased relapse rates upon discontinuation, and are not recommended for long-term maintenance. Guideline Protocol: Interoceptive exposure exercises in CBT (spinning in chair, hyperventilating, breathing through straw to extinguish conditioned somatic fear); diaphragmatic slow breathing (4 seconds in, 6 seconds out); elimination of caffeine and energy drinks; regular aerobic exercise. Thresholds: PDSS score reduction ≥ 40% represents significant clinical response; PDSS ≤ 3 indicates remission.

Within minutes, your heart pounds, your chest tightens, and you feel dizzy and terrified that you are having a heart attack or losing your mind.

title: Social Anxiety Disorder (Social Phobia): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (The Lancet Psychiatry)
snippet: Social anxiety disorder is characterized by marked, persistent fear or anxiety about one or more social situations in which the individual is exposed to possible scrutiny by others (social interactions, being observed eating/drinking, performing in front of others), fearing negative evaluation, embarrassment, or humiliation. The largest comprehensive network meta-analysis (Lancet Psychiatry, 101 trials, 13,164 participants) demonstrated that individual Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT based on the Clark and Wells or Heimberg models with video feedback and behavioral experiments) has the largest effect size and longest-lasting benefits. First-line pharmacotherapy for generalized social anxiety disorder is SSRIs (sertraline 50-200 mg, paroxetine 20-50 mg, escitalopram 10-20 mg) or SNRIs (venlafaxine XR 75-225 mg). For discrete performance-only social anxiety (e.g., public speaking, musical performances), as-needed non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol 10-40 mg orally taken 30-60 minutes before the event) effectively suppress peripheral autonomic somatic symptoms (tremors, tachycardia, voice shaking) without cognitive sedation. Guideline Protocol: Individual CBT incorporating video feedback and behavioral experiments (testing catastrophic predictions about social blunders); gradual social exposure hierarchies; eliminating 'safety behaviors' (avoiding eye contact, rehearsing phrases, hiding face). Thresholds: LSAS score reduction ≥ 30% indicates treatment response; LSAS ≤ 30 indicates minimal social anxiety symptoms.

title: Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Am J Psychiatry)
snippet: Diagnostic criteria (DSM-5) require ≥ 2 of 11 criteria over a 12-month period, categorized into mild (2-3), moderate (4-5), and severe (≥6 criteria: tolerance, withdrawal, craving, inability to cut down, spending excess time obtaining/using, neglecting social/occupational roles). Acute alcohol withdrawal is managed with protocolized symptom-triggered benzodiazepines (CIWA-Ar protocol). First-line FDA-approved pharmacotherapies for maintaining abstinence and reducing heavy drinking days: Oral naltrexone (50 mg daily) or once-monthly extended-release injectable naltrexone (Vivitrol 380 mg IM; opioid receptor antagonist reducing the dopamine-mediated reinforcing reward of alcohol; Cochrane review confirms 28% reduction in heavy drinking days; contraindicated in patients taking opioid analgesics or in acute hepatitis/liver failure); and Acamprosate (666 mg TID; modulates NMDA glutamate neurotransmission, ideal for maintaining abstinence in patients with liver disease; cleared renally, contraindicated if CrCl < 30 mL/min). Disulfiram is second-line. Combining pharmacotherapy with evidence-based psychosocial interventions (Motivational Interviewing, CBT, Twelve-Step Facilitation) optimizes recovery outcomes. Guideline Protocol: Participation in mutual-help support groups (Alcoholics Anonymous, SMART Recovery); structured Motivational Enhancement Therapy or CBT; complete household removal of all alcohol; identify and manage relapse triggers (HALT: Hungry, Angry, Lonely, Tired). Thresholds: CIWA-Ar score > 8 indicates need for protocolized symptom-triggered benzodiazepines; CIWA-Ar > 15 warrants inpatient medical detoxification.

title: Uterine Leiomyomas (Fibroids): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Obstet Gynecol)
snippet: Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) are benign monoclonal smooth muscle neoplasms of the myometrium, occurring in up to 70-80% of women by age 50. Symptoms depend on anatomical location (FIGO classification: submucosal [Types 0-2], intramural [Types 3-5], subserosal [Types 6-7]). Submucosal and intramural fibroids distorting the uterine cavity cause heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB / menorrhagia) leading to iron deficiency anemia; large fibroids cause pelvic pressure, urinary frequency, and hydronephrosis. Transvaginal ultrasonography is first-line imaging; saline-infusion sonohysterography (SIS) or pelvic MRI defines submucosal mapping. Medical therapy for HMB: Levonorgestrel-releasing IUD (52 mg LNG-IUD; reduces menstrual blood loss by >80%), tranexamic acid (1,300 mg TID during heavy flow), or oral GnRH antagonists combined with add-back hormone therapy (elagolix or relugolix combination therapy; FDA-approved, suppresses HMB while preventing bone loss). Uterine artery embolization (UAE), hysteroscopic/laparoscopic myomectomy, or radiofrequency ablation provide fertility-preserving or uterine-preserving procedural options; hysterectomy is definitive. Guideline Protocol: Dietary iron and vitamin C supplementation to treat associated microcytic anemia; structured symptom tracking with menstrual diary; pelvic floor conditioning. Thresholds: Submucosal fibroids (FIGO Types 0-2) are primarily amenable to outpatient hysteroscopic resection, restoring normal cavity architecture and reducing bleeding.

title: Postpartum Depression (PPD): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Am J Psychiatry)
snippet: Postpartum depression affects ~10-15% of women following childbirth, defined as a major depressive episode occurring during pregnancy or within the first 12 months postpartum (distinguished from transient 'postpartum blues' which peak at 3-5 days and resolve by 10-14 days without functional impairment). Presentation features persistent sadness, profound emotional detachment or anhedonia toward the newborn, excessive guilt, sleep disturbance unrelated to infant wakings, severe anxiety, and obsessive fears of infant harm. The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) is the validated screening standard (score ≥ 10-12 indicates positive screen). Mild-to-moderate PPD responds well to evidence-based psychotherapy (Interpersonal Psychotherapy [IPT] or CBT). Moderate-to-severe PPD warrants pharmacotherapy: SSRIs (sertraline is preferred during breastfeeding due to minimal infant breastmilk excretion and low relative infant dose <0.5%). The breakthrough GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator zuranolone (50 mg orally once nightly with fatty food for 14 days; SKYLARK phase 3 trial) demonstrated rapid, statistically significant reduction in HAM-D depression scores by day 3 with sustained remission at day 45. Guideline Protocol: Structured family support plan prioritizing uninterrupted 4-6 hour maternal sleep blocks; peer postpartum support groups; Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT); registered lactation consultant support if breastfeeding difficulties exacerbate distress. Thresholds: EPDS score ≥ 10 or any positive score on Question 10 (suicidal thoughts) mandates immediate comprehensive clinical evaluation.

It is not a sign of personal weakness or being a 'bad mother'. It causes deep sadness, feeling disconnected from your baby, and overwhelming anxiety that can be effectively treated.

title: Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Cochrane Database Syst Rev)
snippet: Croup is an acute viral infection of the upper airway primarily caused by human parainfluenza virus type 1 (70-80%), peaking in infants and toddlers aged 6 months to 3 years during autumn/early winter. Inflammatory subglottic edema leads to the hallmark clinical triad: barking cough (resembling a seal or dog), inspiratory stridor, and hoarseness, characteristically worsening at night. Severity is stratified via the Westley Croup Score (evaluating stridor, retractions, air entry, cyanosis, and level of consciousness). Cochrane meta-analyses definitively prove that a single dose of oral dexamethasone (0.15-0.6 mg/kg, max 16 mg) significantly reduces hospital admissions (RR 0.52), shortens length of emergency department stay, reduces return visits, and decreases the need for nebulized epinephrine across all severity grades (mild, moderate, and severe). For moderate-to-severe croup with resting stridor and retractions, nebulized racemic epinephrine (0.5 mL of 2.25% solution) or L-epinephrine provides rapid subglottic vasoconstriction and symptom relief within 10-30 minutes, requiring a 2-4 hour observation window to monitor for post-epinephrine rebound stridor. Guideline Protocol: Keep the child calm and comforted in the parent's lap (agitation and crying dramatically increases negative intrathoracic airway pressure and worsens subglottic collapse); avoid painful or intrusive procedures (e.g., throat exams or IVs unless necessary); cool mist humidification. Thresholds: Resting stridor, sternal/intercostal retractions, or agitation indicates moderate-to-severe croup requiring nebulized epinephrine in addition to oral dexamethasone.

title: Pediatric Bronchiolitis (RSV): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Pediatrics)
snippet: Bronchiolitis is the leading cause of hospitalization in infants < 12 months, predominantly caused by Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV, 70-80%). Viral necrosis of bronchiolar epithelium, mucus plugging, and submucosal edema produce air trapping, tachypnea, expiratory wheezing, diffuse crackles, and increased work of breathing (nasal flaring, subcostal retractions). AAP evidence-based guidelines emphasize supportive care as the foundation of management: nasal suctioning (saline drops and bulb suction) and maintenance of adequate hydration (oral feeds or IV/nasogastric fluids if tachypneic with respiratory rate > 60-70 breaths/min risking aspiration). The AAP guideline explicitly recommends AGAINST the routine use of bronchodilators (albuterol), systemic corticosteroids, or chest physiotherapy, as randomized trials demonstrate they do not alter disease progression, reduce hospitalizations, or shorten stay. Supplemental oxygen is indicated only if pulse oximetry persistently falls below 90%. High-risk infants benefit from immunoprophylaxis with the long-acting monoclonal antibody nirsevimab (Beyfortus; single IM injection providing >75-80% protection against RSV lower respiratory infection; MELODY trial; NEJM 2022). Guideline Protocol: Nasal bulb or mechanical suctioning with gentle isotonic saline drops before every feeding and before sleep; small, frequent feedings to avoid fatigue and vomiting; strict hand hygiene; eliminate infant exposure to secondhand tobacco smoke. Thresholds: Sustained pulse oximetry < 90% or inability to maintain oral hydration due to severe tachypnea (>60-70 breaths/min) mandates inpatient admission.

Babies start with common cold symptoms before developing fast breathing, wheezing, and a chest that sucks in when inhaling.

title: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg)
snippet: BPPV is the most common cause of peripheral vertigo, caused by otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) dislodged from the utricular macula migrating into a semicircular canal (canalithiasis; posterior canal involved in 85-95%). Pathognomonic presentation is brief (<1 minute), intense episodes of rotational spinning vertigo provoked by head position changes relative to gravity (rolling over in bed, looking up at a high shelf, bending forward). Gold standard diagnosis is the Dix-Hallpike maneuver, which elicits torsional, upbeating nystagmus with a 2-5 second latency and duration < 60 seconds that fatigues upon repeated testing. First-line definitive therapy is the canalith repositioning procedure (Epley maneuver; Cochrane systematic review proves >80-90% resolution of vertigo and negative Dix-Hallpike after 1-2 treatments vs 30% control, NNT=1.5). Vestibular suppressant medications (meclizine, benzodiazepines) are explicitly NOT recommended for routine treatment because they impair central compensation, cause cognitive blunting, and do not resolve otoconia displacement. Guideline Protocol: Canalith repositioning procedure (Epley maneuver performed by a trained clinician); Brandt-Daroff home habituation exercises for persistent residual mild dizziness; fall prevention precautions when getting out of bed. Thresholds: Positive Dix-Hallpike test with classic torsional upbeating nystagmus confirms posterior canal BPPV; negative test confirms successful repositioning.

patient_plain_language: BPPV is a common inner-ear balance disorder where tiny calcium 'ear stones' come loose from their normal spot and float into the semicircular balance canals. When you tilt your head or roll over in bed, the loose crystals slosh the ear fluid, tricking your brain into feeling like the room is violently spinning.

title: Diabetic Retinopathy: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Ophthalmology)
snippet: Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of preventable blindness in working-age adults, caused by chronic microvascular damage from hyperglycemia leading to retinal capillary basement membrane thickening, pericyte loss, microaneurysms, retinal hemorrhages, and vascular leakage. Classified into Non-Proliferative (NPDR: mild, moderate, severe based on 4-2-1 rule: retinal hemorrhages in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2 quadrants, IRMA in 1 quadrant) and Proliferative (PDR: pathological neovascularization of the disc [NVD] or retina [NVE] driven by VEGF ischemia, risking vitreous hemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment). Diabetic macular edema (DME: fluid accumulation in the fovea) can occur at any stage. Foundational systemic control (UKPDS and DCCT trials) reduces retinopathy progression: HbA1c < 7.0%, blood pressure < 130/80 mmHg, and lipid management. First-line therapy for center-involved DME with visual impairment is intravitreal anti-VEGF injections (aflibercept, ranibizumab, or faricimab; Protocol T trial showed aflibercept achieved superior visual gains in eyes with initial visual acuity 20/50 or worse). Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) laser or anti-VEGF therapy stabilizes high-risk PDR. Guideline Protocol: Strict glycemic control (HbA1c target < 7.0%); blood pressure target < 130/80 mmHg; manage dyslipidemia; smoking cessation; aerobic exercise. Thresholds: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrating central macular thickness > 300 µm with intraretinal cysts indicates center-involved diabetic macular edema requiring intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy.

patient_plain_language: Diabetic retinopathy is damage to the delicate blood vessels in the light-sensing retina at the back of your eye caused by high blood sugar. In its early stages, weak spots leak fluid into the center of vision; in later stages, abnormal fragile blood vessels sprout that can bleed into the eye, causing dark floaters or vision loss.

solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrating central macular thickness > 300 µm with intraretinal cysts indicates center-involved diabetic macular edema requiring intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy.

title: Mitral Valve Regurgitation: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (COAPT Trial) & ACC/AHA)
snippet: In the landmark COAPT trial (n=614 heart failure patients with secondary mitral regurgitation), transcatheter mitral-valve repair (MitraClip) plus guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) significantly reduced annual hospitalization for heart failure compared with GDMT alone (35.8% vs 67.9% per patient-year; HR 0.53; 95% CI 0.40-0.70; p<0.001) and all-cause 24-month mortality (29.1% vs 46.1%; HR 0.62; 95% CI 0.46-0.82; p<0.001). Number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent 1 death was 5.9. Guideline Protocol: Strict daily dietary sodium restriction to <2,000 mg/day; daily morning weight tracking; supervised cardiac rehabilitation once stabilized. Thresholds: Regurgitant volume >=60 mL/beat, effective regurgitant orifice area (EROA) >=0.40 cm2, or LV end-systolic dimension (LVESD) >40 mm triggers urgent heart valve team review.
