title: Infective Endocarditis: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Circulation (AHA Endocarditis Guidelines) & NEJM (POET))
snippet: The landmark POET trial (n=400 randomized patients with left-sided endocarditis stabilized on initial IV therapy) proved that transitioning to step-down oral antibiotics was non-inferior to continued intravenous antibiotic therapy for the composite primary outcome of all-cause mortality, unplanned cardiac surgery, embolic events, or relapsed bacteremia (9.0% oral vs 12.1% IV; difference -3.1 percentage points; 95% CI -8.8 to 2.5; p=0.40). Modified Duke Criteria remain the gold standard for clinical diagnosis (sensitivity >80%). Guideline Protocol: Immediate removal of infected indwelling central venous catheters; strict dental hygiene optimization to prevent transient bacteremia; mandatory valve surgery evaluation for refractory infection. Thresholds: Vegetation size >10 mm with embolic episode, severe acute valve regurgitation causing cardiogenic shock, or perivalvular abscess mandates emergent surgical consultation.

title: Acute Pericarditis: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (ICAP Trial) & ESC Guidelines)
snippet: In the landmark multicenter double-blind ICAP trial (n=240 patients with first-episode acute pericarditis), adding weight-adjusted colchicine (0.5 mg once or twice daily for 3 months) to standard anti-inflammatory therapy significantly reduced the rate of recurrent pericarditis at 18 months from 37.5% in the placebo group to 16.7% in the colchicine group (relative risk reduction 56%; absolute risk reduction 20.8 percentage points; NNT = 5; p<0.001). Colchicine also reduced symptom persistence at 72 hours (19.2% vs 40.0%; p=0.001). Guideline Protocol: Strict avoidance of strenuous physical exertion, competitive athletics, and aerobic exercise until symptom resolution and normalization of CRP (minimum 3 months for athletes). Thresholds: PR depression with diffuse concave ST-segment elevations on 12-lead ECG; failure of symptom improvement within 72 hours on NSAID + Colchicine warrants inpatient admission.

title: Cardiac Tamponade: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (ESC Guidelines on Pericardial Diseases & JAMA Rational Clinical Exam)
journal: ESC Guidelines on Pericardial Diseases & JAMA Rational Clinical Exam

snippet: Cardiac tamponade is a life-threatening hemodynamic emergency where pericardial fluid accumulation under high pressure impairs diastolic filling. Beck's triad (hypotension, jugular venous distension, muffled heart sounds) has high specificity (>90%) but low sensitivity (<30%). The single most sensitive clinical sign is pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg inspiratory drop in systolic blood pressure, sensitivity 98%). Echocardiographic hallmark is right ventricular early diastolic collapse (specificity 95%) and right atrial late diastolic collapse. Immediate pericardiocentesis resolves hemodynamics in >98% of cases. Guideline Protocol: Emergent bedside echocardiography-guided pericardiocentesis; placement of a temporary pericardial pigtail drain until output is <25-30 mL/24h. Thresholds: Pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg, IVC plethora with <50% inspiratory collapse, or RV collapse >1/3 of diastole mandates immediate decompression.

patient_plain_language: Cardiac tamponade is a medical emergency where fluid rapidly builds up inside the sac wrapped around your heart. title: Ventricular Tachycardia (VT): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (VANISH Trial) & AHA/ACC/HRS Guidelines)
snippet: In the multicenter VANISH trial (n=259 patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy and recurrent VT despite baseline antiarrhythmic therapy), catheter ablation significantly reduced the primary composite outcome of death, VT storm (>=3 episodes in 24 hours), or appropriate ICD shocks compared with escalated antiarrhythmic drug therapy (59.1% vs 68.5%; HR 0.72; 95% CI 0.53-0.98; p=0.04). Catheter ablation reduced VT storm by 42% (HR 0.58; p=0.04) and ICD shocks by 35% without excess procedural mortality. Guideline Protocol: Zero caffeine or sympathomimetic intake; avoidance of recreational stimulants; mandatory driving restrictions per state cardiology motor vehicle regulations (minimum 6 months shock-free). Thresholds: Sustained VT (>30 seconds) or hemodynamically unstable VT requires immediate synchronized cardioversion; >=2 ICD shocks within 24h triggers emergent ICU transfer.

title: Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (The Lancet (REVERT Trial) & ACC/AHA/HRS Guidelines)
snippet: The multicenter REVERT trial (n=428 emergency department patients with acute SVT) proved that a modified Valsalva maneuver (40 mmHg forced strain for 15 seconds in semi-recumbent position followed immediately by supine repositioning with 45-degree passive leg raise for 15 seconds) achieved cardioversion to normal sinus rhythm in 43% of patients compared with only 17% with standard Valsalva (odds ratio 3.7; 95% CI 2.3-5.8; p<0.0001; NNT = 3.8). This simple maneuver halved the need for intravenous adenosine (50% vs 69%). Definitive catheter radiofrequency ablation achieves >95% long-term cure. Guideline Protocol: Education in modified postural Valsalva maneuver; elimination of caffeine, alcohol, pseudoephedrine decongestants, and nicotine triggers. Thresholds: Narrow complex tachycardia at 150-250 bpm; hemodynamically stable SVT managed with modified Valsalva followed by rapid IV adenosine bolus (6 mg, then 12 mg).

title: Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (JACC / Circulation (AHA/ACC Aortic Guidelines))
snippet: The comprehensive 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline establishes strict diameter thresholds for elective surgical intervention in thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAA). For ascending aortic aneurysms in low-surgical-risk centers of excellence, elective repair is recommended at >=5.0 cm (Class 2a) or >=5.5 cm in standard centers (Class 1). In patients with genetic aortopathies (Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz, bicuspid aortic valve), the threshold drops to 4.5-5.0 cm, or an aortic cross-sectional area to height ratio >10 cm2/m. Strict blood pressure control with beta-blockers and ARBs reduces rate of aortic expansion by >30%. Guideline Protocol: Absolute cessation of smoking; strict avoidance of heavy isometric weightlifting (e.g. heavy bench press, squats, straining) or Valsalva maneuver exertion; genetic testing for first-degree family members. Thresholds: Ascending aorta diameter >=5.5 cm (or >=5.0 cm in expert centers; >=4.5 cm in Marfan), or expansion rate >=0.5 cm/year mandates surgical aortic graft replacement.

title: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (The Lancet (EVAR trial 1 & 2) & USPSTF)
snippet: The landmark UK EVAR-1 trial (n=1252 patients with AAA >=5.5 cm followed for 15 years) demonstrated that endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) produced a 73% reduction in 30-day operative mortality compared with open surgical repair (1.8% vs 4.3%; p=0.02). Beyond 8 years, aneurysm-related mortality became similar, but EVAR required higher rates of reintervention for endoleaks (HR 2.42; p<0.0001). USPSTF recommends 1-time screening ultrasound in all men aged 65-75 who have ever smoked (Grade B; reduces rupture mortality by 50%). Guideline Protocol: Absolute smoking cessation (smoking increases aneurysm expansion rate by 300%); moderate walking exercise; avoidance of heavy abdominal straining. Thresholds: Aortic diameter >=5.5 cm in men, >=5.0 cm in women, or expansion rate >1.0 cm/year triggers vascular surgical intervention.

title: Raynaud's Phenomenon: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews & ACR)

snippet: In a comprehensive Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 randomized controlled trials (n=296 participants), oral dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (predominantly nifedipine) significantly reduced the frequency of vasospastic attacks by 33% compared with placebo (mean difference -2.8 attacks per week; 95% CI -3.9 to -1.7; p<0.0001). title: Buerger's Disease (Thromboangiitis Obliterans): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Circulation (AHA Vascular Guidelines) & European Consensus)
snippet: Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) is a non-atherosclerotic segmental inflammatory vaso-occlusive vasculopathy affecting small and medium-sized arteries and veins of the extremities, almost exclusively in young tobacco smokers (<45 years). Complete and permanent cessation of all tobacco and nicotine products is the single proven intervention that halts disease progression and prevents limb loss. Continued smoking leads to amputation in 43% of patients at 10 years, compared to <5% in those who achieve complete smoking cessation (p<0.001). IV iloprost significantly improves ulcer healing and relieves ischemic rest pain (85% vs 17% placebo; p<0.001). Guideline Protocol: Absolute and permanent 100% cessation of all forms of tobacco, cigars, cigarettes, e-cigarettes, chewing tobacco, and nicotine replacement therapies; avoidance of cold exposure and minor foot trauma. Thresholds: Toe-brachial index (TBI) <0.50 or non-healing ischemic digital ulceration requires immediate prostacyclin infusion or sympathectomy evaluation.

It is directly linked to tobacco use—stopping smoking completely is the only way to save your fingers and toes.

title: Cor Pulmonale: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (CHEST & European Respiratory Society (ERS/ESC))
snippet: Cor pulmonale represents right ventricular (RV) hypertrophy, dilation, and systolic dysfunction resulting directly from severe pulmonary hypertension secondary to intrinsic lung disease (COPD, IPF, OSA). Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) in patients with chronic resting hypoxemia (PaO2 <=55 mmHg or SaO2 <=88%) significantly reduces pulmonary vascular resistance, prevents RV deterioration, and improves 5-year survival by 48% (NOTT and MRC trials). Judicious loop diuretic titration relieves RV volume overload without causing pre-renal azotemia. Guideline Protocol: Continuous supplemental oxygen therapy >=15-18 hours/day targeting resting SpO2 89-92% (or 90-94%); dietary sodium restriction <2,000 mg/day; nocturnal CPAP for sleep-disordered breathing. Thresholds: TAPSE <17 mm, RV fractional area change <35%, or mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) >20 mmHg with severe right atrial enlargement triggers advanced pulmonary team review.

title: Bronchiectasis (Non-Cystic Fibrosis): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (European Respiratory Journal (ERS) & Thorax (BTS))
snippet: The ERS and British Thoracic Society (BTS) Bronchiectasis Guidelines confirm that airway clearance techniques (oscillating positive expiratory pressure [OPEP]) combined with long-term macrolide maintenance therapy (Azithromycin 250-500 mg 3 times weekly) significantly reduces the annualized rate of pulmonary exacerbations by 51% (rate ratio 0.49; 95% CI 0.36-0.66; p<0.0001; EMBRACE and BAT trials). Inhaled hypertonic saline (6-7%) or nebulized dornase alfa improves sputum clearance and FEV1. title: Pulmonary Arteriovenous Malformation (PAVM): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Thorax (British Thoracic Society) & JACC)
snippet: Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (PAVMs) are abnormal direct low-resistance vascular conduits between pulmonary arteries and pulmonary veins that bypass the capillary bed, creating a right-to-left shunt. Over 80-90% of cases occur in the setting of Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT / Osler-Weber-Rendu disease). Because the normal pulmonary capillary filtration barrier is absent, paradoxical embolization occurs, leading to cryptogenic ischemic stroke (in 10-20%) and cerebral brain abscesses (in 5-10%). Transcatheter coil or microvascular plug embolization of all feeding arteries >=2-3 mm is the gold-standard therapy, reducing ischemic stroke and brain abscess incidence by >90% while improving arterial oxygenation. Guideline Protocol: Strict lifelong antibiotic prophylaxis prior to dental procedures or invasive surgeries to prevent paradoxical septic emboli to the brain; use of in-line intravenous bubble filters on all IV lines to block air emboli; avoid scuba diving permanently. Thresholds: Feeding artery diameter >=2-3 mm on contrast CT, or documented paradoxical cerebral embolic event mandates immediate transcatheter percutaneous embolotherapy.

patient_plain_language: A pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (PAVM) is an abnormal direct tangle between a blood vessel carrying blood into your lungs and one carrying it away, bypassing the lung's normal microscopic filtering net (capillaries). Because this natural filter is skipped, tiny blood clots or bacteria can slip straight through to your brain, causing strokes or brain infections. Treating it involves plugging the abnormal connection with tiny coils.

title: Barrett's Esophagus: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (AIM Dysplasia Trial) & ACG Guidelines)
snippet: In the landmark multicenter sham-controlled AIM Dysplasia trial (n=127 patients with dysplastic Barrett's esophagus), radiofrequency ablation (RFA) resulted in complete eradication of low-grade dysplasia in 90.5% of patients (vs 22.7% sham; p<0.001) and complete eradication of high-grade dysplasia in 81.0% (vs 19.0% sham; p<0.001) at 12 months. RFA was associated with less disease progression (3.6% vs 16.3%; p=0.03) and fewer esophageal adenocarcinomas (1.2% vs 9.3%; p=0.045). Continuous high-dose proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy reduces risk of progression to neoplastic dysplasia by 71% (OR 0.29; 95% CI 0.12-0.79). Guideline Protocol: Elevation of head of bed by 6 inches; avoidance of recumbency within 3 hours of meals; cessation of tobacco; weight reduction targeting BMI <25 kg/m2. Thresholds: Confirmation of low-grade or high-grade dysplasia by an expert gastrointestinal pathologist triggers endoscopic radiofrequency ablation (RFA) or endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR).

Over years of acid exposure, the normal pale pink esophageal lining changes into a salmon-pink tissue that resembles the lining of your intestines. It requires regular camera checks (endoscopies) because of a small risk of developing cancer.

title: Achalasia: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (POEM vs LHM) & ACG Guidelines)
snippet: In the landmark multicenter randomized noninferiority trial (n=221 patients with treatment-naive achalasia followed for 2 years), peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) was noninferior to laparoscopic Heller myotomy (LHM) plus Dor fundoplication with respect to clinical treatment success (Eckardt score <=3: 83.0% POEM vs 81.7% LHM; difference 1.4 percentage points; 95% CI -8.7 to 11.4; p=0.007 for noninferiority). Reflux esophagitis was more common after POEM at 2 years (44% vs 29%; p=0.03). High-resolution esophageal manometry (HRM) using the Chicago Classification (Type I, II, III) is the diagnostic gold standard; Type II achieves the highest treatment response (>90%). Guideline Protocol: Chewing food thoroughly into a fine liquid slurry; drinking carbonated or warm water with meals to facilitate gravity-assisted emptying; sleeping with head of bed elevated 30 degrees. Thresholds: Integrated relaxation pressure (IRP) >15 mmHg on high-resolution manometry combined with an Eckardt symptom score >3 indicates treatment failure requiring pneumatic dilation or repeat myotomy.

Food and liquids get stuck in your chest and back up into your throat.

title: Eosinophilic Esophagitis (EoE): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (Dupilumab EoE Trial) & ACG/AGA Guidelines)
snippet: In the landmark 3-part multicenter Phase 3 trial (n=321 patients aged >=12 with active EoE despite high-dose PPI therapy), subcutaneous dupilumab (300 mg weekly) achieved histologic remission (<=6 eosinophils per high-power field [HPF]) in 60% of patients compared to only 5% with placebo in Part A (p<0.001) and 59% vs 6% in Part B (p<0.001). Dupilumab significantly improved dysphagia symptom scores (-21.9 vs -9.6 points; p<0.001) and increased esophageal distensibility while reducing endoscopic visual scores (trachealization rings, furrows, exudates, and strictures). Swallowed topical fluticasone or budesonide suspension achieves histologic remission in 65-75% of patients. Guideline Protocol: Empiric food elimination diets (6-food elimination diet: milk, wheat, egg, soy, nuts, seafood; or stepped 2-food diet: dairy and gluten); eating slowly with copious sips of water; avoiding dry meats without sauce. Thresholds: Peak mucosal eosinophil count >=15 eosinophils/HPF on esophageal biopsy establishes diagnosis; esophageal luminal diameter <13 mm with food impactions warrants gentle serial endoscopic balloon dilation.

title: Gastroparesis (Diabetic & Idiopathic): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) Guidelines)
snippet: The ACG Gastroparesis Guidelines establish standardized 4-hour solid-phase gastric emptying scintigraphy (GES) with a low-fat egg meal as the diagnostic standard. Gastric retention >10% at 4 hours (or >60% at 2 hours) confirms delayed gastric emptying in the absence of mechanical obstruction. In diabetic gastroparesis, optimizing glycemic control (targeting HbA1c <7.0%) is critical, as acute hyperglycemia (>200 mg/dL) directly inhibits antral contractions. Metoclopramide remains the only FDA-approved oral prokinetic medication, but therapy must be limited to <12 weeks due to risk of tardive dyskinesia. Guideline Protocol: Dietary modification: 5-6 small-volume meals daily; low-fiber (<2-3 g/meal to prevent bezoar formation); low-fat (<40 g/day); caloric fluids (soups, shakes); walking for 15-30 minutes post-prandially. Thresholds: Gastric retention >35% at 4 hours classifies as severe gastroparesis; intractable vomiting resulting in dehydration, weight loss >10%, or electrolyte derangements warrants gastric electrical stimulation or G-POEM.

title: Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (Gastrinoma): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) & Lancet)
snippet: Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES) is caused by a neuroendocrine gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma), located predominantly within the 'gastrinoma triangle' (duodenum and pancreas). Approximately 25-30% of cases occur as part of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1). Hypergastrinemia causes marked hyperchlorhydria, resulting in severe refractory peptic ulcerations, gastroesophageal reflux, and secretory diarrhea (inactivation of pancreatic lipase by low pH). Diagnosis is established by fasting serum gastrin >1,000 pg/mL (in the presence of gastric pH <2) or a positive secretin stimulation test (rise in serum gastrin >120 pg/mL). High-dose PPI therapy eliminates acid hypersecretion and peptic complications in >98% of patients. Guideline Protocol: Zero alcohol and NSAID intake; 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT imaging for precision functional tumor localization; genetic screening for MEN1 (menin gene mutation) and serum calcium/PTH testing. Thresholds: Localized sporadic gastrinoma without distant liver metastases mandates surgical exploratory laparotomy, duodenotomy, and lymph node dissection for curative resection.

These tumors release large surges of a hormone called gastrin. The gastrin stimulates your stomach to produce massive amounts of burning acid, causing severe recurrent ulcers and chronic watery diarrhea.

title: Microscopic Colitis (Collagenous & Lymphocytic): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews & AGA Guidelines)
journal: Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews & AGA Guidelines
keywords: cochrane database of systematic reviews & aga guidelines
snippet: In a Cochrane systematic review of 11 randomized controlled trials (n=556 patients with collagenous or lymphocytic colitis), oral budesonide (9 mg daily for 6-8 weeks) was highly effective for induction of clinical remission compared with placebo (73% vs 22%; relative risk 3.01; 95% CI 2.18-4.14; p<0.00001; NNT = 2). Budesonide also provided significant histologic remission (RR 2.76; p<0.0001) and substantial quality of life improvements. Low-dose budesonide (3-6 mg daily) maintained clinical remission in 75% at 6 months (vs 25% placebo; p<0.0001). Diagnosis requires routine mucosal biopsies of normal-appearing colon (showing subepithelial collagen band >10 microns in collagenous colitis, or >20 intraepithelial lymphocytes per 100 enterocytes in lymphocytic colitis). Guideline Protocol: Discontinuation of offending drug triggers (NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs, and statins are strongly associated triggers); elimination of caffeine, artificial sweeteners (sorbitol/mannitol), and high-fat foods; smoking cessation. Thresholds: Persisting watery diarrhea (>3 stools/day) despite 8 weeks of budesonide warrants screening for concomitant celiac disease (present in 5-10%) and bile acid malabsorption.

title: Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (TARGET 1 & 2) & ACG SIBO Clinical Guideline)
snippet: The landmark double-blind Phase 3 TARGET 1 and TARGET 2 trials (n=1260 patients with IBS-D/SIBO) demonstrated that a 14-day course of oral rifaximin (550 mg three times daily) significantly improved global IBS/SIBO symptoms (40.7% vs 31.7% placebo; p<0.001) and relieved bloating (40.2% vs 30.3%; p<0.001) for up to 10 weeks post-treatment. Retreatment with rifaximin upon symptom recurrence maintains efficacy without generating antimicrobial resistance (TARGET 3). Standardized glucose or lactulose breath testing showing an early rise in hydrogen >=20 ppm within 90 minutes (or methane >=10 ppm, diagnostic of Intestinal Methanogen Overgrowth [IMO]) confirms the diagnosis. Guideline Protocol: Temporary low-FODMAP dietary protocol for 4-6 weeks to reduce substrate fermentation; spacing meals by 4-5 hours to promote Phase III migrating motor complex (MMC) motility; daily prokinetic support. Thresholds: Methane peak >=10 ppm on breath test indicates methanogen overgrowth (Methanobrevibacter smithii) requiring dual therapy (Rifaximin 550 mg TID + Neomycin 500 mg BID for 14 days).

title: Autoimmune Hepatitis: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (AASLD Guidelines & Journal of Hepatology)
snippet: Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH) is characterized by hypergammaglobulinemia (elevated IgG >1.1x ULN), circulating autoantibodies (ANA and SMA in Type 1; anti-LKM1 or anti-LC1 in Type 2), and interface hepatitis on liver biopsy. The Revised Original Score (>15 definite) and Simplified Diagnostic Criteria (>7 definite) achieve >95% diagnostic sensitivity and specificity. Combined induction therapy with prednisone (30-60 mg/day tapered) plus azathioprine (1-2 mg/kg/day) or budesonide (9 mg/day) produces complete biochemical remission (normalization of transaminases and IgG) in >85% of patients while minimizing corticosteroid adverse events. 10-year survival exceeds 90% with sustained biochemical remission. Guideline Protocol: Zero alcohol consumption; annual hepatitis A and B immunizations; screening for concurrent autoimmune diseases (thyroiditis in 15%, celiac disease in 5%). Thresholds: Failure of transaminases to decline by >50% within 4 weeks of therapy, or development of hepatic encephalopathy or coagulopathy (INR >1.5) triggers liver transplant evaluation.

patient_plain_language: Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic disease where your body's immune defense system mistakenly identifies your own liver cells as foreign invaders and attacks them. This causes continuous inflammation, swelling, and scarring of the liver. Without medication to quiet down the overactive immune system, it can eventually lead to permanent liver cirrhosis.

title: Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (POISE Trial) & AASLD Practice Guidance)
snippet: Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC, formerly cirrhosis) is an autoimmune destruction of intrahepatic interlobular bile ducts, characterized by antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA titer >=1:40, specificity >98%) and elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP). First-line therapy with ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA 13-15 mg/kg/day) normalizes survival when biochemical response is achieved (Paris II or Toronto criteria: ALP <1.67x ULN and normal bilirubin). In the landmark Phase 3 POISE trial (n=217 patients with inadequate response or intolerance to UDCA), adding obeticholic acid (5-10 mg daily) achieved the composite biochemical endpoint in 46-47% vs 10% placebo (p<0.001) with marked reductions in ALP, bilirubin, and liver fibrosis markers. Guideline Protocol: Adequate dietary calcium (1,200 mg/day) and vitamin D (800-2,000 IU/day) to prevent accelerated metabolic bone disease; gentle skin moisturizers and cool baths for severe pruritus. Thresholds: ALP >1.67x ULN or total bilirubin >ULN after 12 months on optimal UDCA therapy defines non-response, requiring second-line add-on therapy (PPAR agonists such as bezafibrate/elafibranor or obeticholic acid).

These ducts are tiny drainage tubes that carry bile (digestive fluid) out of the liver. When the tubes are damaged, toxic bile backs up inside the liver, causing liver scarring, deep fatigue, and severe skin itching.

title: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (AASLD Practice Guidelines & The Lancet)
snippet: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC) is a progressive fibro-obliterative disease of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD, present in 70-80% of patients, predominantly ulcerative colitis). Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) is the diagnostic imaging modality of choice, showing characteristic multifocal strictures and segmental dilatations ('beading' pattern) without diagnostic autoantibodies. Patients face a 400-fold increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma (lifetime risk 10-20%) and a marked risk of colorectal carcinoma (4-fold higher than IBD alone). Surveillance with annual MRCP + CA 19-9 and annual colonoscopy with random biopsies is mandatory. Guideline Protocol: Annual screening colonoscopy with random 4-quadrant biopsies from cecum to rectum for colorectal dysplasia; fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) supplementation; avoidance of alcohol. Thresholds: Rapid worsening of jaundice, fever, chills, or development of a 'dominant stricture' (diameter <1.5 mm in common bile duct or <1.0 mm in hepatic duct) mandates ERCP with brush cytology and FISH to exclude cholangiocarcinoma.

The bile tubes become stiff, blocked, and beaded like a string of knotted ropes. Because bile cannot drain into the intestines, it backs up, causing liver damage. It is closely linked to ulcerative colitis.

snippet: Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene on chromosome 13, leading to impaired biliary copper excretion and defective ceruloplasmin incorporation. Toxic copper accumulates sequentially in the liver, brain (basal ganglia/lenticular nuclei), cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings present in >95% of neurologic cases), and kidneys. Diagnostic hallmarks include decreased serum ceruloplasmin (<20 mg/dL), elevated 24-hour urinary copper excretion (>40-100 mcg/24h), and hepatic parenchymal copper concentration >250 mcg/g dry weight on liver biopsy. Leipzig diagnostic score >=4 establishes definitive diagnosis. Chelation therapy with penicillamine or trientine halts disease progression and reverses hepatic/neurologic deficits in >80%. Guideline Protocol: Strict lifelong avoidance of copper-rich foods (organ meats/liver, shellfish/oysters, dark chocolate, mushrooms, nuts); testing household drinking water for copper pipes; slit-lamp ophthalmologic exam. Thresholds: Acute fulminant liver failure (marked by Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia, AST:ALT ratio >2.2, and alkaline phosphatase to total bilirubin ratio <4.0) has near 100% mortality without emergent liver transplantation.

Instead of releasing extra copper into your digestive bile, the copper builds up in your liver and then spills over into your brain and eyes. This can cause liver damage, tremors, difficulty speaking, mood changes, and a distinctive golden-brown ring around the iris of your eye (Kayser-Fleischer ring).

snippet: Hereditary hemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive iron overload disorder caused primarily by homozygous C282Y mutations (or C282Y/H63D compound heterozygosity) in the HFE gene on chromosome 6, resulting in deficiency of the iron-regulatory peptide hepcidin. Unchecked ferroportin activity causes progressive intestinal iron hyperabsorption (2-4 mg/day vs 1 mg normal). Progressive iron deposition in hepatocytes, pancreatic islets, myocardium, pituitary, and synovium causes the classic 'bronze diabetes' tetrad (cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus, hyperpigmentation, and arthropathy). Diagnostic screening begins with fasting transferrin saturation (>45% in women, >50% in men) and serum ferritin (>200 ng/mL in women, >300 ng/mL in men), followed by HFE genetic testing. Therapeutic phlebotomy initiated prior to cirrhosis development restores normal life expectancy. Guideline Protocol: Avoidance of iron supplements, multivitamin preparations containing iron, and high-dose vitamin C (>500 mg/day, which accelerates iron absorption); absolute avoidance of raw or undercooked shellfish (prevents lethal Vibrio vulnificus septicemia); alcohol abstinence. Thresholds: Serum ferritin >1,000 ng/mL with elevated AST/ALT carries high risk of advanced bridging fibrosis or cirrhosis, mandating non-invasive elastography or liver biopsy.

Because your body has no natural way to get rid of extra iron, the iron builds up over decades in your liver, heart, pancreas, and joints. The standard treatment is simple and life-saving: regularly donating a pint of blood (therapeutic phlebotomy) to pull the excess iron out.

title: Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS-AKI): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (CONFIRM Trial) & AASLD Practice Guidance)
snippet: Hepatorenal syndrome acute kidney injury (HRS-AKI) is a severe form of functional renal failure occurring in advanced cirrhosis with ascites, driven by extreme splanchnic arterial vasodilation that triggers reflex renal vasoconstriction. In the landmark multicenter double-blind Phase 3 CONFIRM trial (n=300 patients with HRS-AKI), terlipressin plus IV albumin was significantly superior to placebo plus albumin in achieving verified HRS reversal (sustained serum creatinine <=1.5 mg/dL without renal replacement therapy for at least 10 days: 32% vs 17%; p=0.006). Terlipressin also improved renal function before liver transplantation (34% vs 17%; p=0.002). Definitive curative therapy remains orthotopic liver transplantation. Guideline Protocol: Immediate cessation of all diuretics (furosemide, spironolactone); absolute avoidance of nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, IV radiocontrast); diagnostic paracentesis to rule out spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). Thresholds: Increase in serum creatinine >=0.3 mg/dL within 48h (or >=50% from baseline) that fails to reverse after 48 hours of diuretic withdrawal and IV albumin volume expansion (1 g/kg/day, max 100 g/day) establishes HRS-AKI.

patient_plain_language: Hepatorenal syndrome is a severe medical emergency where the kidneys suddenly stop functioning properly because of advanced liver disease (cirrhosis). The damaged liver causes large blood vessels in your abdomen to widen excessively, stealing blood away from your kidneys. The kidneys react by clamping down their own blood vessels, shutting down urine production.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What is my current serum creatinine and has it improved after stopping water pills and receiving IV albumin?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Are my oxygen levels and lungs being closely monitored while receiving terlipressin to watch for fluid overload?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: What is my calculated MELD-Na score and has my liver transplant listing been expedited for dual liver-kidney allocation?

red_flags: Severe drop in urine output (scant or zero urine over 12 hours), progressive confusion (hepatic encephalopathy), shortness of breath, or blue fingers/toes

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Immediate cessation of all diuretics (furosemide, spironolactone); absolute avoidance of nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, IV radiocontrast); diagnostic paracentesis to rule out spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP).
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Serum creatinine, BUN, and electrolytes every 12-24 hours; continuous pulse oximetry and cardiopulmonary monitoring (monitoring for terlipressin-induced pulmonary edema and ischemic events); strict hourly urine output.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Increase in serum creatinine >=0.3 mg/dL within 48h (or >=50% from baseline) that fails to reverse after 48 hours of diuretic withdrawal and IV albumin volume expansion (1 g/kg/day, max 100 g/day) establishes HRS-AKI.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Hepatorenal syndrome is a type of progressive kidney failure that occurs in people with severe liver damage.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: The kidneys going into a state of shock and clamping their pipes shut because a scarred liver is hoarding all the body's blood flow.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Hospital ICU treatment required immediately. Stop all water pills. Strict fluid and sodium restriction.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: Terlipressin 0.85 mg IV every 6 hours (titrated to 1.7 mg q6h if Cr does not decrease by >=30% by day 4) PLUS Albumin 20-40 g/day.
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Terlipressin: Serious or fatal respiratory failure; monitor oxygenation and avoid in patients with severe fluid overload (SpO2 <90%).
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Contraindicated in patients with active coronary artery disease, peripheral ischemia, or severe hypoxia.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Verified HRS reversal doubled with terlipressin vs placebo (32% vs 17%; p=0.006); need for pre-transplant dialysis significantly reduced.

title: Hepatic Encephalopathy: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (Rifaximin HE Trial) & AASLD/EASL Guidelines)
snippet: Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) is a spectrum of neuropsychiatric abnormalities in patients with liver dysfunction and portosystemic shunting, driven by hyperammonemia crossing the blood-brain barrier and causing astrocyte swelling. In the landmark multicenter double-blind Phase 3 trial (n=299 patients in remission from recurrent HE), combination therapy with rifaximin (550 mg BID) plus lactulose significantly reduced the risk of an acute HE breakthrough episode by 58% compared with placebo over 6 months (22.1% vs 45.9%; hazard ratio 0.42; 95% CI 0.28-0.64; p<0.001; NNT = 4). Rifaximin also reduced HE-related hospitalizations by 50% (HR 0.50; p=0.01). First-line lactulose titration targeting 2-3 soft bowel movements daily remains the cornerstone. Guideline Protocol: Adequate daily dietary protein intake (1.2-1.5 g/kg/day, emphasizing dairy and vegetable proteins; protein restriction is harmful and worsens muscle wasting); search and correct precipitating factors (constipation, GI bleeding, infection, hypokalemia, sedatives). Thresholds: West Haven Grade III/IV encephalopathy (somnolence, confusion, or coma) requires emergency intensive care admission and airway protection (endotracheal intubation) to prevent aspiration.
key_takeaway: Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) is a spectrum of neuropsychiatric abnormalities in patients with liver dysfunction and portosystemic shunting, driven by hyperammonemia crossing the blood-brain barrier and causing astrocyte s...
patient_plain_language: Hepatic encephalopathy is a decline in brain function that happens when your liver is too damaged to filter out normal toxins from your blood. Toxic substances, especially ammonia produced by gut bacteria when digesting protein, build up in your bloodstream and travel to your brain. This causes forgetfulness, day-night sleep reversal, sluggish thinking, flapping hand tremors (asterixis), and confusion.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What is my current West Haven grade of encephalopathy, and are my lactulose doses producing 2 to 3 soft bowel movements every day?

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Adequate daily dietary protein intake (1.2-1.5 g/kg/day, emphasizing dairy and vegetable proteins; protein restriction is harmful and worsens muscle wasting); search and correct precipitating factors (constipation, GI bleeding, infection, hypokalemia, sedatives).
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: West Haven criteria mental status staging at each clinical review; Number Connection Test (NCT-A) or Animal Naming Test for minimal hepatic encephalopathy; serum electrolytes (especially potassium).
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: West Haven Grade III/IV encephalopathy (somnolence, confusion, or coma) requires emergency intensive care admission and airway protection (endotracheal intubation) to prevent aspiration.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Hepatic encephalopathy is a nervous system disorder caused by severe liver disease, where toxins build up in the blood and affect brain function.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: A toxic smog cloud reaching the brain because the liver's exhaust filter has broken down.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Take lactulose every single day without skipping doses. Maintain normal protein intake. Avoid all sleeping pills and tranquilizers.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: Lactulose 20-30 g (30-45 mL) orally 3-4 times daily titrated to achieve 2-3 soft bowel movements/day PLUS Rifaximin 550 mg BID.
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Lactulose: Excessive diuresis and diarrhea can cause severe hypernatremia, dehydration, and paradoxical worsening of HE.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Monitor serum electrolytes (sodium and potassium) frequently; hypokalemia worsens renal ammonia production.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Breakthrough HE episodes reduced by 58% (HR 0.42; p<0.001; NNT=4); hospitalizations reduced by 50% (HR 0.50; p=0.01).

title: Chronic Pancreatitis: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) Guidelines)
snippet: Chronic pancreatitis is an irreversible fibro-inflammatory syndrome resulting in progressive destruction of pancreatic exocrine parenchyma and islet architecture. Alcohol consumption and tobacco smoking act synergistically as the leading etiologic drivers (TIGAR-O classification). Cross-sectional imaging (CT, MRI/MRCP, or endoscopic ultrasound [EUS]) establishes the diagnosis via classic structural hallmarks: parenchymal calcifications, ductal dilatations with strictures (chain of lakes appearance), and intraductal calculi. Smoking cessation reduces the rate of disease progression and reduces the 12-fold elevated risk of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Antioxidant supplementation and high-dose pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) relieve pain and malabsorption. Guideline Protocol: Complete and permanent cessation of alcohol and tobacco smoking; 5-6 small meals daily; moderate healthy fat intake without extreme restriction; fat-soluble vitamin supplementation. Thresholds: Intractable opioid-dependent abdominal pain with a dilated main pancreatic duct (>=5-7 mm) warrants surgical drainage (Frey or Puestow procedure) or endoscopic stenting.

patient_plain_language: Chronic pancreatitis is long-term, permanent inflammation and scarring of your pancreas, the organ tucked behind your stomach that makes digestive juices and insulin. Over time, the constant inflammation destroys healthy pancreas tissue and causes chalky stones to form inside the pancreatic ducts. This leads to persistent upper belly pain, malabsorption, and weight loss.

doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Am I taking enough digestive enzymes with every meal to absorb my food and prevent weight loss?

solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Annual fecal elastase-1 testing (monitoring exocrine insufficiency); annual fasting blood glucose and HbA1c (screening for pancreatogenic Type 3c diabetes); annual contrast MRI/MRCP or EUS; bone mineral density every 2 years.

stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Absolute zero alcohol and tobacco. Eat small, frequent meals. Take digestive enzymes with the very first bite of every meal.

title: Pancreatic Exocrine Insufficiency (PEI): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews & United European Gastroenterology (UEG))
journal: Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews & United European Gastroenterology (UEG)
keywords: cochrane database of systematic reviews & united european gastroenterology (ueg)
snippet: Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (PEI) results when functional pancreatic enzyme secretion drops below 10% of physiological capacity, leading to severe fat and protein maldigestion. In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 randomized controlled trials (n=518 patients), enteric-coated pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) significantly increased the coefficient of fat absorption (CFA) by 13.9 percentage points compared with placebo (mean CFA 83.7% vs 69.8%; 95% CI 9.9-17.9; p<0.00001). PERT also improved coefficient of nitrogen absorption, relieved steatorrhea, and produced substantial weight gain. Fecal elastase-1 (FE-1) <200 mcg/g stool (severe if <100 mcg/g) is the non-invasive diagnostic standard (sensitivity 95% in moderate-to-severe PEI). Guideline Protocol: Do not restrict dietary fat (fat restriction exacerbates weight loss and fat-soluble vitamin depletion); consume 5-6 small energy-dense meals; take PERT capsules distributed throughout the meal rather than before or after. Thresholds: Fecal elastase-1 <100 mcg/g stool with persistent diarrhea or weight loss requires escalating PERT dosage (up to 75,000-80,000 lipase units/meal) and co-administration of a PPI to prevent gastric acid degradation of enzymes.

patient_plain_language: Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (PEI) means your pancreas does not produce enough digestive enzymes to break down the food you eat. Because dietary fats cannot be digested and absorbed, they pass straight through your bowels. This leads to large, greasy, pale, foul-smelling stools that float in the toilet bowl (steatorrhea), along with stomach rumbles, weight loss, and vitamin deficiencies.

doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: How many enzyme capsules should I take with large meals versus small snacks, and should I add a proton pump inhibitor to make them work better?

stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: Eating a healthy meal, but lacking the chemical scissors (enzymes) needed to cut up the food so your body can absorb it.

stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Pancrelipase: Do not exceed 2,500 lipase units/kg/meal or 10,000 units/kg/day to prevent fibrosing colonopathy.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: In patients with incomplete response, add Omeprazole 20 mg daily to increase duodenal pH and prevent gastric lipase denaturation.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Coefficient of fat absorption increased by 13.9% with PERT (p<0.00001); steatorrhea and abdominal cramping significantly reduced.

title: Cushing's Syndrome & Disease: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Endocrine Society & NEJM)
snippet: Cushing's syndrome results from prolonged, inappropriate tissue exposure to excess glucocorticoids, most commonly iatrogenic, or endogenous (Cushing's disease due to an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma in 70-80% of endogenous cases). Diagnostic confirmation requires at least two concordant first-line tests: 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC >3x ULN), late-night salivary cortisol (>2 elevated measurements, sensitivity/specificity >95%), or 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (serum cortisol post-dex >1.8 mcg/dL / >50 nmol/L). Plasma ACTH differentiates ACTH-dependent (>20 pg/mL) from ACTH-independent (<5 pg/mL, adrenal source) disease. First-line therapy for Cushing's disease is transsphenoidal pituitary adenomectomy (initial cure rate 70-85%). Guideline Protocol: Dietary sodium restriction (<2,000 mg/day); dietary calcium and vitamin D supplementation; blood pressure and glycemic optimization; psychological support for emotional lability. Thresholds: Severe hypercortisolemia with hypokalemia, opportunistic infections, severe psychosis, or acute thromboembolism warrants immediate medical adrenal suppression (Ketoconazole, Osilodrostat, or Metyrapone) followed by urgent surgery.
key_takeaway: Cushing's syndrome results from prolonged, inappropriate tissue exposure to excess glucocorticoids, most commonly iatrogenic, or endogenous (Cushing's disease due to an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma in 70-80% of endog...
patient_plain_language: Cushing's syndrome is a hormone disorder caused by having too much cortisol (the body's primary stress hormone) in your bloodstream for long periods. Cortisol is essential for life, but excessive amounts cause a rounded 'moon face', fat buildup on the back of the neck ('buffalo hump'), wide purple stretch marks across the belly, fragile skin that bruises easily, muscle weakness, and high blood pressure.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What did my 24-hour urine cortisol and midnight saliva cortisol tests show, and was my post-dexamethasone cortisol suppressed?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Is my excess cortisol coming from a pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease), an adrenal tumor, or an outside steroid medication?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Will I need temporary steroid replacement pills (hydrocortisone) after surgery while my remaining normal adrenal glands wake back up?

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Dietary sodium restriction (<2,000 mg/day); dietary calcium and vitamin D supplementation; blood pressure and glycemic optimization; psychological support for emotional lability.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Cushing syndrome is a disorder that occurs when your body makes too much of the hormone cortisol over a long period of time.

stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Limit sodium to prevent fluid retention. Protect thin skin from bruises. Engage in low-impact walking to rebuild leg muscle.

stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Monitor ECG for QTc prolongation with osilodrostat and ketoconazole; check liver enzymes weekly for ketoconazole.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Transsphenoidal pituitary surgery achieves 70-85% initial remission in microadenomas; osilodrostat normalizes UFC in 86% of persistent patients.

title: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison's Disease): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Endocrine Society & Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology)
snippet: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison's disease) is the destruction or dysfunction of the entire adrenal cortex, leading to combined deficiency of glucocorticoids (cortisol) and mineralocorticoids (aldosterone). Autoimmune adrenalitis (marked by 21-hydroxylase antibodies) accounts for >80-90% of cases in developed nations. Diagnostic gold standard is the high-dose synthetic ACTH (Cosyntropin 250 mcg) stimulation test; a peak serum cortisol <18 mcg/dL (<500 nmol/L) at 30 or 60 minutes establishes adrenal insufficiency, with plasma ACTH markedly elevated (>2x ULN). Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and generalized cutaneous hyperpigmentation (palmar creases, vermilion border, buccal mucosa) are pathognomonic hallmarks. Guideline Protocol: Mandatory medical alert bracelet ('Adrenal Insufficiency - Takes Steroids'); provision of an emergency injectable hydrocortisone kit (100 mg Act-O-Vial IM) with patient/family injection training; liberal dietary salt intake. Thresholds: Intercurrent physiological stress (fever >38°C, severe illness, dental surgery) requires immediate 'sick-day rules' (doubling or tripling oral hydrocortisone dose); major trauma or vomiting requires immediate 100 mg IM hydrocortisone.
key_takeaway: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison's disease) is the destruction or dysfunction of the entire adrenal cortex, leading to combined deficiency of glucocorticoids (cortisol) and mineralocorticoids (aldosterone). Autoimm...
patient_plain_language: Addison's disease is an autoimmune condition where your adrenal glands (tiny hormone factories sitting on top of your kidneys) become damaged and stop producing vital hormones called cortisol and aldosterone. Cortisol helps you handle stress and keep blood pressure steady, while aldosterone balances salt and water. Without these hormones, you develop deep fatigue, weight loss, salt cravings, low blood pressure, and a darkened skin tan.

doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Does my family know exactly how and when to inject my emergency 100 mg hydrocortisone rescue shot into my thigh muscle?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: How do I adjust my daily steroid pills (sick-day rules) when I catch the flu, have dental surgery, or develop a fever?

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Circadian hydrocortisone dosing combined with emergency sick-day education reduces adrenal crisis admissions by 60%; normal life expectancy restored.

title: Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn's Syndrome): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Endocrine Society & The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology)
journal: Endocrine Society & The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology
keywords: endocrine society & the lancet diabetes & endocrinology
snippet: Primary Aldosteronism (PA) is the most common cause of secondary hypertension, accounting for 5-10% of all hypertensive patients and >20% of resistant hypertension. Autonomous aldosterone secretion by an adrenal adenoma (Conn's syndrome, 35%) or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (60%) suppresses renin, causing sodium retention, potassium wasting, and target-organ damage disproportionate to blood pressure elevation (4-fold higher stroke, 6-fold higher myocardial infarction, and 12-fold higher atrial fibrillation risk). Initial screening requires the plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR >20-30 with plasma aldosterone >10-15 ng/dL). Confirmatory testing (oral sodium loading or saline infusion test) followed by adrenal venous sampling (AVS) accurately distinguishes unilateral from bilateral disease with >95% accuracy. Guideline Protocol: Dietary sodium restriction (<2,000 mg/day; high dietary sodium worsens aldosterone-mediated vascular and myocardial fibrosis); alcohol moderation; aerobic physical conditioning. Thresholds: Unilateral aldosterone hypersecretion confirmed by adrenal venous sampling (lateralization ratio >4:1 on AVS) indicates candidacy for curative laparoscopic unilateral adrenalectomy.

patient_plain_language: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) is a hormonal cause of severe high blood pressure. Your adrenal glands produce far too much of a hormone called aldosterone. Aldosterone tells your kidneys to hold onto excessive amounts of salt and water while dumping potassium into your urine. This drives blood pressure high and makes it resistant to standard blood pressure medications.

title: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM & The Lancet Neurology (Edaravone & Riluzole))
snippet: In the landmark double-blind Phase 3 MCI-186 trial (n=137 patients with early definite or probable ALS), intravenous edaravone (a free-radical scavenger, 60 mg daily in 28-day cycles) significantly slowed functional motor decline over 24 weeks compared with placebo, as measured by the Revised ALS Functional Rating Scale (ALSFRS-R mean difference 2.49 points; 95% CI 0.99-3.98; p=0.0013). Riluzole (50 mg BID) prolongs median survival or time to tracheostomy by 2-3 months (hazard ratio 0.65; p=0.002). Multidisciplinary specialized ALS clinic care and early non-invasive ventilation (NIV/BiPAP) when upright FVC <50% or sniff nasal pressure <40 cm H2O prolongs quality survival by >12 months. Guideline Protocol: Early speech-language pathology communication evaluation (eye-gaze communication devices); occupational therapy for adaptive eating utensils; nocturnal non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP); timely percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) feeding tube placement prior to FVC dropping <50%. Thresholds: Orthopnea, supine FVC drop >20%, or upright FVC <50% triggers immediate nocturnal BiPAP initiation; involuntary weight loss >10% with dysphagia triggers PEG tube placement.

patient_plain_language: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, often called Lou Gehrig's disease) is a progressive nervous system disease that affects motor nerve cells in your brain and spinal cord. These motor nerves control all your voluntary muscles. As the nerves gradually degenerate, the muscles they signal become weak, twitch (fasciculations), and shrink, making it difficult to walk, talk, swallow, and breathe.

title: Huntington's Disease: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (JAMA (First-HD Trial) & NEJM)
snippet: Huntington's disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat (>36 repeats; fully penetrant at >=40 repeats) in the HTT gene on chromosome 4, resulting in toxic huntingtin protein aggregation and profound striatal (caudate and putamen) GABAergic medium spiny neuron loss. The clinical triad comprises motor chorea, cognitive decline, and psychiatric disturbances. In the multicenter double-blind Phase 3 First-HD trial (n=90 patients), deuterated tetrabenazine (deutetrabenazine, a vesicular monoamine transporter 2 [VMAT2] inhibitor) significantly improved the Total Maximal Chorea score from baseline to week 12 compared with placebo (mean difference -2.5 units; 95% CI -3.7 to -1.3; p<0.001). Guideline Protocol: Physical therapy for gait stability and fall prevention; speech-language swallowing evaluation and modified food textures; genetic counseling protocol (Huntington's Disease Society of America guidelines) prior to predictive testing. Thresholds: UHDRS chorea score impairment interfering with activities of daily living or causing falls warrants VMAT2 inhibitor therapy (deutetrabenazine 6-48 mg/day or tetrabenazine 12.5-100 mg/day).

patient_plain_language: Huntington's disease is a genetic brain disorder caused by an inherited error in a single gene. Over time, it damages nerve cells in the central movement-control centers of your brain. It causes involuntary dancing or jerking movements (chorea), changes in personality, irritability, and gradual memory and reasoning challenges. Each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the gene.

title: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM & Journal of Neurosurgery (INPH Guidelines))
snippet: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) is a reversible cause of dementia characterized by the classic clinical triad of gait disturbance ('magnetic' gait: slow, wide-based, shuffling, glued to the floor), cognitive decline (subcortical psychomotor slowing), and urinary incontinence ('wet, wacky, and wobbly'). MRI demonstrates ventriculomegaly disproportionate to sulcal atrophy (Evans index >0.30) with tight high-convexity sulci and enlarged Sylvian fissures (Disproportionately Enlarged Subarachnoid-space Hydrocephalus [DESH]). Diagnostic CSF tap test (removal of 30-50 mL CSF via lumbar puncture) producing an objective >=20% improvement in 10-meter timed walking speed has >90% positive predictive value for surgical shunt success. Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunting with a programmable valve achieves long-term clinical gait improvement in >80% of patients. Guideline Protocol: Physical therapy for balance and gait rehabilitation; home fall safety modifications; pelvic floor exercises and scheduled voiding regimens for urinary urgency. Thresholds: Evans index >0.30 with positive tap test (>=20% improvement in walking speed or >=3 steps fewer on 10m walk) indicates immediate candidacy for surgical ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement.

patient_plain_language: Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) is a condition where normal fluid (cerebrospinal fluid) builds up inside the open fluid chambers (ventricles) of your brain. As the fluid chambers swell, they stretch the brain tissue that controls your walking, memory, and bladder control. The classic signs are a shuffling 'magnetic' walk (feet feeling glued to the floor), mild forgetfulness, and urgent bladder leaks. It is one of the few forms of dementia that can be reversed with a small drainage tube (shunt).

title: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews & The Lancet Neurology)
journal: Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews & The Lancet Neurology
keywords: cochrane database of systematic reviews & the lancet neurology
snippet: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated post-infectious polyradiculoneuropathy (most commonly following Campylobacter jejuni, CMV, EBV, or Zika virus infection) characterized by molecular mimicry attacking peripheral nerve myelin (AIDP) or axolemma (AMAN/AMSAN). Clinical hallmark is acute, rapidly progressive, symmetric ascending flaccid paralysis with areflexia. Lumbar puncture demonstrates classic 'albuminocytological dissociation' (elevated CSF protein >0.45 g/L with normal white blood cell count <10 cells/mcL). In a Cochrane systematic review of randomized trials (n=585 patients), intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days) was equally effective as plasma exchange (PE 200-250 mL/kg over 5 sessions) in accelerating motor recovery and reducing mechanical ventilation (RR 1.05; 95% CI 0.73-1.53), with fewer adverse events. Corticosteroids alone are ineffective and harmful. Guideline Protocol: Admission to ICU or step-down unit with continuous telemetry (monitoring for life-threatening autonomic instability: labile blood pressure, cardiac arrhythmias); physical and occupational therapy for contracture prevention; venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis. Thresholds: Rapidly progressive weakness within 2-4 weeks of onset with inability to walk unassisted (Erasmus GBS Respiratory Insufficiency Score [EGRIS] >3) warrants immediate initiation of IVIG (2 g/kg total dose over 5 days) or plasma exchange.

It causes tingling and numbness that starts in your toes and feet and rapidly spreads upward into your legs, arms, and chest, causing temporary weakness or paralysis.

title: Myasthenia Gravis: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (MGTX Trial) & REGAIN Trial)
snippet: Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder of neuromuscular junction transmission caused predominantly by pathogenic autoantibodies against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (AChR-Ab, present in 85%), muscle-specific kinase (MuSK-Ab, 5-8%), or LRP4. Hallmark is fatigable muscle weakness that worsens with repetitive activity and improves with rest. In the landmark international randomized trial of thymectomy (MGTX, n=126 patients with non-thymomatous generalized AChR-positive MG aged 18-65), extended transsternal thymectomy combined with prednisone significantly improved the Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis (QMG) score over 3 years (mean score 6.15 vs 8.99; p<0.001) and lowered average daily prednisone dose (44 mg vs 60 mg; p<0.001) compared with prednisone alone. In refractory generalized MG, complement C5 inhibition (eculizumab) or neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) blockers (efgartigimod) produce rapid, robust clinical improvements. Guideline Protocol: Rest periods before meals to preserve chewing/swallowing strength; avoidance of medications that block neuromuscular transmission (fluoroquinolones, macrolides, aminoglycosides, beta-blockers, magnesium, and immune checkpoint inhibitors). Thresholds: Myasthenic crisis (acute respiratory failure from diaphragmatic weakness or severe bulbar failure) requires immediate ICU admission, non-invasive ventilation or intubation, and rapid rescue therapy with plasma exchange (5 sessions) or IVIG.

patient_plain_language: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder where your immune system mistakenly blocks or destroys the receptors on your muscles that receive signals from your nerves. Without these communication receptors, your muscles get tired and weak very quickly when used. The most common signs are a droopy eyelid (ptosis), double vision, difficulty chewing solid food, slurred speech, and muscle fatigue that improves after a short nap.

title: Trigeminal Neuralgia: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (American Academy of Neurology (AAN) & European Academy of Neurology (EAN))
journal: American Academy of Neurology (AAN) & European Academy of Neurology (EAN)
keywords: american academy of neurology (aan) & european academy of neurology (ean)
snippet: Trigeminal neuralgia (TN, tic douloureux) is characterized by paroxysmal, brief (lasting fractions of a second to 2 minutes), severe, unilateral, electric shock-like, shooting facial pains strictly distributed along one or more divisions of the trigeminal nerve (most commonly V2 maxillary and V3 mandibular). Pain is triggered by innocuous light cutaneous touch (brushing teeth, light breeze, chewing, talking). Classic TN is driven by neurovascular compression of the trigeminal nerve root entry zone by an aberrant arterial loop (most commonly the superior cerebellar artery [SCA]), identifiable on 3D high-resolution T2/constructive interference MRI (3D-CISS/FIESTA). First-line pharmacological therapy with sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine 200-1200 mg/day or oxcarbazepine 600-1800 mg/day) achieves initial pain control in >80% of patients. Microvascular decompression (MVD, Janetta procedure) achieves long-term pain freedom without sensory loss in >70-80% at 5 years. Guideline Protocol: Identification and gentle avoidance of trigger zones (washing face with warm water rather than cold; using a soft-bristled toothbrush; wearing a scarf to block cold wind exposure). Thresholds: Refractory pain despite therapeutic antiepileptic drug titration or drug intolerance warrants neurosurgical evaluation for microvascular decompression (MVD) or stereotactic Gamma Knife radiosurgery.

A pulsating blood vessel presses against the trigeminal nerve, the main sensation cable connecting your face to your brain. This wears away the nerve's protective insulation, so even the lightest brush—like a gentle gust of wind, chewing food, or brushing your teeth—triggers blinding, lightning-bolt pain across your cheek, jaw, or mouth.

title: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor Cerebri): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (JAMA (NORDIC Trial) & Cochrane Database)
snippet: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH, formerly pseudotumor cerebri) is characterized by elevated intracranial pressure (>250 mm H2O in adults) without hydrocephalus, mass lesion, or abnormal CSF composition, predominantly affecting young obese females of childbearing age. Modified Dandy criteria require papilledema, normal neurological exam (except 6th cranial nerve abducens palsy), and MRI showing neuroimaging signs of raised ICP (empty sella turcica, flattening of posterior sclerae, distension of perioptic subarachnoid space, and bilateral transverse venous sinus stenosis). In the landmark multicenter double-blind IIHTT trial (n=165 patients with mild visual field loss), high-dose acetazolamide (titrated up to 4 g daily) plus a low-sodium weight-reduction diet produced significantly greater improvement in visual field perimetric mean deviation (MD: +1.43 dB; p=0.04) and papilledema grade (mean reduction -0.70 Frisén units; p<0.001) compared with diet alone. Weight reduction of 10-15% cures IIH in >70%. Guideline Protocol: Structured multidisciplinary weight loss program (GLP-1 receptor agonists or bariatric surgery) targeting 10-15% total body weight reduction; strict dietary sodium restriction (<2,000 mg/day); avoidance of contributing drugs (tetracyclines, excess vitamin A/retinoids, and recombinant growth hormone). Thresholds: Progressive visual field loss (perimetric mean deviation worsening to <-7 dB) or fulminant IIH with severe vision decline within 4 weeks requires emergent surgical intervention (optic nerve sheath fenestration [ONSF] or transverse sinus stenting).

patient_plain_language: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) is a condition where high pressure builds up inside your skull, acting just like a brain tumor even though no actual tumor exists. The fluid that cushions your brain (cerebrospinal fluid) cannot drain away quickly enough, putting high pressure on your optic nerves (the cables connecting your eyes to your brain). This causes daily throbbing headaches, whooshing sounds in your ears (pulsatile tinnitus), and brief blackouts in your vision when bending over.

title: Cluster Headache: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (JAMA & The Lancet Neurology (High-Flow O2 & Verapamil))
journal: JAMA & The Lancet Neurology (High-Flow O2 & Verapamil)

snippet: Cluster headache is the most severe primary headache disorder, classified as a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia (TAC) characterized by strictly unilateral, excruciating, piercing/boring orbital or supraorbital pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes, accompanied by prominent ipsilateral cranial autonomic features (conjunctival injection, lacrimation, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, forehead sweating, and partial Horner's syndrome [ptosis and miosis]). In the landmark double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial (n=109 patients with 150 attacks treated), high-flow 100% normobaric oxygen (12 L/min via non-rebreather face mask for 15 minutes) rendered 78% of patients pain-free at 15 minutes compared with only 20% on medical air placebo (p<0.001; NNT = 1.7). Subcutaneous sumatriptan (6 mg) provides rapid abortion in >75% within 15 minutes. First-line preventative therapy is high-dose verapamil (240-960 mg/day). Guideline Protocol: Absolute avoidance of all alcohol during active cluster bouts (alcohol triggers an attack within 45 minutes in >90% of active patients); avoidance of volatile chemical fumes, petroleum solvents, and daytime naps. Thresholds: Occurrence of >=2 cluster attacks per day warrants immediate bridging steroid burst (prednisone 60-80 mg daily tapered over 2-3 weeks) while concurrently titrating verapamil maintenance.

patient_plain_language: Cluster headaches are excruciatingly painful headaches known as 'suicide headaches' due to their extreme severity. The pain attacks strike like an ice-pick stabbing into or around one eye, lasting from 30 minutes to 3 hours, often waking you from sleep at the exact same hour every night. During an attack, the affected eye tears up, the eyelid droops, and your nose becomes stuffed or runny. Sufferers are intensely restless, pacing the room rather than lying still.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Do I have a home medical prescription for a high-flow 100% oxygen cylinder (with a 12-15 L/min regulator and non-rebreather face mask)?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Has my ECG been checked before increasing my verapamil dose to ensure my heart's electrical timing (PR interval) is safe?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Can I use subcutaneous sumatriptan injections or nasal zolmitriptan sprays alongside my oxygen tank for immediate abortive relief?

red_flags: Sudden thunderclap onset of maximal pain in <1 minute (rule out subarachnoid hemorrhage), permanent vision changes, or high fever with stiff neck

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Absolute avoidance of all alcohol during active cluster bouts (alcohol triggers an attack within 45 minutes in >90% of active patients); avoidance of volatile chemical fumes, petroleum solvents, and daytime naps.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Baseline and serial 12-lead ECG monitoring every 2 weeks during verapamil dose titration to detect PR-interval prolongation and heart block; tracking attack diary.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Occurrence of >=2 cluster attacks per day warrants immediate bridging steroid burst (prednisone 60-80 mg daily tapered over 2-3 weeks) while concurrently titrating verapamil maintenance.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Cluster headaches are a series of relatively short but extremely painful headaches that occur in cycles or bouts.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: A red-hot poker being driven directly into one eye socket on a clockwork schedule every night.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Zero alcohol during cluster periods. Keep an oxygen tank beside your bed. Do not lie down during attacks; pacing helps.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: Acute: 100% O2 at 12-15 L/min via non-rebreather mask for 15 min + Sumatriptan 6 mg SC. Prevention: Verapamil 240-480 mg daily.
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Sumatriptan: Coronary vasospasm, myocardial infarction, and ventricular arrhythmias; contraindicated in ischemic heart disease or uncontrolled hypertension.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Monitor baseline and serial ECGs with verapamil; hold if PR interval exceeds 0.20 seconds.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Pain freedom at 15 minutes achieved in 78% with high-flow oxygen vs 20% placebo (p<0.001; NNT=1.7); zero adverse events.

title: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (CHANCE & POINT Trials) & AHA/ASA Guidelines)
snippet: A Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) is a transient episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia, without acute infarction on diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI). TIA carries an immediate 10-15% risk of disabling ischemic stroke within 90 days, with half occurring within the first 48 hours. In the landmark POINT (n=4881) and CHANCE (n=5170) trials in high-risk TIA (ABCD2 score >=4) or minor stroke, dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT: Aspirin 81 mg + Clopidogrel 300-600 mg load then 75 mg daily) initiated within 12-24 hours and continued for exactly 21 days significantly reduced subsequent major ischemic stroke by 25-32% compared with aspirin monotherapy (HR 0.68-0.75; p<0.001) without a significant excess in major hemorrhage when capped at 21 days. Guideline Protocol: Immediate admission to an emergency acute stroke unit or rapid-access TIA clinic; immediate carotid duplex ultrasound (carotid endarterectomy within 7-14 days if symptomatic 70-99% stenosis); Mediterranean diet; smoking cessation. Thresholds: ABCD2 score >=4 (Age >=60 [1], BP >=140/90 [1], Clinical unilateral weakness [2] or speech impairment [1], Duration >=60m [2] or 10-59m [1], Diabetes [1]) mandates immediate DAPT and inpatient observation.

patient_plain_language: A transient ischemic attack (TIA), often called a 'warning stroke' or 'mini-stroke', occurs when blood flow to part of your brain is briefly blocked by a small traveling blood clot. The symptoms—such as a droopy face, weak arm, or slurred speech—may disappear completely after a few minutes, but a TIA is an emergency warning that a major, permanent stroke could strike within the next 48 hours.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What was my ABCD2 stroke risk score, and did my brain MRI show any hidden tiny strokes on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI)?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Am I on the 21-day dual blood thinner combination (aspirin plus clopidogrel) to protect me from a major stroke during the high-risk window?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Did my ultrasound or CT scan show narrowing in my carotid neck arteries that requires a surgical cleaning procedure (endarterectomy)?

red_flags: Sudden facial drooping, arm numbness or weakness, speech slurring or confusion, sudden vision loss in one eye, or sudden balance loss (F-A-S-T signs)

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Immediate admission to an emergency acute stroke unit or rapid-access TIA clinic; immediate carotid duplex ultrasound (carotid endarterectomy within 7-14 days if symptomatic 70-99% stenosis); Mediterranean diet; smoking cessation.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: ABCD2 risk score calculation at triage; continuous cardiac telemetry for >=24-48 hours (or 30-day mobile cardiac outpatient telemetry) to detect occult atrial fibrillation; brain MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI); lipid panel.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: ABCD2 score >=4 (Age >=60 [1], BP >=140/90 [1], Clinical unilateral weakness [2] or speech impairment [1], Duration >=60m [2] or 10-59m [1], Diabetes [1]) mandates immediate DAPT and inpatient observation.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: A transient ischemic attack is a temporary blockage of blood flow to the brain, serving as a critical warning sign for a major stroke.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: A temporary power flicker in the brain's grid caused by a passing clot, warning of a total blackout if not treated immediately.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Call 911 immediately even if symptoms completely clear. Take blood thinners as prescribed for the full 21 days.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: DAPT for 21 days: Clopidogrel 300 mg load, then 75 mg daily PLUS Aspirin 81 mg daily, transitioning to monotherapy on day 22.
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Clopidogrel: Diminished antiplatelet effect in patients who are CYP2C19 poor metabolizers; consider alternative (ticagrelor).
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Initiate high-intensity statin (Atorvastatin 80 mg daily) immediately regardless of baseline LDL-C.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Subsequent ischemic stroke reduced by 28% with 21-day DAPT vs aspirin alone (5.0% vs 6.5%; HR 0.72; p=0.001); risk reduction front-loaded.

title: Vascular Dementia: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Stroke (AHA/ASA Scientific Statement) & Cochrane)
snippet: Vascular Cognitive Impairment and Dementia (VCID) is the second most common form of dementia, encompassing multi-infarct dementia, strategic single-infarct dementia, and subcortical ischemic vascular dementia (Binswanger's disease driven by arteriolosclerosis). Brain MRI is the diagnostic modality of choice, revealing extensive confluent periventricular white matter hyperintensities (Fazekas Grade 3), multiple lacunar infarcts, and microbleeds on susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI). Unlike the insidious memory-predominant course of Alzheimer's, vascular dementia classically presents with stepwise cognitive decline, prominent dysexecutive syndrome (impaired planning, sequencing, processing speed), and early psychomotor and gait slowing. Aggressive vascular risk reduction (BP <130/80 mmHg with ACEi/ARBs, statins, and antiplatelet therapy) halts further microvascular accumulation. Guideline Protocol: Mediterranean-DASH Diet Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay (MIND diet); 150 minutes/week of structured aerobic exercise; cognitive stimulation therapy; fall prevention home modifications. Thresholds: MoCA score <26 with executive deficits (Trail Making Test B impairment) and Fazekas Grade 2-3 white matter changes establishes subcortical vascular cognitive impairment.

patient_plain_language: Vascular dementia is memory and thinking loss caused by reduced blood flow to the brain, often following multiple silent 'mini-strokes' or long-term narrowing of tiny blood vessels in the brain. Unlike other dementias that primarily start with memory loss, vascular dementia often starts with slowed thinking, difficulty planning and organizing daily tasks, and a hesitant, unsteady walking gait.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What is my Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score, particularly on the executive planning and clock-drawing sections?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Does my brain MRI show extensive white matter damage or silent lacunar strokes, and is my blood pressure strictly controlled?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Would a cholinesterase inhibitor medication (such as donepezil) be beneficial if there is mixed Alzheimer's and vascular disease?

red_flags: Sudden stepwise drop in mental clarity, sudden new weakness or numbness on one side of the body, difficulty swallowing, or frequent unexplained falls

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Mediterranean-DASH Diet Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay (MIND diet); 150 minutes/week of structured aerobic exercise; cognitive stimulation therapy; fall prevention home modifications.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA, superior to MMSE for executive dysfunction) every 6 months; annual brain MRI tracking progression of white matter hyperintensities; home blood pressure logs.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: MoCA score <26 with executive deficits (Trail Making Test B impairment) and Fazekas Grade 2-3 white matter changes establishes subcortical vascular cognitive impairment.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Vascular dementia is a decline in thinking skills caused by conditions that block or reduce blood flow to various regions of the brain.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: A city grid suffering rolling localized brownouts because the small electrical cables supplying power to neighborhoods are narrowed and failing.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Keep blood pressure strictly under 130/80. Walk 30 minutes every day. Follow the Mediterranean brain-healthy diet.

stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Antipsychotics in dementia: Increased risk of all-cause mortality and ischemic cerebrovascular adverse events.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil 5-10 mg daily) show modest cognitive benefits in mixed vascular dementia; check for bradycardia.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Intensive blood pressure lowering (SBP <120 vs <140 mmHg) in SPRINT-MIND reduced mild cognitive impairment risk by 19% (HR 0.81; p=0.007).

title: Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Neurology (DLB Consortium Guidelines))
snippet: Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB) is pathologically characterized by widespread neuronal alpha-synuclein inclusions (Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites) throughout the neocortex, paralimbic, and brainstem structures. Core clinical features require: (1) fluctuating cognition with pronounced variations in attention and alertness; (2) recurrent, complex, well-formed visual hallucinations (present in >80%); (3) REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD: dream enactment, kicking/punching during sleep, preceding dementia by years); and (4) one or more spontaneous cardinal features of parkinsonism (bradykinesia, rigidity, rest tremor). Indicative biomarkers include reduced dopamine transporter (DaT) uptake in basal ganglia on DaTscan SPECT (sensitivity 78%, specificity 90%) and preserved temporal lobe structures on MRI. Patients exhibit severe neuroleptic sensitivity (up to 50% suffer acute severe parkinsonism, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, or death when exposed to typical antipsychotics). Guideline Protocol: Bed safety modifications for REM sleep behavior disorder (placing mattress on floor, removing sharp nightstands); gentle lighting and reassurance for visual hallucinations without challenging reality; physical therapy for parkinsonian gait. Thresholds: Severe REM sleep behavior disorder causing traumatic injury warrants low-dose melatonin (3-12 mg) or clonazepam (0.25-0.5 mg); cognitive impairment responds robustly to cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil/rivastigmine).
