patient_plain_language: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is a progressive brain condition caused by abnormal microscopic protein deposits called Lewy bodies forming inside your brain cells. It causes memory and thinking problems that fluctuate dramatically from hour to hour, realistic visual hallucinations (often seeing people or animals that are not there), physically acting out dreams while asleep (kicking or shouting), and Parkinson's-like stiffness and shuffling.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Does my brain DaTscan or FDG-PET scan show the distinctive loss of dopamine transporters in the basal ganglia confirming Lewy body disease?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Is my medical chart clearly flagged with an allergy alert to NEVER give me standard antipsychotic tranquilizers (like haloperidol)?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: How will we balance taking carbidopa/levodopa for my motor stiffness without worsening my visual hallucinations?

red_flags: Acute severe muscle rigidity with high fever and altered consciousness after receiving an anti-nausea or psychiatric pill (Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome)

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Bed safety modifications for REM sleep behavior disorder (placing mattress on floor, removing sharp nightstands); gentle lighting and reassurance for visual hallucinations without challenging reality; physical therapy for parkinsonian gait.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Quarterly clinical tracking of cognitive fluctuations, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, and UPDRS motor scores; bone mineral density scan (high fall and fracture risk); formal depression screening.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Severe REM sleep behavior disorder causing traumatic injury warrants low-dose melatonin (3-12 mg) or clonazepam (0.25-0.5 mg); cognitive impairment responds robustly to cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil/rivastigmine).

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies is a progressive dementia that leads to a decline in thinking, reasoning, and independent function, combined with movement problems.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: Protein clumps cluttering brain wiring, causing fluctuating mental brownouts, visual hallucinations, and dream-enacting sleep.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Pad bedroom walls and bedside floor. Avoid all older psychiatric sedatives. Maintain steady daily routines.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: First-line: Donepezil 5-10 mg daily or Rivastigmine patch 4.6-9.5 mg/24h. For motor parkinsonism: Low-dose Carbidopa/Levodopa 25/100 mg TID.
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Antipsychotics: Severe neuroleptic sensitivity; typical neuroleptics (haloperidol) can trigger irreversible rigidity and fatal cardiovascular collapse.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: If an antipsychotic is absolutely necessary for distressing psychosis, only Quetiapine (12.5-25 mg) or Pimavanserin is tolerated.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Cholinesterase inhibitors improve cognitive fluctuation and attention scores by 30%; DaTscan provides 90% diagnostic specificity vs Alzheimer's.

title: Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Brain & The Lancet Neurology (FTDC Criteria))
snippet: Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD / Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration [FTLD]) is the most common cause of early-onset dementia in patients <65 years, pathologically driven by tau inclusions (Pick bodies), TDP-43, or FUS aggregates. The behavioral variant (bvFTD) is diagnosed via the international FTDC criteria requiring at least 3 of 6 core features: (1) early behavioral disinhibition (socially inappropriate actions, loss of manners); (2) early apathy or inertia; (3) early loss of empathy or sympathy; (4) early perseverative, stereotyped, or compulsive behavior; (5) hyperorality and dietary changes (gluttony, sweet cravings); and (6) executive cognitive deficits with relative sparing of episodic memory and visuospatial function. Structural MRI shows asymmetric knife-blade atrophy of frontal and anterior temporal lobes. Genetic mutations (C9orf72 hexanucleotide expansion, GRN, MAPT) account for 30-40% of familial cases. Guideline Protocol: Structured environmental routines; secure lockboxes for food and finances (protecting against hyperorality and impulsive financial disinhibition); specialized caregiver support groups and respite care; genetic counseling for first-degree relatives. Thresholds: Emergence of motor neuron disease features (fasciculations, muscle wasting, hyperreflexia indicating FTD-ALS overlap) or progressive dysphagia requires immediate multidisciplinary palliative and swallowing evaluation.
key_takeaway: Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD / Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration [FTLD]) is the most common cause of early-onset dementia in patients <65 years, pathologically driven by tau inclusions (Pick bodies), TDP-43, or FUS aggre...
patient_plain_language: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a group of brain disorders caused by nerve cell damage and shrinking in the front and side regions of your brain (the frontal and temporal lobes). Because these areas govern your personality, behavior, judgment, empathy, and language, FTD typically starts with major personality shifts—such as socially inappropriate comments, loss of sympathy for family, obsessive rituals, or a craving for sweets—often while memory remains intact.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Does my brain MRI show frontotemporal lobar atrophy, and should we order a C9orf72 genetic test for familial frontotemporal degeneration?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Why are standard Alzheimer's medications (like donepezil or memantine) not recommended, and could they make my behavioral symptoms worse?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: What medications (such as SSRIs like sertraline or trazodone) can help safely tone down compulsive habits and emotional agitation?

red_flags: Rapid muscle twitching, muscle wasting, and weakness in hands or legs (suspect FTD-ALS overlap), severe choking on food, or dangerous impulsive behaviors

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Structured environmental routines; secure lockboxes for food and finances (protecting against hyperorality and impulsive financial disinhibition); specialized caregiver support groups and respite care; genetic counseling for first-degree relatives.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Frontal Behavioral Inventory (FBI) and Clinical Dementia Rating scale modified for FTLD (CDR-FTLD) every 6 months; speech-language evaluation for primary progressive aphasia variants; annual caregiver burden assessments.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Emergence of motor neuron disease features (fasciculations, muscle wasting, hyperreflexia indicating FTD-ALS overlap) or progressive dysphagia requires immediate multidisciplinary palliative and swallowing evaluation.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Frontotemporal dementia is a group of disorders caused by progressive nerve cell loss in the brain's frontal lobes or its temporal lobes, affecting personality and speech.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: The brain's behavioral filter and social conductor wearing away, so personal judgment and emotional empathy are lost.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Secure bank accounts and credit cards. Lock the pantry if sweet bingeing occurs. Establish peaceful, consistent routines.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: SSRIs (Sertraline 50-150 mg daily or Paroxetine 20-40 mg daily) significantly reduce repetitive behaviors, disinhibition, and carbohydrate binging.
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Cholinesterase inhibitors (Donepezil/Galantamine): May worsen behavioral agitation in FTD; generally avoided.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Avoid typical antipsychotics; if low-dose atypical antipsychotics are required, obtain informed family consent.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Revised FTDC criteria achieve 95% sensitivity for pathologically confirmed bvFTD; SSRIs significantly reduce Frontal Behavioral Inventory scores.

title: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews & American Psychiatric Association)
journal: Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews & American Psychiatric Association
keywords: cochrane database of systematic reviews & american psychiatric association
snippet: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is characterized by intrusive, distressing, ego-dystonic thoughts, urges, or images (obsessions) that trigger repetitive mental or physical behaviors (compulsions) performed to neutralize anxiety, consuming >1 hour daily. In a comprehensive network meta-analysis of 54 randomized trials (n=6652 patients), Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) behavioral therapy combined with high-dose Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) was significantly superior to either intervention alone for reduction in Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) scores (standardized mean difference -1.18; 95% CI -1.45 to -0.91; p<0.0001). SSRI doses required for OCD are typically substantially higher than for major depression (e.g. Fluoxetine up to 80 mg/day, Sertraline up to 200 mg/day) and require 8-12 weeks to assess clinical response. Guideline Protocol: Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) psychotherapy: creating a graded hierarchy of feared triggers (in vivo and imaginal exposure) with deliberate, prolonged refusal to engage in neutralizing rituals; mindfulness techniques. Thresholds: Y-BOCS score >=24 indicates severe OCD; failure to respond to two successive trials of high-dose SSRIs for 12 weeks warrants augmentation with an atypical antipsychotic (Aripiprazole 2-10 mg or Risperidone 0.5-2 mg) or deep brain stimulation (DBS).

patient_plain_language: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a mental health condition driven by a cycle of obsessions and compulsions. Obsessions are unwanted, intrusive, frightening thoughts or doubts (like fears of germs, harm, or symmetry) that get stuck on repeat in your mind, triggering intense anxiety. Compulsions are repetitive mental acts or physical behaviors (like washing hands, checking door locks, or tapping) you feel driven to perform to relieve the anxiety.

doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Is my SSRI medication dose high enough for OCD, and have we allowed a full 8 to 12 weeks to judge whether it is working?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: How can I be connected with an OCD-specialist therapist trained in Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) therapy?

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) psychotherapy: creating a graded hierarchy of feared triggers (in vivo and imaginal exposure) with deliberate, prolonged refusal to engage in neutralizing rituals; mindfulness techniques.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) score tracking at baseline and every 4 weeks (clinical response defined as >=25-35% reduction in Y-BOCS); screen for co-occurring major depressive disorder and suicidality.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Y-BOCS score >=24 indicates severe OCD; failure to respond to two successive trials of high-dose SSRIs for 12 weeks warrants augmentation with an atypical antipsychotic (Aripiprazole 2-10 mg or Risperidone 0.5-2 mg) or deep brain stimulation (DBS).

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Obsessive-compulsive disorder is a common, chronic disorder in which a person has uncontrollable, recurring thoughts and behaviors that they feel the urge to repeat.

stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Monitor for QTc prolongation and anticholinergic side effects with tricyclic Clomipramine; check baseline ECG.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: ERP therapy combined with SSRIs achieves significant Y-BOCS reduction (SMD -1.18; p<0.0001); 65% achieve long-term clinical remission.

title: Panic Disorder & Agoraphobia: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews & Lancet Psychiatry)
journal: Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews & Lancet Psychiatry
keywords: cochrane database of systematic reviews & lancet psychiatry
snippet: Panic disorder is characterized by recurrent unexpected panic attacks (abrupt surges of intense fear or intense discomfort reaching a peak within minutes, with at least 4 of 13 autonomic symptoms: palpitations, sweating, trembling, dyspnea, choking sensation, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills/heat, paresthesias, derealization/depersonalization, fear of losing control, and fear of dying) followed by at least 1 month of persistent worry about further attacks or maladaptive avoidance behavior (agoraphobia). In a network meta-analysis of 87 randomized controlled trials (n=12,823 patients), Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT with interoceptive exposure) combined with an SSRI/SNRI achieved superior remission of panic attacks and reduction in agoraphobic avoidance compared with either treatment alone (odds ratio 2.45; 95% CI 1.72-3.48; p<0.0001). Long-term benzodiazepine monotherapy is discouraged due to tolerance and rebound panic. Guideline Protocol: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT): interoceptive exposure (deliberately inducing physical sensations like hyperventilation, spinning, or breath-holding to extinguish catastrophic misinterpretation of body cues); diaphragmatic breathing; elimination of caffeine and stimulants. Thresholds: PDSS score reduction >=40% denotes clinical response; absence of panic attacks for 12 consecutive months on maintenance SSRI therapy warrants considering very slow medication taper.

patient_plain_language: Panic disorder is an anxiety condition where you experience sudden, terrifying surges of overwhelming fear and physical sensations called panic attacks. Out of nowhere, your heart pounds rapidly, your chest tightens, you gasp for breath, and you feel like you are having a heart attack, fainting, or dying. Because these attacks strike without warning, many people develop agoraphobia—avoiding crowded places, stores, or driving out of fear of having another attack.

doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: How does interoceptive exposure therapy work in CBT to train my brain that racing heart sensations are harmless adrenaline rushes?

title: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews & JAMA Psychiatry)
journal: Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews & JAMA Psychiatry
keywords: cochrane database of systematic reviews & jama psychiatry
snippet: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is characterized by a pervasive pattern of emotional dysregulation, instability of interpersonal relationships, unstable self-image, marked impulsivity (spending, sex, substance abuse), recurrent suicidal behavior, gestures, or self-harm (NSSI), and chronic feelings of emptiness. In a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis of 33 randomized controlled trials (n=2256 patients), specialized psychotherapies—most notably Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT, standardized mean difference -0.34; p=0.005) and Mentalization-Based Therapy (MBT)—significantly reduced self-harm, suicidal gestures, emergency department visits, and BPD core symptom severity compared with treatment as usual. Pharmacotherapy has no primary disease-modifying FDA approval; low-dose second-generation antipsychotics or mood stabilizers offer modest adjunctive control for severe affective lability. Guideline Protocol: Comprehensive Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT): weekly individual therapy, weekly DBT skills training group (mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness), and between-session phone coaching; written crisis safety plan. Thresholds: Acute life-threatening self-harm or active suicidal crisis requires immediate safety planning and brief crisis stabilization; avoid prolonged psychiatric hospitalizations which cause regression.

Sufferers experience emotions like emotional third-degree burns—feeling emotional pain far more intensely and for longer than others. This leads to dramatic mood shifts, intense fears of abandonment, rocky relationships, impulsive actions, and self-harm when distress becomes overwhelming.

doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: How can I join a certified Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) skills training group to learn emotion regulation tools?

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Comprehensive Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT): weekly individual therapy, weekly DBT skills training group (mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness), and between-session phone coaching; written crisis safety plan.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Zanarini Rating Scale for Borderline Personality Disorder (ZAN-BPD) every 3 months; structured continuous suicide and self-harm risk assessments; regular review of medication polypharmacy.

title: Meniere's Disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery (AAO-HNS Guidelines))
snippet: Meniere's disease is an inner ear disorder pathologically characterized by endolymphatic hydrops (fluid distension of the endolymphatic system in the cochlea and vestibular labyrinth). The definitive diagnostic criteria established by AAO-HNS and the Bárány Society require: (1) two or more spontaneous episodes of rotational vertigo lasting between 20 minutes and 12 hours; (2) audiometrically documented low-to-medium frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the affected ear on at least one occasion before, during, or after an episode; and (3) fluctuating aural fullness or tinnitus in the affected ear. First-line conservative management with dietary sodium restriction (<1,500-2,000 mg/day) and oral diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide/triamterene) or betahistine reduces vertigo attack frequency in >70-80% of patients. Intratympanic dexamethasone or gentamicin is effective in refractory cases. Guideline Protocol: Strict daily dietary sodium restriction (<1,500-2,000 mg/day without sudden fluctuations); elimination of caffeine, alcohol, and excessive monosodium glutamate (MSG); vestibular rehabilitation therapy between acute attacks. Thresholds: Disabling Tumarkin 'otolithic drop attacks' (sudden falls without loss of consciousness) or intractable vertigo spells despite 3 months of medical therapy warrants intratympanic gentamicin chemical labyrinthectomy or surgical endolymphatic sac decompression.

patient_plain_language: Meniere's disease is an inner ear disorder caused by excess fluid pressure building up inside the hearing and balance chambers of your inner ear. This fluid buildup triggers sudden attacks of violent room-spinning dizziness (vertigo) that last for hours, accompanied by nausea, a roaring sound in your ear (tinnitus), a clogged feeling of pressure in the ear, and temporary loss of low-pitched hearing.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Does my audiogram hearing test show the classic low-frequency hearing loss that confirms Meniere's disease?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: What is my daily sodium limit, and should I take a mild water pill (diuretic) to prevent fluid pressure from building up in my inner ear?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: What rescue medication (like meclizine or sublingual ondansetron) should I carry with me at all times for acute vertigo attacks?

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Strict daily dietary sodium restriction (<1,500-2,000 mg/day without sudden fluctuations); elimination of caffeine, alcohol, and excessive monosodium glutamate (MSG); vestibular rehabilitation therapy between acute attacks.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Serial pure-tone audiometry at 3, 6, and 12 months; vestibular function testing (caloric testing and video head impulse test [vHIT]); vertigo attack diary tracking frequency and duration.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Disabling Tumarkin 'otolithic drop attacks' (sudden falls without loss of consciousness) or intractable vertigo spells despite 3 months of medical therapy warrants intratympanic gentamicin chemical labyrinthectomy or surgical endolymphatic sac decompression.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Meniere's disease is an inner ear disorder that causes episodes in which you feel as if you are spinning (vertigo), and you have fluctuating hearing loss.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: High water pressure inside the inner ear's delicate canals, disrupting both hearing and balance gyroscopes at the same time.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Limit sodium strictly under 2,000 mg daily. Spread water intake evenly. Keep emergency vertigo pills in your pocket.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: Prevention: Triamterene 37.5 mg / HCTZ 25 mg daily. Acute attacks: Meclizine 25-50 mg PO + Ondansetron 4-8 mg ODT.

stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Monitor serum electrolytes and renal function periodically on thiazide diuretics.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Dietary sodium restriction and diuretics control vertigo attack frequency in >75%; intratympanic gentamicin achieves >85% vertigo control.

title: Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SSNHL): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery & JAMA Otolaryngology)
journal: Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery & JAMA Otolaryngology
keywords: otolaryngology-head and neck surgery & jama otolaryngology
snippet: Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SSNHL) is an otologic emergency defined as a rapid sensorineural hearing loss of >=30 decibels (dB) across at least 3 contiguous audiometric frequencies occurring within a 72-hour window. Approximately 90% of cases are idiopathic, with vascular ischemia, viral labyrinthitis, or cochlear autoimmune reactions implicated. Immediate initiation of high-dose systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day, maximum 60 mg daily for 7-14 days followed by a taper) or intratympanic corticosteroid injections (dexamethasone 10-24 mg/mL or methylprednisolone) within the first 14 days achieves meaningful hearing recovery in 65-80% of patients. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) within 1 month of onset provides significant additional hearing gain (odds ratio 1.43). Gadolinium-enhanced brain MRI of the internal auditory canal (IAC) is mandatory to rule out vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma, found in 3-5%). Guideline Protocol: Immediate emergency audiology pure-tone audiometry within 24-48 hours; strict avoidance of loud noise exposure; hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) sessions within 2-4 weeks; contrast-enhanced MRI of internal auditory canals. Thresholds: Sensorineural hearing drop >=30 dB across 3 frequencies warrants immediate high-dose oral steroids; incomplete recovery (<10 dB improvement) at 2-3 weeks triggers salvage intratympanic steroid injections.

patient_plain_language: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (often called sudden deafness) is an ear emergency where you suddenly wake up with one ear completely blocked or hearing muffled, or notice the hearing vanish over a few hours. Many people mistakenly think their ear is just plugged with earwax or water, but it is actually damage to the nerve hair cells in your inner ear. Beginning steroid treatment within the first few days gives you the highest chance of getting your hearing back permanently.

doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Have we started high-dose oral prednisone immediately, or should we add direct steroid injections through my eardrum (intratympanic)?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Is an MRI scan of my internal auditory canals scheduled to rule out a benign acoustic neuroma tumor on the hearing nerve?

solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Repeat pure-tone audiometry at 2 weeks, 4 weeks, and 3 months to monitor decibel recovery and word recognition score (WRS); brain MRI with IAC protocol.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Sensorineural hearing drop >=30 dB across 3 frequencies warrants immediate high-dose oral steroids; incomplete recovery (<10 dB improvement) at 2-3 weeks triggers salvage intratympanic steroid injections.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Sudden deafness is an unexplained, rapid loss of hearing that happens all at once or over a few days.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: A blown fuse in the inner ear's electrical hearing microphone; emergency steroid treatment can reset the fuse if started within days.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Do not wait for it to clear. Go to an ENT specialist or emergency clinic immediately. Protect the ear from loud noises.

stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Delays beyond 2 to 4 weeks significantly reduce likelihood of hearing recovery, resulting in permanent deafness.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Monitor blood glucose in diabetic patients on high-dose steroids; intratympanic injection avoids systemic steroid side effects.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: High-dose corticosteroids started within 14 days achieve significant hearing recovery in 75%; salvage intratympanic injections restore hearing in 40% of non-responders.

title: Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (AION): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) & Ophthalmology)
snippet: Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (AION) is infarction of the optic nerve head supplied by the short posterior ciliary arteries, presenting as sudden, painless, unilateral vision loss accompanied by optic disc edema. It is critically bifurcated into: (1) Arteritic AION (A-AION, accounting for 10-15%), an ophthalmic emergency caused by Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) in patients >=50 years, marked by high ESR (>50-100 mm/h) and elevated CRP; and (2) Non-Arteritic AION (NA-AION, 85-90%), driven by nocturnal arterial hypotension and microvascular hypoperfusion in structurally crowded optic discs ('disc-at-risk': small or absent optic cup). Visual field testing classically reveals an inferior altitudinal visual field defect. In A-AION, emergent high-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3 days) is mandatory to prevent fellow eye blindness (which occurs in up to 50% within days if untreated). Guideline Protocol: Immediate ESR and CRP blood testing in all patients >=50; avoidance of nocturnal blood pressure overtreatment (avoid taking antihypertensives right before bedtime to prevent nocturnal hypotensive optic ischemia); CPAP for sleep apnea. Thresholds: Suspected Arteritic AION with scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, or ESR >50 mm/h warrants immediate emergency IV methylprednisolone prior to waiting for temporal artery biopsy results.

patient_plain_language: Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AION) is often described as a 'stroke of the optic nerve'. The small blood vessels carrying oxygen to the optic nerve (the main visual cable transmitting images from your eye to your brain) suddenly become blocked. This causes sudden, painless loss of vision in one eye, typically leaving the lower or upper half of your vision completely dark.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Were my ESR and CRP inflammation markers checked immediately to rule out Giant Cell Arteritis (temporal arteritis)?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Should I avoid taking my blood pressure medications right at bedtime to prevent my blood pressure from dipping too low while I sleep?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Do I have a 'crowded optic disc' in my other eye, and what steps should I take to protect my remaining good eye?

red_flags: Severe headache at the temples, pain when chewing food (jaw claudication), scalp tenderness when brushing hair, or sudden vision loss spreading to the other eye

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Immediate ESR and CRP blood testing in all patients >=50; avoidance of nocturnal blood pressure overtreatment (avoid taking antihypertensives right before bedtime to prevent nocturnal hypotensive optic ischemia); CPAP for sleep apnea.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Humphrey 24-2 visual field perimetry and optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL); temporal artery biopsy (minimum 2 cm specimen) within 1-2 weeks if arteritic form suspected.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Suspected Arteritic AION with scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, or ESR >50 mm/h warrants immediate emergency IV methylprednisolone prior to waiting for temporal artery biopsy results.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Ischemic optic neuropathy is a loss of vision caused by damage to the optic nerve from poor blood flow.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: A blood clot or drop in water pressure cutting off blood flow to the optic nerve cable, turning off half the picture.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Emergency eye clinic exam immediately. Never take blood pressure pills right at bedtime. Treat sleep apnea.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: For Arteritic AION: Methylprednisolone 1g IV daily for 3 days, followed by oral Prednisone 1 mg/kg daily. NA-AION: Aspirin 81 mg daily.
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: High-dose systemic steroids: Monitor for acute psychosis, acute peptic ulceration, and severe hyperglycemia.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) carry an FDA warning for NA-AION; avoid in patients with prior NA-AION in one eye.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Immediate IV steroids in Arteritic AION reduces fellow-eye blindness from 50% to <5%; NA-AION fellow eye involvement 15% at 5 years.

title: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Stroke (AHA Scientific Statement on CRAO) & Ophthalmology)
journal: Stroke (AHA Scientific Statement on CRAO) & Ophthalmology
keywords: stroke (aha scientific statement on crao) & ophthalmology
snippet: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) is an acute ischemic stroke of the eye, characterized by sudden, painless, profound monocular vision loss (visual acuity counting fingers or worse in >90%). Fundoscopy reveals a pale, edematous retina with the classic 'cherry-red spot' at the fovea (where the thin foveal retina allows the underlying red choroid to shine through). The AHA scientific statement emphasizes that CRAO must be triaged as an acute ischemic stroke code; the retina suffers irreversible ischemic infarction within 240 minutes (4 hours) of complete occlusion. Over 70% of CRAO patients have concurrent high-grade ipsilateral carotid artery stenosis or cardioembolic sources. Emergency intravenous thrombolysis (IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg) within 4.5 hours of symptom onset produces visual recovery in 37% vs 17% conventional conservative therapy (p=0.002). Guideline Protocol: Immediate emergency 911 activation and transport to a comprehensive stroke center; conservative bedside maneuvers (ocular massage with Goldman lens, rebreathing into a paper bag to induce hypercapnic vasodilation) while preparing thrombolysis; emergency anterior chamber paracentesis. Thresholds: Onset of visual loss <4.5 hours without contraindications warrants emergency evaluation for intravenous tissue plasminogen activator (IV alteplase) by the acute stroke neurology team.

patient_plain_language: Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is an eye stroke. Just like an ischemic stroke in the brain, a small traveling blood clot gets stuck in the main artery supplying blood and oxygen to your retina (the visual film lining the back of your eye). This causes sudden, painless blindness in one eye, like a dark window shade pulling shut. It is a critical medical emergency requiring immediate emergency room stroke evaluation.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Am I within the 4.5-hour time window to receive emergency clot-busting medication (IV tPA / alteplase)?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Did my emergency neck CT angiogram or carotid ultrasound show a severe blockage in my carotid artery?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: What blood thinner and cholesterol medication do I need to start immediately to prevent a major brain stroke?

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Immediate emergency 911 activation and transport to a comprehensive stroke center; conservative bedside maneuvers (ocular massage with Goldman lens, rebreathing into a paper bag to induce hypercapnic vasodilation) while preparing thrombolysis; emergency anterior chamber paracentesis.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Emergent non-contrast head CT and CT angiography (CTA) of head/neck vessels; continuous telemetry for atrial fibrillation; transthoracic/transesophageal echocardiogram (TTE/TEE); dilated retinal examination at 2-4 weeks to screen for iris neovascularization (neovascular glaucoma).
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Onset of visual loss <4.5 hours without contraindications warrants emergency evaluation for intravenous tissue plasminogen activator (IV alteplase) by the acute stroke neurology team.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Central retinal artery occlusion is a blockage of the blood flow in the central retinal artery that carries oxygen to the retina, causing sudden blindness.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: A stroke of the eye: a blood clot plugging the main pipe that powers the eye's visual camera screen.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Call 911 immediately. Treat this as an acute stroke. Every minute counts to preserve retinal nerve tissue.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: Within 4.5 hours: IV Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg; 10% bolus over 1 min, remaining 90% over 60 min). Secondary: High-intensity statin + Aspirin.
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Alteplase: Intracranial hemorrhage and fatal systemic bleeding; strict adherence to stroke thrombolysis exclusion criteria.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Screen for neovascular glaucoma with panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) or anti-VEGF if ocular neovascularization develops.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours improves visual recovery rate from 17% to 37% (p=0.002); stroke workup identifies surgical carotid stenosis in >25%.

title: Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Ophthalmology (AAO Preferred Practice Pattern) & Cochrane)
snippet: Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (RRD) is an ophthalmic surgical emergency occurring when a full-thickness retinal tear or break (rhegma), most commonly triggered by posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) or lattice degeneration in myopic eyes, allows liquefied vitreous fluid to dissect into the subretinal space, separating the neurosensory retina from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Cardinal premonitory symptoms include sudden photopsia (flashes of light), sudden shower of black floaters, and a progressive dark peripheral curtain/shadow advancing toward the central vision. In the primary repair of uncomplicated RRD, surgical reattachment via pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) or scleral buckle achieves primary anatomic reattachment in >85-90% of cases and final attachment in >95%. Preserving visual acuity depends critically on whether the macula is still attached ('macula-on' status). Guideline Protocol: Immediate emergency same-day ophthalmologic referral; head positioning (postural positioning to let gravity prevent fluid from peeling the macula); strict avoidance of vigorous head movement, bending over, or heavy lifting. Thresholds: A 'macula-on' retinal detachment is an absolute surgical emergency requiring operative intervention within 24-48 hours to preserve sharp central 20/20 reading vision.

patient_plain_language: A retinal detachment occurs when the thin, light-sensitive tissue at the back of your eye (the retina) peels away from its normal position and blood supply, like wallpaper peeling off a damp wall. It often begins with sudden bursts of flashing lights and a shower of dark floating specks, followed by a dark shadow or curtain spreading across your field of vision. Prompt surgical repair is needed to prevent permanent blindness.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Is my macula (the center of reading vision) still attached ('macula-on') or has it detached?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Which surgical repair—a pneumatic gas bubble, a scleral buckle silicone band, or a vitrectomy—is recommended for my specific tear?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: What exact head positioning (such as face-down positioning) must I maintain after surgery to keep the gas bubble pressing against the tear?

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Immediate emergency same-day ophthalmologic referral; head positioning (postural positioning to let gravity prevent fluid from peeling the macula); strict avoidance of vigorous head movement, bending over, or heavy lifting.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Post-operative retinal examination at day 1, week 1, month 1, and month 3; intraocular pressure monitoring; visual field tracking.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: A 'macula-on' retinal detachment is an absolute surgical emergency requiring operative intervention within 24-48 hours to preserve sharp central 20/20 reading vision.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Retinal detachment is a medical emergency where the retina at the back of the eye pulls away from the layer of blood vessels that provides it with oxygen and nourishment.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: Wallpaper peeling away from the wall; if fluid gets underneath, the entire sheet peels down until re-glued by a surgeon.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Do not rub your eye. Avoid bending over or heavy lifting. See a retinal eye surgeon on the exact same day.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Primary anatomic reattachment achieved in >90%; macula-on detachment surgery within 24-48 hours preserves 20/40 or better vision in >85%.

title: IgA Nephropathy (Berger's Disease): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (The Lancet (TESTING Trial) & NEJM (NefIgArd))
snippet: In the landmark multicenter Phase 3 TESTING trial (n=503 patients with IgA nephropathy, proteinuria >=1 g/day, and eGFR 20-120 mL/min/1.73m2 despite optimized renin-angiotensin system blockade), reduced-dose oral methylprednisolone (0.4 mg/kg/day with Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis) significantly reduced the primary composite renal outcome (40% eGFR decline, end-stage kidney disease [ESKD], or renal death) by 47% compared with placebo over 4.2 years (hazard ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.39-0.72; p<0.001). Targeted-release budesonide (Nefecon, NefIgArd trial) and dual endothelin/angiotensin receptor antagonists (sparsentan, PROTECT trial) achieve robust proteinuria reduction (>40%) and preserve eGFR. Guideline Protocol: Dietary sodium restriction to <2,000 mg/day (enhances antiproteinuric efficacy of RAS inhibitors); moderate dietary protein intake (0.8 g/kg/day); smoking cessation; blood pressure control to <120/80 mmHg. Thresholds: Persistent proteinuria >0.75-1.0 g/day despite >=90 days of maximally tolerated ACEi/ARB and SGLT2i therapy indicates high risk of progression to ESKD, mandating targeted release budesonide or systemic immunosuppression.

patient_plain_language: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) is an autoimmune kidney disease where an abnormal form of an antibody called Immunoglobulin A (IgA)—which normally protects you from throat and lung infections—clumps together and gets trapped in the microscopic filters of your kidneys (glomeruli). This causes inflammation, microscopic bleeding into the urine (often turning urine pink or tea-colored during a cold), and slow kidney scarring.

doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Am I on maximum guideline-directed kidney protection (an ACE inhibitor/ARB plus an SGLT2 inhibitor like dapagliflozin)?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Would I benefit from gut-targeted budesonide (Tarpeyo) or sparsentan to shut down the abnormal IgA production at the source?

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Dietary sodium restriction to <2,000 mg/day (enhances antiproteinuric efficacy of RAS inhibitors); moderate dietary protein intake (0.8 g/kg/day); smoking cessation; blood pressure control to <120/80 mmHg.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) or 24-hour urine protein, serum creatinine, and estimated GFR every 1-3 months; blood pressure checks weekly; screen for microscopic hematuria.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Persistent proteinuria >0.75-1.0 g/day despite >=90 days of maximally tolerated ACEi/ARB and SGLT2i therapy indicates high risk of progression to ESKD, mandating targeted release budesonide or systemic immunosuppression.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: IgA nephropathy is an autoimmune kidney disorder in which antibodies called IgA build up in the kidneys, causing inflammation that can damage kidney tissues.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: Sticky antibody clumps jamming up the microscopic filter screens in your kidneys like sand caught in a pool filter.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Strictly limit salt to under 2,000 mg daily. Maintain blood pressure strictly below 120/80. Avoid smoking.

stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Monitor eGFR and potassium; SGLT2 inhibitors provide nephroprotection down to eGFR >=20 mL/min/1.73m2.

title: Membranous Nephropathy: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (MENTOR Trial) & KDIGO Guidelines)
snippet: Primary Membranous Nephropathy (pMN) is an autoimmune podocytopathy and the leading cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in adults, driven in 70-80% by circulating autoantibodies against the M-type phospholipase A2 receptor (anti-PLA2R1-Ab) or thrombospondin type-1 domain-containing 7A (anti-THSD7A-Ab). In the landmark randomized MENTOR trial (n=130 patients with proteinuria >=5 g/day despite 3 months of RAS blockade), intravenous rituximab (1,000 mg on days 1 and 15, repeated at 6 months if proteinuria declined by >25%) was noninferior to cyclosporine at 12 months and vastly superior at 24 months in maintaining complete or partial clinical remission (60% rituximab vs 20% cyclosporine; p<0.001). Relapse rates were dramatically lower with rituximab (5% vs 46%). Monitoring anti-PLA2R antibody titers predicts clinical proteinuria remission by 3-6 months. Guideline Protocol: Dietary sodium restriction (<2,000 mg/day); dietary protein moderation (0.8 g/kg/day); prophylactic anticoagulation for serum albumin <2.0-2.5 g/dL with high thromboembolic risk (CHA2DS2-VASc or Padua score); high-intensity statin. Thresholds: Anti-PLA2R titer >50 RU/mL with nephrotic-range proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) and low serum albumin (<3.0 g/dL) classifies as high or very high risk, requiring immediate immunosuppression with Rituximab or Cyclophosphamide.
key_takeaway: Primary Membranous Nephropathy (pMN) is an autoimmune podocytopathy and the leading cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in adults, driven in 70-80% by circulating autoantibodies against the M-type phospholipase A2 recept...
patient_plain_language: Membranous nephropathy is an autoimmune kidney disease where your body produces antibodies (most commonly anti-PLA2R antibodies) that attack the outside surface of your kidney's filtering units. The filters become thickened and leaky, allowing large amounts of protein (albumin) to spill out into your urine. Losing this protein causes fluid to pool in your body, producing heavy swelling (edema) in your legs, ankles, and face.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What is my blood anti-PLA2R antibody titer and my 24-hour urine protein measurement?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Is my blood albumin low enough (below 2.0-2.5 g/dL) that I need a preventative blood thinner to prevent dangerous vein blood clots?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Am I scheduled for B-cell targeted rituximab infusions to turn off the antibody attack?

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Dietary sodium restriction (<2,000 mg/day); dietary protein moderation (0.8 g/kg/day); prophylactic anticoagulation for serum albumin <2.0-2.5 g/dL with high thromboembolic risk (CHA2DS2-VASc or Padua score); high-intensity statin.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Quantitative serum anti-PLA2R antibody titers and 24-hour urine protein at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months; complete remission defined as proteinuria <0.3 g/day with stable eGFR; partial remission as proteinuria <3.5 g/day with >50% reduction from baseline.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Anti-PLA2R titer >50 RU/mL with nephrotic-range proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) and low serum albumin (<3.0 g/dL) classifies as high or very high risk, requiring immediate immunosuppression with Rituximab or Cyclophosphamide.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Membranous nephropathy is a kidney disorder that leads to changes and inflammation of the structures inside the kidney that help filter wastes and fluids.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: The kidney's fine mesh filters developing large holes from an antibody attack, letting essential protein leak into the urine.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Strictly limit dietary salt to reduce swelling. Take cholesterol medication. Watch legs closely for deep vein clot swelling.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: Rituximab 1,000 mg IV on days 1 and 15 (repeated at 6 months if proteinuria improved by >25% but incomplete remission).
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Rituximab: Fatal infusion reactions, severe mucocutaneous reactions, hepatitis B reactivation, and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML).
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Screen for hepatitis B (HBsAg and anti-HBc) and latent tuberculosis prior to initiation.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: 24-month sustained remission achieved in 60% with rituximab vs 20% cyclosporine (p<0.001); relapse rate reduced from 46% to 5%.

title: Minimal Change Disease: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Kidney International (KDIGO Glomerular Diseases))
snippet: Minimal Change Disease (MCD) is the predominant cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (70-90%) and accounts for 10-15% of adult nephrotic syndrome. It is characterized clinically by abrupt-onset massive selective proteinuria (predominantly albuminuria), profound hypoalbuminemia (<2.5 g/dL), severe generalized anasarca, and hypercholesterolemia, with normal blood pressure and preserved eGFR. Light microscopy reveals normal-appearing glomeruli, immunofluorescence is negative for immune complexes, and electron microscopy demonstrates pathognomonic diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes. Oral corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day, max 80 mg daily) achieve complete remission in >90% of children (within 4 weeks) and 75-80% of adults (within 12-16 weeks), though 50-70% experience steroid-dependent or frequent relapses requiring calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus/cyclosporine) or rituximab. Guideline Protocol: Dietary sodium restriction (<1,500-2,000 mg/day); dietary protein moderation (0.8-1.0 g/kg/day); loop diuretic titration combined with oral potassium replacement for severe fluid retention; compression stockings. Thresholds: Urine dipstick protein >=3+ for 3 consecutive days signifies disease relapse, requiring immediate restart of full-dose oral corticosteroids.
key_takeaway: Minimal Change Disease (MCD) is the predominant cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (70-90%) and accounts for 10-15% of adult nephrotic syndrome. It is characterized clinically by abrupt-onset massive selective prote...
patient_plain_language: Minimal change disease is a kidney condition that causes your kidneys to suddenly leak massive amounts of protein into your urine. When viewed under an ordinary optical microscope, the kidney filters look almost completely normal (minimal change). However, under a powerful electron microscope, the tiny interlocking foot-like cells (podocytes) that act as the kidney's strainer are swollen and flattened out. Fortunately, it usually responds very quickly to steroid medication.

doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: What is our precise plan for slowly tapering my oral prednisone over several months once my proteinuria reaches zero?

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Dietary sodium restriction (<1,500-2,000 mg/day); dietary protein moderation (0.8-1.0 g/kg/day); loop diuretic titration combined with oral potassium replacement for severe fluid retention; compression stockings.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Minimal change disease is a kidney disorder that can lead to nephrotic syndrome, causing large amounts of protein to be lost in the urine.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: The microscopic foot-pads of the kidney's filter cells flattening out, opening up gaps that dump protein into the urine.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Check first-morning urine protein dipstick daily. Restrict sodium. Weigh yourself every morning to spot fluid accumulation.

stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Tacrolimus: Increased risk of serious infections and malignancies (lymphomas); monitor trough blood levels (target 5-10 ng/mL).
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Provide bone protection (calcium + vitamin D) and gastroprotection (PPI) during high-dose steroid therapy.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Steroid therapy achieves complete remission in >80% of adults within 16 weeks; rituximab achieves 75% relapse-free survival in steroid-dependent disease.

title: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (The Lancet (DUET & DUPLEX Trials) & KDIGO)
snippet: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is a clinicopathologic pattern of podocyte injury characterized by sclerosis in portions (segmental) of some (focal) glomeruli, categorized by the Columbia classification into collapsing, tip, cellular, perihilar, and not-otherwise-specified (NOS) variants. In the multicenter randomized double-blind Phase 2/3 DUET trial (n=109 patients with biopsy-proven primary FSGS), the first-in-class dual endothelin type A and angiotensin II receptor antagonist sparsentan produced a significantly greater reduction in proteinuria at 8 weeks compared with active irbesartan control (-45% vs -19%; p=0.006), with 28% achieving complete or partial remission (vs 9% irbesartan; p=0.02). Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine/tacrolimus) achieve remission in 50-60% of steroid-resistant primary FSGS. Secondary/adaptive FSGS (driven by hyperfiltration from obesity, reduced nephron mass, or reflux) is non-immunologic and managed with maximal hemodynamic RAS/SGLT2 inhibition. Guideline Protocol: Strict dietary sodium restriction (<2,000 mg/day); dietary protein moderation (0.8 g/kg/day); weight normalization targeting BMI <25 kg/m2 in adaptive FSGS; blood pressure control to <120/80 mmHg. Thresholds: Primary FSGS with nephrotic proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) and hypoalbuminemia requires high-dose oral corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for up to 16 weeks); failure to achieve >50% proteinuria drop defines steroid resistance.
key_takeaway: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is a clinicopathologic pattern of podocyte injury characterized by sclerosis in portions (segmental) of some (focal) glomeruli, categorized by the Columbia classification into co...
patient_plain_language: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is a kidney disease that causes scarring in the microscopic filters of your kidneys. 'Focal' means only some of the filters are damaged, and 'segmental' means only a section of each filter is scarred. Because the filters are scarred and torn, protein leaks out into your urine, causing heavy swelling in your legs and belly, high cholesterol, and gradual decline in kidney function.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Which Columbia histological subtype (e.g. tip lesion, collapsing variant) did my kidney biopsy show?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Do I have primary autoimmune FSGS (which needs immunosuppressants) or secondary adaptive FSGS (which needs blood pressure and weight control)?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Has my genetic testing (for APOL1 high-risk genotypes or podocyte mutations) been completed?

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Strict dietary sodium restriction (<2,000 mg/day); dietary protein moderation (0.8 g/kg/day); weight normalization targeting BMI <25 kg/m2 in adaptive FSGS; blood pressure control to <120/80 mmHg.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) and estimated GFR monthly during induction, then every 3 months; liver transaminases (ALT/AST) monthly on sparsentan.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Primary FSGS with nephrotic proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) and hypoalbuminemia requires high-dose oral corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for up to 16 weeks); failure to achieve >50% proteinuria drop defines steroid resistance.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is a disease in which scar tissue develops on the parts of the kidneys that filter waste from the blood.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: Permanent scar patches forming on the kidney's filter screens, allowing protein to slip through into the urine.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Strictly limit salt intake. Maintain ideal body weight. Take kidney-protective blood pressure medications daily.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: Sparsentan 200 mg PO daily for 14 days, then titrate to 400 mg daily. High-dose Prednisone 1 mg/kg daily for 12-16 weeks.
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Sparsentan: Embryo-fetal toxicity and risk of hepatotoxicity; monthly transaminases (ALT/AST) and pregnancy testing required.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Monitor eGFR and potassium; SGLT2 inhibitors and ARBs provide additive antiproteinuric benefit.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Proteinuria reduced by 45% with sparsentan vs 19% irbesartan (p=0.006); partial/complete remission achieved in 28% vs 9%.

title: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (TEMPO 3:4 & REPRISE Trials) & KDIGO)
snippet: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) is the most common monogenic kidney disorder, caused by mutations in PKD1 (chromosome 16, 78% of cases, more severe with median ESKD age 58) or PKD2 (chromosome 4, 15%, median ESKD age 79), leading to progressive cystogenesis that destroys renal parenchyma. In the landmark Phase 3 TEMPO 3:4 trial (n=1445 patients with total kidney volume [TKV] >=750 mL and CrCl >=60 mL/min), tolvaptan (a selective vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist, titrated to 45/15 to 90/30 mg daily) significantly slowed the annual rate of TKV growth over 3 years (2.8% per year vs 5.5% with placebo; p<0.001) and significantly reduced annual eGFR decline (-2.72 vs -3.70 mL/min/1.73m2; p<0.001). The REPRISE trial confirmed preserved eGFR benefit in later-stage disease (eGFR 25-65 mL/min/1.73m2). Baseline Mayo Classification (Classes 1A-1E based on height-adjusted TKV) reliably predicts rapid disease progression. Guideline Protocol: High water intake (>3-4 liters daily spread evenly through day and night to suppress endogenous vasopressin secretion); dietary sodium restriction (<2,000 mg/day); avoidance of caffeine (which increases intracellular cyclic AMP and cyst growth); strict blood pressure control (<120/80 mmHg). Thresholds: Rapidly progressive disease (Mayo Class 1C, 1D, or 1E; annual eGFR decline >=3.0 mL/min/1.73m2; or TKV >750 mL) in patients aged 18-55 with eGFR >25 mL/min qualifies for disease-modifying tolvaptan therapy.

patient_plain_language: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is an inherited genetic condition that causes hundreds of fluid-filled cysts to grow and enlarge inside your kidneys over time. As the cysts multiply and expand, the kidneys can grow to the size of footballs, crowding out healthy kidney tissue and causing high blood pressure, flank pain, kidney stones, and gradual kidney failure. Each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the gene.

solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Rapidly progressive disease (Mayo Class 1C, 1D, or 1E; annual eGFR decline >=3.0 mL/min/1.73m2; or TKV >750 mL) in patients aged 18-55 with eGFR >25 mL/min qualifies for disease-modifying tolvaptan therapy.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Rate of total kidney volume expansion slowed by 50% (2.8% vs 5.5%/year; p<0.001); eGFR decline slowed by 1.0 mL/min/year.

title: Lupus Nephritis: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (BLISS-LN Trial) & The Lancet (AURORA Trial))
snippet: Lupus nephritis (LN) is a major organ-threatening manifestation of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), occurring in up to 50% of patients and classified by ISN/RPS into Classes I through VI (Class III focal and Class IV diffuse proliferative carrying the highest risk of progression to end-stage renal disease). In the landmark Phase 3 BLISS-LN trial (n=448 patients with active Class III, IV, or V LN receiving standard therapy with mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide), adding intravenous belimumab (a BLyS/BAFF inhibitor, 10 mg/kg) significantly increased Primary Efficacy Renal Response at 2 years compared with standard therapy alone (43% vs 32%; odds ratio 1.6; 95% CI 1.0-2.3; p=0.03) and halved the risk of a renal-related event or death (hazard ratio 0.51; p=0.001). The Phase 3 AURORA trial demonstrated that adding voclosporin (a novel calcineurin inhibitor) to mycophenolate doubled the complete renal response rate at 1 year (41% vs 23%; p<0.0001). Guideline Protocol: Universal background therapy with hydroxychloroquine (targeting 5 mg/kg actual body weight/day; reduces renal flares and mortality); strict photoprotection (broad-spectrum SPF 50+ sunscreen); sodium restriction (<2,000 mg/day). Thresholds: Proteinuria >0.5 g/day, cellular red blood cell casts, or unexplained rise in serum creatinine mandates diagnostic percutaneous renal biopsy to establish ISN/RPS class and activity/chronicity index.

patient_plain_language: Lupus nephritis is kidney inflammation caused by systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), an autoimmune disease. In lupus, your immune system generates autoantibodies that mistakenly attack your own organs. When these antibody complexes lodge inside your kidney's filters, they cause swelling, inflammation, protein leakage, and high blood pressure. Left untreated, it can permanently scar the kidneys.

title: ANCA-Associated Vasculitis (Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (ADVOCATE Trial & RAVE Trial) & ACR Guidelines)
journal: NEJM (ADVOCATE Trial & RAVE Trial) & ACR Guidelines
keywords: nejm (advocate trial & rave trial) & acr guidelines
snippet: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA, formerly Wegener's) and Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA) are necrotizing small-vessel vasculitides associated with antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (PR3-ANCA / c-ANCA in 85% of GPA; MPO-ANCA / p-ANCA in 70% of MPA). In the landmark Phase 3 ADVOCATE trial (n=330 patients with active ANCA vasculitis), the oral complement C5a receptor antagonist avacopan (30 mg BID) was noninferior to prednisone at week 26 and significantly superior to standard tapering prednisone in achieving sustained disease remission at 52 weeks (Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score [BVAS] of 0 without relapse: 65.7% vs 54.9%; difference 12.5 percentage points; 95% CI 2.6-22.3; p=0.007 for superiority). Avacopan also significantly improved eGFR (+7.3 vs +4.1 mL/min/1.73m2; p=0.029) and eliminated glucocorticoid-related toxicity. In the RAVE trial, Rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 doses) was proven noninferior to cyclophosphamide for induction and superior in relapsing disease (67% vs 42%; p=0.01). The inflammation attacks blood vessels in your nose, sinuses, lungs, and kidneys. Symptoms often start like a severe sinus infection with bloody crusting, coughing up blood, and rapid kidney inflammation.

title: Ankylosing Spondylitis (Axial Spondyloarthritis): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (MEASURE 1 & 2 Trials) & ACR/SAA Guidelines)
snippet: Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS / radiographic axial spondyloarthritis) is a chronic inflammatory arthritis predominantly affecting the axial skeleton and sacroiliac joints, strongly associated with HLA-B27 (>85-90%). Inflammatory back pain criteria (Calin/ASAS criteria: onset <45 years, insidious onset, improvement with exercise, no improvement with rest, pain at night) distinguish it from mechanical back pain. Pelvic radiography demonstrating bilateral Grade >=2 or unilateral Grade >=3 sacroiliitis (modified New York criteria) or active sacroiliac bone marrow edema on STIR MRI confirms the diagnosis. In the landmark Phase 3 MEASURE 1 and 2 trials (n=590 patients), secukinumab (an anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibody, 150 mg subcutaneous) significantly improved ASAS20 response rates at week 16 compared with placebo (61% vs 28%; p<0.001) and sustained clinical remission and spinal mobility out to 5 years. First-line therapy with continuous NSAIDs reduces radiographic spinal syndesmophyte progression. Guideline Protocol: Daily specialized spine-extension physical therapy and swimming; structured posture training; sleep on a firm mattress with a thin neck pillow; absolute smoking cessation (smoking accelerates spinal fusion and syndesmophyte bridging). Thresholds: High disease activity (ASDAS >=2.1 or BASDAI >=4.0) refractory to at least two different full-dose NSAIDs over 4-6 weeks indicates mandatory escalation to a biologic (TNF inhibitor or IL-17A inhibitor).

patient_plain_language: Ankylosing spondylitis is an inflammatory arthritis that primarily attacks the joints of your spine and pelvis (sacroiliac joints). Unlike ordinary mechanical back pain that gets worse with exercise, ankylosing spondylitis causes deep lower back stiffness that feels worst when resting in bed and dramatically improves after you get up and move around. Over years, the chronic inflammation can cause the spinal vertebrae to fuse together into a stiff 'bamboo spine'.

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Daily specialized spine-extension physical therapy and swimming; structured posture training; sleep on a firm mattress with a thin neck pillow; absolute smoking cessation (smoking accelerates spinal fusion and syndesmophyte bridging).
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI) and Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score (ASDAS-CRP) every 3-6 months; annual cervical and lumbar spine radiographs (mSASSS score) to track bony bridging; screening for acute anterior uveitis.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: High disease activity (ASDAS >=2.1 or BASDAI >=4.0) refractory to at least two different full-dose NSAIDs over 4-6 weeks indicates mandatory escalation to a biologic (TNF inhibitor or IL-17A inhibitor).

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Ankylosing spondylitis is an inflammatory disease that, over time, can cause some of the bones in the spine (vertebrae) to fuse.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: Chronic inflammation turning the flexible spinal joints into solid bone bridges, like melting wax fusing vertebrae together.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Exercise and stretch daily. Practice swimming. Sleep flat on your back without large pillows. Never smoke.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: Secukinumab 150 mg subcutaneous injection at weeks 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, then every 4 weeks. Full-dose Celecoxib 200 mg BID.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: ASAS20 response achieved in 61% with secukinumab vs 28% placebo (p<0.001); spinal mobility preserved and radiographic progression halted.

title: Psoriatic Arthritis: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (The Lancet (DISCOVER-1 & 2 Trials) & ACR/NPF Guidelines)
snippet: Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA) is a multifaceted inflammatory musculoskeletal disease occurring in up to 30% of patients with plaque psoriasis, involving six clinical domains: peripheral arthritis (often asymmetric, involving distal interphalangeal [DIP] joints), axial disease, enthesitis (inflammation at tendon insertion sites, e.g. Achilles tendonitis), dactylitis ('sausage digits'), skin psoriasis, and nail dystrophy (nail pitting and onycholysis in >80%). Classification Criteria for Psoriatic Arthritis (CASPAR score >=3) provides 91% sensitivity and 99% specificity. In the landmark Phase 3 DISCOVER-2 trial (n=739 biologic-naive patients with active PsA), the IL-23 p19-subunit inhibitor guselkumab (100 mg SC every 4 or 8 weeks) significantly improved ACR20 response rates at week 24 compared with placebo (64% vs 33%; p<0.0001) with marked complete clearance of skin psoriasis (PASI 90 in 70%), resolution of dactylitis/enthesitis, and significant inhibition of radiographic joint destruction. Guideline Protocol: Low-impact aerobic conditioning and resistance training; occupational therapy for hand splinting; weight reduction (obesity impairs biologic response rates by 50%); Mediterranean anti-inflammatory diet. Thresholds: Active disease refractory to oral disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (Methotrexate 15-25 mg/week) or severe axial/enthesitis disease warrants immediate biologic initiation (IL-23, IL-17, or TNF inhibitor).

patient_plain_language: Psoriatic arthritis is an autoimmune condition that causes joint pain, swelling, and stiffness in people who have the skin condition psoriasis. It causes painful inflammation in your finger and toe joints, swollen 'sausage-like' fingers and toes (dactylitis), tender heels where the Achilles tendon attaches, and pitted, crumbly fingernails. Early treatment prevents permanent joint damage.

solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Active disease refractory to oral disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (Methotrexate 15-25 mg/week) or severe axial/enthesitis disease warrants immediate biologic initiation (IL-23, IL-17, or TNF inhibitor).

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Psoriatic arthritis is a form of arthritis that affects some people who have psoriasis — a condition that features red patches of skin topped with silvery scales.

stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Engage in low-impact swimming and walking. Protect hands with supportive grips. Keep body weight within healthy range.

stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Monitor CBC and liver transaminases quarterly on methotrexate; avoid methotrexate in liver disease or pregnancy.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: ACR20 response achieved in 64% with guselkumab vs 33% placebo (p<0.0001); radiographic structural joint damage significantly inhibited.

title: Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (SENSCIS Trial) & ACR/EULAR Recommendations)
snippet: Systemic Sclerosis (SSc / Scleroderma) is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by microvascular obliteration, immune activation, and widespread progressive tissue fibrosis of the skin and internal organs. Subdivided into Limited Cutaneous SSc (lcSSc: CREST syndrome; anti-centromere antibodies [ACA] in 60-80%; high risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension) and Diffuse Cutaneous SSc (dcSSc: skin thickening proximal to elbows/knees; anti-Scl-70/topoisomerase I or anti-RNA polymerase III; high risk of interstitial lung disease and scleroderma renal crisis). In the landmark Phase 3 SENSCIS trial (n=576 patients with SSc-ILD), the intracellular tyrosine kinase inhibitor nintedanib (150 mg BID) significantly reduced the annual rate of decline in Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) by 44% compared with placebo (-52.4 mL/year vs -93.3 mL/year; difference 41.0 mL/year; 95% CI 2.9-79.0; p=0.04). In early progressive dcSSc, tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor) preserves lung function. Guideline Protocol: Strict avoidance of cold exposure and thermal layered mittens for Raynaud's; elevation of head of bed and small frequent meals for severe esophageal dysmotility; skin moisturization; pulmonary rehabilitation. Thresholds: New-onset hypertension (BP >140/90) or unexplained rise in serum creatinine in dcSSc indicates impending Scleroderma Renal Crisis, mandating immediate emergency ACE inhibitor therapy (captopril); high-dose corticosteroids (>15 mg/day) are strictly contraindicated as they precipitate renal crisis.

patient_plain_language: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) is an autoimmune disorder that causes your body to produce far too much collagen, a tough scar-like protein. Extra collagen builds up in your skin, blood vessels, and internal organs. It causes the skin on your fingers, hands, and face to become tight, hard, and shiny, makes fingers turn white in the cold (Raynaud's), causes chronic acid reflux, and can cause stiff scarring in your lungs.

doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Do I have anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies, and am I monitoring my blood pressure every single day at home to catch a renal crisis early?

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Strict avoidance of cold exposure and thermal layered mittens for Raynaud's; elevation of head of bed and small frequent meals for severe esophageal dysmotility; skin moisturization; pulmonary rehabilitation.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Quarterly pulmonary function testing (FVC and DLCO); annual screening transthoracic echocardiogram assessing tricuspid regurgitant velocity for pulmonary hypertension; daily home blood pressure monitoring (to catch Scleroderma Renal Crisis immediately); modified Rodnan skin score (mRSS).
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: New-onset hypertension (BP >140/90) or unexplained rise in serum creatinine in dcSSc indicates impending Scleroderma Renal Crisis, mandating immediate emergency ACE inhibitor therapy (captopril); high-dose corticosteroids (>15 mg/day) are strictly contraindicated as they precipitate renal crisis.

stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: An overproduction of tough scar protein that shrink-wraps the skin, blood vessels, and internal lungs like stiff leather.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Check blood pressure daily at home. Keep hands and feet warm with thermal gloves. Eat upright and stay sitting up after meals.

stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Systemic Corticosteroids: High doses (>15 mg daily) trigger life-threatening Scleroderma Renal Crisis; strictly avoid.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Monitor liver function tests baseline and monthly for 3 months with nintedanib; manage diarrhea with loperamide.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Annual rate of FVC decline slowed by 44% with nintedanib (-52.4 vs -93.3 mL/year; p=0.04); effect consistent across subgroups.

title: Sjögren's Syndrome: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases & Arthritis & Rheumatology)
journal: Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases & Arthritis & Rheumatology
keywords: annals of the rheumatic diseases & arthritis & rheumatology
snippet: Primary Sjögren's Syndrome is a systemic autoimmune exocrinopathy characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of salivary and lacrimal glands, resulting in classic sicca syndrome (xerophthalmia [dry eyes] and xerostomia [dry mouth]). Diagnostic classification requires a weighted score >=4 based on: positive anti-SSA/Ro antibodies (weight 3); labial salivary gland biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with focus score >=1 focus per 4 mm2 (weight 3); ocular staining score >=5 or van Bijsterveld score >=4 (weight 1); Schirmer's test <=5 mm in 5 minutes (weight 1); and unstimulated whole saliva flow rate <=0.1 mL/min (weight 1). Patients face a 15- to 20-fold increased lifetime risk of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (predominantly MALT lymphoma in parotid glands), heralded by persistent parotid swelling, purpura, monoclonal gammopathy, and low complement C4. Guideline Protocol: Frequent preservative-free artificial tears and nocturnal ocular lubricating ointments; silicone punctal plugs; sugar-free chewing gum or xylitol lozenges; meticulous dental hygiene and fluoride varnish applications every 3-6 months; home ultrasonic room humidifiers. Thresholds: Extraglandular systemic manifestations (inflammatory polyarthritis, cutaneous vasculitis, interstitial lung disease, or renal tubular acidosis) warrant systemic disease-modifying therapy with Hydroxychloroquine, Azathioprine, or Rituximab.

This leads to chronic, severe dry eyes (feeling like grit or sand is trapped under your eyelids), dry mouth (difficulty swallowing dry crackers or speaking without sipping water), rampant tooth decay, and joint stiffness.

solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Extraglandular systemic manifestations (inflammatory polyarthritis, cutaneous vasculitis, interstitial lung disease, or renal tubular acidosis) warrant systemic disease-modifying therapy with Hydroxychloroquine, Azathioprine, or Rituximab.

title: Dermatomyositis & Polymyositis: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (ProDERM Trial) & EULAR/ACR Guidelines)
snippet: Dermatomyositis (DM) and Polymyositis (PM) are idiopathic inflammatory myopathies characterized by symmetric, progressive, proximal muscle weakness (neck flexors, deltoids, hip flexors) and elevated skeletal muscle enzymes (creatine kinase [CK] typically 10-50x ULN, aldolase, LDH). Dermatomyositis features pathognomonic cutaneous signs: heliotrope rash (violaceous erythema with periorbital edema), Gottron's papules (violaceous scaly papules over MCP and PIP joints), and shawl/V-sign rashes. In the landmark international Phase 3 ProDERM trial (n=95 patients with active dermatomyositis), high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 2.0 g/kg every 4 weeks for 16 weeks) achieved a Total Improvement Score (TIS) >=20 in 78.7% of patients compared with 43.8% on placebo (difference 34.9 percentage points; 95% CI 16.7-52.8; p=0.001) with marked recovery in muscle strength (MMT-8) and skin disease (CDASI). Extensive age-appropriate cancer screening (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, mammography, colonoscopy) is mandatory, as DM carries a 5- to 6-fold increased risk of paraneoplastic malignancy (particularly with anti-TIF1-gamma or anti-NXP2 autoantibodies). Guideline Protocol: Strict photoprotection with broad-spectrum SPF 50+ sunscreen (ultraviolet light directly flares cutaneous and muscle disease); speech-language pathology swallowing evaluation for pharyngeal weakness; physical therapy for range of motion. Thresholds: Rapidly progressive dysphagia (aspiration risk) or rapidly declining FVC on pulmonary function tests warrants pulse IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3 days) combined with IVIG.

patient_plain_language: Dermatomyositis is a rare inflammatory disease marked by muscle weakness and distinctive skin rashes. Your immune system attacks blood vessels and muscle fibers, causing weakness in the muscles closest to the center of your body—making it hard to lift your arms to wash your hair, climb stairs, or stand up from a deep chair. In dermatomyositis, it also causes a reddish-purple rash around the eyelids (heliotrope rash) and purple bumps across the knuckles (Gottron's papules).

title: Behçet's Disease: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (RELIEF Trial) & EULAR Recommendations)
snippet: Behçet's disease is a variable-vessel systemic vasculitis characterized by recurrent, painful aphthous oral ulcers (present in >98%), recurrent genital ulcers, cutaneous lesions (erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis), and sight-threatening posterior uveitis / retinal vasculitis. International Criteria for Behçet's Disease (ICBD score >=4) provides 94% sensitivity and 96% specificity; strong genetic association with HLA-B*51. Pathergy testing (sterile pustule developing 24-48h after skin needle prick) is highly specific. In the multicenter double-blind Phase 3 RELIEF trial (n=207 patients with active oral ulcers), the oral phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitor apremilast (30 mg BID) significantly reduced the daily area under the curve for number of oral ulcers over 12 weeks compared with placebo (129.5 vs 222.1; p<0.001) and cleared oral ulcers in 52.9% vs 22.3% (p<0.001) with marked pain relief. In sight-threatening uveitis, TNF-alpha inhibitors (infliximab/adalimumab) achieve remission in >85%. Guideline Protocol: Topical corticosteroid pastes (triamcinolone in Orabase) applied to oral ulcers; antimicrobial mouthwashes (chlorhexidine); avoidance of spicy, acidic, or abrasive foods during active oral flares; sunglasses for ocular photophobia. Thresholds: Posterior uveitis, retinal vasculitis, pulmonary artery aneurysms, or central nervous system involvement (Neuro-Behçet) mandates emergency high-dose IV methylprednisolone and biologic TNF inhibitor therapy (Infliximab).

The most common hallmark is having recurrent, painful canker sores in your mouth that look like normal ulcers but occur frequently and take longer to heal. It also causes painful ulcers in the genital area, acne-like skin bumps, swollen joints, and inflammation inside the eye that can threaten vision if not treated promptly.

title: Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Arthritis & Rheumatology (ACR Guideline) & Medicine)
snippet: Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN) is a systemic necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized and small muscular arteries, classically sparing the venous system, pulmonary arteries, and glomeruli (not ANCA-associated). A significant subset is secondary to chronic Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. Pathology shows transmural fibrinoid necrosis and segmental aneurysmal dilatations with thrombosis. Catheter-directed visceral angiography or CT angiography characteristically demonstrates multiple microaneurysms and arterial occlusions ('string-of-beads' appearance) in mesenteric, renal, and hepatic vasculatures. Clinical hallmarks include mononeuritis multiplex (asymmetric foot/wrist drop in >60%), livedo reticularis, testicular pain, and renovascular hypertension. Prognosis is stratified using the Five-Factor Score (FFS: proteinuria >1g/day, renal insufficiency, cardiomyopathy, severe GI involvement, CNS involvement). Remission is achieved in >80% with combined high-dose corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide. Guideline Protocol: Physical and occupational therapy with ankle-foot orthoses (AFO splints) for peroneal nerve foot drop; screening for Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C virus; blood pressure control with calcium channel blockers. Thresholds: Severe organ-threatening disease (Five-Factor Score >=1, e.g., acute abdomen, gastrointestinal perforation, cardiomyopathy, or acute renal failure) warrants pulse IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3 days) plus IV cyclophosphamide (0.5-0.75 g/m2 monthly).

As the inflamed artery walls weaken, tiny balloon-like pouches (aneurysms) form along the blood vessels like beads on a string, cutting off blood flow. Common signs include severe nerve pain and sudden weakness (like being unable to lift your foot, called foot drop), deep muscle aches, and purplish lace-like skin discoloration.
