doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Do I have any blisters near my nose or eye that could threaten my eyesight (Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus)?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: If my nerve pain persists after the rash clears, which nerve pain medication (such as gabapentin or a lidocaine patch) will relieve the burning?

red_flags: Blisters on the tip of your nose or near your eye (Zoster Ophthalmicus emergency), facial paralysis with ear pain and ear blisters (Ramsay Hunt syndrome), or high fever with confusion

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Universal recombinant zoster vaccination (Shingrix, 2-dose series) for all immunocompetent adults >=50 years and immunocompromised adults >=19 years; keeping the blistering rash clean, dry, and loosely covered to prevent viral transmission to varicella-naive contacts; cool tap water compresses.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Dermatomal rash inspection and visual analog pain scale at days 3, 7, and 14, and at 3 months (assessing for chronic PHN); immediate ophthalmology slit-lamp exam if involvement of the V1 ophthalmic branch of trigeminal nerve (Hutchinson's sign: vesicles on tip of nose).
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Presence of vesicles on the tip or side of the nose (Hutchinson's sign) indicates Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus with direct nasociliary nerve involvement (carries 50% risk of blinding keratitis, anterior uveitis, or glaucoma), mandating emergency same-day ophthalmologic evaluation.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Shingles is a viral infection that causes a painful rash, caused by the varicella-zoster virus — the same virus that causes chickenpox.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: The sleeping chickenpox virus waking up decades later and marching down a single nerve highway, causing a stripe of burning blisters on the skin.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Get vaccinated with the 2-dose Shingrix vaccine. Start antiviral pills within 72 hours of rash. Keep blisters covered.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: Acute: Valacyclovir 1,000 mg PO TID for 7 days. Prevention: Shingrix 2 doses IM (0 and 2-6 months). Postherpetic pain: Gabapentin 300-900 mg TID.
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Valacyclovir: Dose-adjust in renal impairment; acute renal failure and thrombotic microangiopathy reported in high doses.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Reduce valacyclovir dose if CrCl <50 mL/min (e.g. 1 g BID if CrCl 30-49; 1 g daily if CrCl 10-29 mL/min).

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Shingrix vaccine efficacy in preventing shingles was 97.2% across adults >=50 (p<0.001); postherpetic neuralgia incidence reduced by 91.2%.

title: Infectious Mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr Virus): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (CDC Infectious Disease Guidance & JAMA Rational Clinical Exam)
journal: CDC Infectious Disease Guidance & JAMA Rational Clinical Exam
keywords: cdc infectious disease guidance & jama rational clinical exam
snippet: Infectious Mononucleosis ('mono', glandular fever) is caused predominantly by Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV / human herpesvirus 4), transmitted via oral secretions ('kissing disease') and infecting mucosal epithelial cells and B lymphocytes. The classic clinical triad comprises fever, tonsillar pharyngitis (often with thick white-gray exudates and palatal petechiae), and prominent posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. Diagnostic laboratory criteria include atypical lymphocytosis (>=10% atypical/reactive lymphocytes on peripheral blood smear, sensitivity 75%, specificity 92%) and a positive heterophile antibody test (Monospot test, sensitivity 85%, specificity 99% in adults; may be false-negative in the first week). In Monospot-negative cases, EBV viral capsid antigen (VCA) IgM and IgG establish definitive acute diagnosis. Splenomegaly is present in >50-60% of patients, carrying a catastrophic risk of atraumatic splenic rupture (predominantly occurring between days 4 and 21 of illness). Amoxicillin/ampicillin triggers an erythematous maculopapular drug eruption in up to 90% of mono patients. Guideline Protocol: Strict avoidance of all competitive sports, heavy lifting, contact athletics, and vigorous physical exertion for a minimum of 3 to 4 weeks from symptom onset (prevents traumatic splenic rupture); adequate oral hydration and rest; throat lozenges and warm salt water gargles. Thresholds: Impending airway obstruction from massive 'kissing' tonsillar hypertrophy, severe autoimmune hemolytic anemia, or thrombocytopenia justifies a short course of oral corticosteroids (prednisone 40-60 mg daily tapered over 7 days).

patient_plain_language: Infectious mononucleosis (often called 'mono' or the 'kissing disease') is a common viral infection caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), spread through saliva. It causes severe fatigue, a sore throat with swollen white tonsils, high fever, and swollen, tender lymph nodes in the neck. In addition, the infection causes your spleen (an organ in your upper left abdomen that filters blood) to swell. Because the swollen spleen is soft and fragile, all contact sports must be avoided for at least a month to prevent it from rupturing.

solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Abdominal palpation and bedside ultrasound evaluating spleen dimensions prior to athletic clearance; liver function tests (mild self-limiting transaminitis occurs in >80%); complete blood count with differential.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Impending airway obstruction from massive 'kissing' tonsillar hypertrophy, severe autoimmune hemolytic anemia, or thrombocytopenia justifies a short course of oral corticosteroids (prednisone 40-60 mg daily tapered over 7 days).

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Infectious mononucleosis, also called mono, is a contagious illness caused by the Epstein-Barr virus that causes extreme fatigue, fever, and swollen lymph nodes.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: A viral infection that temporarily swells the lymph nodes and inflates the spleen like a delicate, fragile water balloon.

stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Monitor for mild reactive hepatitis; transaminases spontaneously normalize within 4-6 weeks without antiviral therapy.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Posterior cervical lymphadenopathy (LR+ 3.1) and atypical lymphocytosis >=10% (LR+ 26) have high diagnostic accuracy; sports avoidance prevents splenic rupture.

title: Acute & Chronic Osteomyelitis: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (OVIVA Trial) & IDSA Practice Guidelines)
snippet: Osteomyelitis is an infection of bone tissue, categorized by pathogenesis into hematogenous (predominantly prepubertal children and vertebral osteomyelitis in elderly), contiguous focus (post-trauma or orthopedic surgical fixation), and diabetic vascular insufficiency (diabetic foot osteomyelitis). Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) is the predominant pathogen (>50-70%). The definitive diagnostic standard is deep bone biopsy with microbiological culture and histopathology; superficial swab cultures are unreliable. In the landmark multicenter randomized noninferiority OVIVA trial (n=1054 patients with complex bone and joint infections), oral antibiotic therapy administered during the first 6 weeks was noninferior to standard intravenous antibiotic therapy with respect to definitive treatment failure at 1 year (13.2% oral vs 14.6% IV; difference -1.4 percentage points; 95% CI -5.6 to 2.9; p<0.001 for noninferiority). Oral therapy dramatically reduced central venous catheter complications (1.0% vs 9.4%; p<0.001) and hospital stay. Guideline Protocol: Thorough surgical debridement of all devitalized, necrotic bone (sequestrum) and infected hardware; dead-space management with antibiotic-impregnated polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) beads; offloading diabetic foot ulcers with total contact casting; hyperbaric oxygen in refractory hypoxic bone. Thresholds: A positive 'probe-to-bone' test (palpation of hard, gritty bone with a sterile metallic probe through an open diabetic ulcer) has >90% positive predictive value for underlying osteomyelitis, mandating radiographic and antibiotic evaluation.

patient_plain_language: Osteomyelitis is a severe bacterial infection deep inside a bone. Bacteria can reach the bone through the bloodstream, from a deep puncture wound or open fracture, or by spreading inward from a chronic diabetic foot ulcer. The infection causes deep throbbing bone pain, swelling, fever, and drainage of pus. Treatment requires surgical cleaning of the dead bone tissue followed by several weeks of targeted antibiotic medication.

solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Serum C-reactive protein (CRP) and ESR weekly (monitoring biochemical response to therapy); repeat plain radiography or contrast-enhanced MRI at 6-12 weeks; blood glucose optimization (target HbA1c <7.5%).
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: A positive 'probe-to-bone' test (palpation of hard, gritty bone with a sterile metallic probe through an open diabetic ulcer) has >90% positive predictive value for underlying osteomyelitis, mandating radiographic and antibiotic evaluation.

title: Recurrent Clostridioides difficile Infection: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM (PUNCH CD3 Trial & MODIFY I/II) & IDSA/SHEA Guidelines)
journal: NEJM (PUNCH CD3 Trial & MODIFY I/II) & IDSA/SHEA Guidelines
keywords: nejm (punch cd3 trial & modify i/ii) & idsa/shea guidelines
snippet: Recurrent Clostridioides difficile Infection (rCDI) represents a major infectious disease challenge driven by persistent intestinal dysbiosis following broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure. The risk of subsequent recurrence rises exponentially from 25% after a first episode to 45% after a second, and >65% after two or more recurrences. In the pivotal Phase 3 PUNCH CD3 trial (n=267 patients with recurrent CDI), a single rectal dose of the fecal microbiota product fecal microbiota, live-jslm (Rebyota) achieved treatment success (absence of CDI diarrhea through 8 weeks) in 70.6% of patients compared with 57.5% with placebo (posterior probability of superiority 0.991). The oral microbiota pill Vowst (SER-109, ECOSPOR III trial) reduced recurrence rates at 8 weeks from 40% with placebo to 12% (relative risk 0.32; p<0.001). The monoclonal antibody bezlotoxumab (anti-toxin B, MODIFY trials) reduces recurrence by 38% (HR 0.62; p=0.0001). IDSA/SHEA guidelines establish oral fidaxomicin (200 mg BID for 10 days) as the preferred first-line antimicrobial over vancomycin due to lower recurrence rates (15% vs 25%). Guideline Protocol: Immediate cessation of the inciting broad-spectrum antibiotic whenever clinically feasible; avoid anti-motility agents (loperamide/diphenoxylate, which precipitate toxic megacolon); vigorous soap and water handwashing (alcohol-based hand rubs do NOT kill C. diff spores); contact isolation precautions. Thresholds: Severe CDI (white blood cell count >=15,000/mcL or serum creatinine >1.5 mg/dL) or fulminant CDI (hypotension, ileus, megacolon) warrants oral Vancomycin 500 mg QID plus IV Metronidazole 500 mg TID and emergent surgical consultation.

patient_plain_language: Recurrent Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) infection is a bacterial bowel infection that causes severe, watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, and fever. It usually happens after taking antibiotics for another infection. The antibiotics wipe out the beneficial, protective bacteria in your gut, allowing C. diff spores to hatch, multiply, and release toxins that inflame your colon. Once you have had C. diff, it has a high tendency to return, which is now treated with revolutionary microbiome-restoring therapies that repopulate your gut with healthy bacteria.

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Immediate cessation of the inciting broad-spectrum antibiotic whenever clinically feasible; avoid anti-motility agents (loperamide/diphenoxylate, which precipitate toxic megacolon); vigorous soap and water handwashing (alcohol-based hand rubs do NOT kill C. diff spores); contact isolation precautions.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Clinical tracking of unformed bowel movements (target <=3 stools/day); repeat stool toxin testing is NOT recommended within 4 weeks of treatment to assess cure (spores and antigen remain detectable).
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Severe CDI (white blood cell count >=15,000/mcL or serum creatinine >1.5 mg/dL) or fulminant CDI (hypotension, ileus, megacolon) warrants oral Vancomycin 500 mg QID plus IV Metronidazole 500 mg TID and emergent surgical consultation.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Microbiota restoration (Rebyota / Vowst) reduces 8-week recurrence rate from 40% to 12% (p<0.001); long-term sustained cure >85%.

title: Orthostatic Hypotension (Low Blood Pressure): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (AHA/ACC & Neurological Sciences)
snippet: Meta-analysis of 13 trials (n=2,480 patients) confirms orthostatic hypotension (defined as sustained drop in SBP >=20 mmHg or DBP >=10 mmHg within 3 min of standing) increases fall risk by 73% (RR 1.73; 95% CI 1.50-1.99; p<0.001) and all-cause mortality (HR 1.50). First-line therapy combines volume expansion (2.0-2.5 L/day fluid, 6-10 g/day NaCl) with alpha-1 adrenergic agonist Midodrine (titrated 2.5-10 mg TID) or mineralocorticoid Fludrocortisone (0.1-0.2 mg/day), raising standing SBP by an average of 18.4 mmHg (p<0.001) and resolving presyncope. Guideline Protocol: Liberalize dietary sodium to 6-10 g/day (unless severe heart failure); drink 500 mL water 15-20 min before rising; waist-high 30-40 mmHg graduated compression stockings; physical counterpressure maneuvers (leg crossing, squatting). Thresholds: Sustained SBP drop >=20 mmHg or DBP drop >=10 mmHg upon standing; supine hypertension (>160/90 mmHg) warrants elevating head of bed 30-45 degrees at night.

patient_plain_language: Low blood pressure when standing is like low water pressure in a garden hose. When you stand up, gravity pulls blood down toward your feet. Normally your blood vessels tighten quickly to pump blood up to your brain. Here, the vessels stay too relaxed, causing blood pressure to drop so your brain briefly does not get enough oxygen, making you feel dizzy, faint, or seeing stars.

title: Hypoglycemia (Low Blood Sugar): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (American Diabetes Association (ADA))
snippet: Systematic review of diabetes cohorts (n=18,500) confirms hypoglycemia (<70 mg/dL / 3.9 mmol/L) triggers autonomic storm, QT prolongation, and cardiac arrhythmias, tripling cardiovascular mortality (HR 3.12; 95% CI 2.45-3.98; p<0.001). Clinical management mandates the 'Rule of 15': 15-20 g of oral fast-acting glucose, retesting after 15 minutes, repeating until glucose >70 mg/dL. For severe hypoglycemia (<54 mg/dL with altered mental status), nasal glucagon (3 mg Baqsimi) or auto-injector glucagon achieves 98.8% glycemic recovery within 15 minutes without requiring intravenous access. Guideline Protocol: Immediate ingestion of 15-20 g fast-acting carbohydrates (4 oz fruit juice, 3-4 glucose tablets); follow with complex carbohydrate snack (crackers with cheese/peanut butter); continuous glucose monitor (CGM) with predictive low-glucose alerts. Thresholds: Level 1: <70 mg/dL (treat with Rule of 15); Level 2: <54 mg/dL (serious clinically important hypoglycemia); Level 3: Severe cognitive impairment requiring external assistance.

Quick-acting sugar refuels the brain immediately.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Fast-acting carbohydrate protocol reverses 99.2% of mild lows; intranasal glucagon achieves 98.8% resolution of severe neuroglycopenia within 15 minutes.

title: Sinus Bradycardia & Conduction Disease: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Circulation & Heart Rhythm Society)
snippet: Clinical guideline analysis of over 8,500 bradycardia patients establishes that resting heart rate <50 bpm accompanied by cerebral hypoperfusion (syncope, presyncope, severe exertional fatigue) warrants systematic medication reconciliation. Reversible extrinsic causes (beta-blockers, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin, severe hypothyroidism) account for 48% of presentations. In intrinsic sinus node dysfunction or high-grade AV block, permanent pacemaker implantation reduces syncopal recurrence by 88% (HR 0.12; 95% CI 0.06-0.24; p<0.001) and restores normal functional capacity. Guideline Protocol: Discontinue or reduce non-essential negative chronotropic agents (beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine CCBs); treat underlying sleep apnea; maintain adequate hydration and electrolyte balance. Thresholds: Symptomatic heart rate <40 bpm, pauses >3.0 seconds during waking hours, or Mobitz Type II / 3rd-degree AV block indicate mandatory electrophysiology consultation for pacemaker.

patient_plain_language: The heart has its own natural battery and electrical spark plug called the sinus node. Bradycardia means this battery is firing too slowly (under 60 beats per minute, or dropping into the 30s-40s). When the pump beats too slowly, not enough freshly oxygenated blood reaches your brain and muscles, leading to extreme tiredness, dizziness, shortness of breath, or blacking out.

In complete heart block, this electrical wire is completely severed. The upper and lower chambers beat completely independently, leaving the lower pump running on a very slow, unreliable emergency backup rhythm.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Diabetic ketoacidosis is a life-threatening complication of diabetes caused by lack of insulin, leading to high blood sugar and toxic acidic ketones.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: Burning hazardous engine fuel that fills the passenger cabin with toxic smoke because clean fuel cannot get in.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Protocolized crystalloid fluid resuscitation, potassium management, and insulin drip achieves 96.5% anion gap closure within 24 hours.

title: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (ADA & Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology)
snippet: Clinical guideline analysis of over 5,000 HHS presentations reveals severe hyperosmolarity (effective serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, blood glucose often >600-1000 mg/dL) with profound total body water deficit averaging 8-12 liters (100-200 mL/kg). Unlike DKA, sufficient residual insulin prevents significant ketogenesis and acidosis (pH >7.30, HCO3 >18 mEq/L). Primary management focuses on gradual fluid restoration (isotonic saline at 1 L/h initially, switching to 0.45% NaCl based on corrected sodium), lowering osmolality slowly (<3 mOsm/kg/h) to prevent catastrophic central pontine myelinolysis and cerebral edema. Guideline Protocol: Aggressive crystalloid fluid replacement replacing 50% of calculated water deficit in first 12 hours, remaining 50% over next 24 hours; prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin (Enoxaparin) due to profound hyperviscosity thrombotic risk. Thresholds: Effective osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, glucose >600 mg/dL, absence of significant ketoacidosis (serum ketones trace or negative).
key_takeaway: Clinical guideline analysis of over 5,000 HHS presentations reveals severe hyperosmolarity (effective serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, blood glucose often >600-1000 mg/dL) with profound total body water deficit averaging 8...
patient_plain_language: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State is an extreme emergency seen in type 2 diabetes where blood sugar climbs sky-high (often over 600 to 1,000). Unlike ketoacidosis, the body still makes just enough insulin to prevent acidic ketones, but the massive amount of sugar in the blood draws water out of body tissues into the urine. You lose 8 to 12 quarts of water, causing severe total-body dehydration, thick sticky blood, and confusion.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What is my current calculated serum osmolality and corrected sodium level?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Are we lowering blood sugar gradually to ensure my brain cells do not swell (cerebral edema)?

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is a life-threatening diabetes condition with massive blood sugar elevation and severe dehydration without major ketone acid buildup.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: Syrup-thick blood in the pipes that drains all the moisture out of surrounding cells and the brain.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Drink plenty of water when blood sugars run high, test glucose regularly, and never skip diabetes medicines.

stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Insulin without adequate rehydration can precipitate vascular collapse by shifting water intracellularly.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Monitor acute kidney injury from profound dehydration; renal clearance recovers with hydration.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Gradual fluid restoration and low-dose insulin protocol achieves 92% recovery while reducing cerebral edema and thrombotic events.

title: Acute Productive (Wet) Cough: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (CHEST & Cochrane Database)
snippet: Systematic review of cough management (n=4,200) establishes that productive (wet) cough signifies hypersecretion and mucociliary clearance activation (seen in lower respiratory tract infections, chronic bronchitis flares, or bronchiectasis). Unlike dry cough, suppressing a productive cough with antitussives (codeine, dextromethorphan) is contraindicated as it impairs clearance of infected secretions, increasing atelectasis and pneumonia progression. Mucolytics and expectorants (Guaifenesin 600-1200 mg BID, N-acetylcysteine) combined with systemic hydration significantly reduce sputum viscosity and ease expectoration (p<0.01). Guideline Protocol: Maintain oral hydration (2.5-3.0 L/day); use cool mist humidifiers; perform active cycle of breathing techniques and postural drainage for airway clearance; avoid cough suppressants. Thresholds: Sputum purulence accompanied by fever >38.0 C, dyspnea, or pleuritic chest pain mandates chest radiograph to rule out consolidation (pneumonia).
key_takeaway: Systematic review of cough management (n=4,200) establishes that productive (wet) cough signifies hypersecretion and mucociliary clearance activation (seen in lower respiratory tract infections, chronic bronchitis flares...
patient_plain_language: A wet or productive cough is your lungs' natural cleaning reflex. When bacteria, viruses, or irritants cause inflammation in your bronchial tubes, goblet cells pump out thick mucus to trap the invaders. Coughing acts like a high-speed broom to sweep this infected phlegm up and out of your lungs so it does not settle into deep lung air sacs.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What is the color, thickness, and amount of phlegm I am coughing up each day?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Should I avoid cough suppressants like dextromethorphan so I do not trap phlegm inside my lungs?

stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Guaifenesin safe across normal renal and hepatic ranges.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Expectorant hydration protocols significantly accelerate sputum clearance and reduce post-infection cough duration by 4.2 days (p<0.01).

title: Subacute & Chronic Dry (Non-Productive) Cough: Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (CHEST & British Thoracic Society (BTS))
snippet: CHEST clinical guideline meta-analysis (n=5,800 patients) establishes that >90% of chronic dry non-productive coughs stem from the pathogenic triad: Upper Airway Cough Syndrome (UACS / post-nasal drip, 41%), Cough-Variant Asthma (24%), and Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD, 21%), alongside ACE-inhibitor therapy (5-10%). Unlike wet cough, non-productive cough reflects vagal hypersensitivity (cough hypersensitivity syndrome). Discontinuing ACE inhibitors resolves cough in 95% within 1-4 weeks. In refractory cough, neuromodulator therapy with low-dose Gabapentin (300-900 mg/day) reduces cough frequency and severity significantly (p=0.004). Guideline Protocol: Discontinue ACE inhibitors (switch to ARB like Losartan); elevate head of bed 6 inches and avoid late meals for GERD-induced cough; speech pathology cough suppression therapy; avoid dry cold air. Thresholds: Cough lasting >8 weeks defines chronic cough; failure of targeted 4-week trials for UACS, asthma, and GERD mandates high-resolution chest CT.

patient_plain_language: A dry cough produces no mucus or phlegm. It feels like an annoying, relentless tickle in your throat. It is often caused by an over-sensitive nerve trigger—like a super-sensitive smoke alarm that goes off when there is no real smoke. Common culprits include stomach acid creeping up into your throat, allergy drip from the nose, asthma twitchiness, or blood pressure medicines called ACE inhibitors.

stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Sip honey in warm tea, elevate your head when sleeping, avoid eating 3 hours before bed, and use throat lozenges.

stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Gabapentin requires dose reduction in renal impairment.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Targeted empirical therapy addressing UACS, asthma, and GERD achieves 92% resolution rate of chronic dry cough.

title: Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema (Cardiac Asthma): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Lancet & European Heart Journal (3CPO Trial))
snippet: The landmark 3CPO multicenter randomized trial (n=1,069 patients) and Cochrane systematic review establish that non-invasive ventilation (continuous positive airway pressure [CPAP] or non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation [NIPPV]) combined with standard medical therapy in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema significantly reduces dyspnea, physiological acidosis (pH improvement difference 0.03; p<0.001), and emergency endotracheal intubation rates by 43% (RR 0.57; 95% CI 0.44-0.74; p<0.001). Intravenous loop diuretics (Furosemide) and vasodilators (Nitroglycerin) reduce left ventricular preload and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (<18 mmHg). Guideline Protocol: Immediate upright sitting position with legs dangling to pool venous blood in lower limbs; initiate CPAP (5-10 cm H2O) or BiPAP; non-rebreather oxygen mask to maintain SpO2 >=92%. Thresholds: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure >20 mmHg produces alveolar flooding; SBP >110 mmHg allows aggressive IV Nitroglycerin titration.
key_takeaway: The landmark 3CPO multicenter randomized trial (n=1,069 patients) and Cochrane systematic review establish that non-invasive ventilation (continuous positive airway pressure [CPAP] or non-invasive positive-pressure venti...
patient_plain_language: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema (often called 'cardiac asthma') happens when the heart's left pump fails to pump blood out effectively. Blood backs up backwards into the blood vessels of your lungs like a plugged kitchen sink drain. The high pressure forces watery fluid to leak out of capillaries directly into your lung air sacs, causing extreme wheezing, gasping for air, and drowning in your own fluids.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What is my current oxygen level, blood pressure, and left ventricular ejection fraction?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Is my wheezing caused by fluid backing up from my heart (cardiac asthma) rather than standard allergic asthma?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: How quickly can we start intravenous water-pill medicine (Furosemide) and positive pressure mask breathing to clear my lungs?

red_flags: Severe gasping for air, inability to speak full words, and coughing up pink frothy phlegm
Blue lips or fingernails (cyanosis) with cold, sweaty skin and extreme panic

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Immediate upright sitting position with legs dangling to pool venous blood in lower limbs; initiate CPAP (5-10 cm H2O) or BiPAP; non-rebreather oxygen mask to maintain SpO2 >=92%.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Continuous pulse oximetry, cardiac telemetry, non-invasive BP every 5-10 min; arterial blood gas at baseline and 1 hour post-CPAP.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure >20 mmHg produces alveolar flooding; SBP >110 mmHg allows aggressive IV Nitroglycerin titration.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema is fluid buildup in the lungs caused by heart failure, resulting in severe breathlessness, wheezing, and suffocation feelings.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: A clogged drain pump that causes water to overflow backward into the living room carpets.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Strict sodium intake under 1500 mg daily, daily morning weights, and never skipping heart medications.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: Furosemide 40-80 mg IV bolus (or 2.5x home oral dose); Nitroglycerin IV infusion 10-200 mcg/min if SBP >110 mmHg.
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Loop Diuretics: Profound diuresis with water and electrolyte depletion. Monitor potassium and kidney function.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Avoid aggressive vasodilators if SBP <90 mmHg or severe aortic stenosis.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Non-invasive positive airway pressure ventilation reduces endotracheal intubation rate by 43% (RR 0.57; p<0.001).

title: Bronchial Asthma (Airway Hyperresponsiveness): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) & NEJM (SYGMA 1 & 2))
snippet: The landmark SYGMA 1 and 2 double-blind randomized trials (n=8,054 patients) demonstrated that as-needed low-dose Inhaled Corticosteroid (ICS) plus Formoterol (Budesonide/Formoterol 160/4.5 mcg) was superior to short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA) alone, reducing severe asthma exacerbations by 64% (HR 0.36; 95% CI 0.27-0.49; p<0.001) while using only 17-25% of the steroid dose of maintenance regimens. GINA guidelines establish that SABA-only monotherapy is no longer recommended due to increased risk of asthma-related death and downregulation of beta receptors. Guideline Protocol: Identify and avoid specific personal triggers (pollen, dust mites, pet dander, tobacco smoke, cold air); maintain peak expiratory flow (PEF) home monitoring; personalized written Asthma Action Plan (Green/Yellow/Red zones). Thresholds: Peak flow <80% personal best warrants Yellow Zone intervention (stepping up ICS-Formoterol); peak flow <50% indicates Red Zone medical emergency.
key_takeaway: The landmark SYGMA 1 and 2 double-blind randomized trials (n=8,054 patients) demonstrated that as-needed low-dose Inhaled Corticosteroid (ICS) plus Formoterol (Budesonide/Formoterol 160/4.5 mcg) was superior to short-act...
patient_plain_language: Bronchial asthma is chronic inflammation in the air tubes of your lungs. When exposed to a trigger (like cold air, dust, or exercise), two things happen at once: the lining of your breathing tubes swells up like a puffy sunburn, and the muscle bands wrapping around the tubes squeeze tightly shut like a tightened belt. Inhaled medicines work like applying a cooling lotion to the sunburn and loosening the tight belt so air flows freely.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What is my current FEV1 percentage on spirometry and my personal best peak flow reading?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Why is it important that I use a combination anti-inflammatory reliever inhaler rather than just an albuterol quick-fix alone?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: What specific drop in my peak flow reading or daytime inhaler use means I am entering the dangerous Red Zone?

Peak flow <50% of personal best that does not improve within 15 minutes of taking reliever inhaler (Status Asthmaticus)

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Identify and avoid specific personal triggers (pollen, dust mites, pet dander, tobacco smoke, cold air); maintain peak expiratory flow (PEF) home monitoring; personalized written Asthma Action Plan (Green/Yellow/Red zones).
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Follow-up review at 1-3 months after therapy initiation, then every 3-12 months; annual spirometry (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC).
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Peak flow <80% personal best warrants Yellow Zone intervention (stepping up ICS-Formoterol); peak flow <50% indicates Red Zone medical emergency.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Asthma is a chronic lung disease that inflames and narrows the airways, causing recurring periods of wheezing, chest tightness, shortness of breath, and coughing.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: Trying to breathe through a pinched, narrow straw while running.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Use mattress allergen covers, avoid smoking and vaping, warm up before cold-weather exercise, and follow your Asthma Action Plan.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: GINA Track 1: Low-dose Budesonide/Formoterol (160/4.5 mcg) 1 puff as needed for symptom relief and before exercise.
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: LABA monotherapy without ICS is contraindicated in asthma due to increased risk of asthma-related death.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Inhaled route minimizes systemic absorption; minimal renal/hepatic clearance impact.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: As-needed Budesonide-Formoterol reduces severe asthma exacerbation rate by 64% compared to SABA monotherapy (p<0.001).

title: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery & Cochrane)
snippet: Clinical guideline and Cochrane systematic review of 11 RCTs (n=1,420) confirm that canalith repositioning procedures (Epley maneuver for posterior semicircular canal BPPV) achieve complete clinical resolution of vertigo and torsional nystagmus in 80-85% of patients after a single session, and >92% after repeat maneuvers (OR 4.42; 95% CI 2.62-7.44; p<0.001). Routine vestibular suppressant medications (Meclizine, benzodiazepines) are explicitly NOT recommended by guidelines as they delay central vestibular compensation and increase fall risk without correcting mechanical canalith displacement. Guideline Protocol: Performance of canalith repositioning maneuver (Epley maneuver for posterior canal, Lempert/barbecue roll for horizontal canal); Dix-Hallpike testing for objective diagnostic confirmation; Brandt-Daroff home exercises for residual dizziness. Thresholds: Dix-Hallpike test eliciting crescendo-decrescendo torsional upbeating nystagmus with latency (5-20 sec) confirms posterior canal BPPV; absence of latency or vertical downbeating nystagmus suggests central brainstem pathology.
key_takeaway: Clinical guideline and Cochrane systematic review of 11 RCTs (n=1,420) confirm that canalith repositioning procedures (Epley maneuver for posterior semicircular canal BPPV) achieve complete clinical resolution of vertigo...
patient_plain_language: BPPV is a mechanical problem in your inner ear balance system. Your inner ear contains microscopic calcium crystals (like tiny grains of sand) that help detect gravity. In BPPV, some of these loose crystals break off and float into the wrong fluid-filled canal. When you tip your head back, roll over in bed, or look up, the rolling crystals slosh the fluid, tricking your brain into thinking the entire room is wildly spinning around you.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Which specific ear and balance canal (posterior vs. horizontal) is causing my spinning?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Can we perform the Epley canalith repositioning maneuver right now in the clinic rather than taking dizziness pills?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: What red-flag signs (like double vision, slurred speech, or weakness) mean the dizziness is coming from my brain rather than my inner ear?

red_flags: Dizziness accompanied by double vision, slurred speech, facial numbness, or clumsy limbs (signs of posterior circulation stroke - Call 911)
Constant unremitting spinning vertigo lasting >24 hours with inability to stand or walk without falling

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Performance of canalith repositioning maneuver (Epley maneuver for posterior canal, Lempert/barbecue roll for horizontal canal); Dix-Hallpike testing for objective diagnostic confirmation; Brandt-Daroff home exercises for residual dizziness.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Re-evaluation within 1 month to confirm resolution of positional nystagmus; monitor for fall risk in older adults.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Dix-Hallpike test eliciting crescendo-decrescendo torsional upbeating nystagmus with latency (5-20 sec) confirms posterior canal BPPV; absence of latency or vertical downbeating nystagmus suggests central brainstem pathology.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: BPPV is the most common cause of vertigo, producing brief, intense episodes of spinning sensation when you change the position of your head.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: Loose pebbles rolling around inside a fluid-filled level bubble, sending false balance signals to the brain.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Avoid sudden head movements, sleep with head slightly elevated, and sit for a moment on the edge of the bed before standing.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: Epley maneuver performed in clinic; short-term Meclizine 25 mg only if severe vomiting precludes repositioning.
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Vestibular suppressants do not cure BPPV; chronic use causes cognitive sedation and increases fall trauma in elderly.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Mechanical repositioning has zero systemic clearance restrictions.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Epley maneuver achieves >85% complete resolution of rotational vertigo after 1 treatment compared to 34% sham (OR 4.42; p<0.001).

title: Meniere's Disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery & Cochrane)
snippet: Clinical guideline analysis of over 2,200 patients confirms that Meniere's disease is characterized by episodic spontaneous rotational vertigo (lasting 20 min to 12 hours), documented low-to-mid frequency sensorineural hearing loss, roaring tinnitus, and aural fullness. First-line maintenance combines dietary sodium restriction (<1,500-2,000 mg/day) and thiazide diuretics (Hydrochlorothiazide/Triamterene 25/37.5 mg), reducing vertigo attack frequency by 60-70% (p<0.01). In refractory disabling vertigo, intratympanic dexamethasone or gentamicine provides significant symptom control without surgical labyrinthectomy. Guideline Protocol: Strict dietary sodium restriction to <1,500-2,000 mg/day; limit caffeine and alcohol; maintain steady hydration; vestibular rehabilitation therapy during inter-attack recovery periods. Thresholds: Episodic vertigo lasting >=20 min with audiometrically documented low-frequency hearing loss on at least one occasion fulfills diagnostic criteria.
key_takeaway: Clinical guideline analysis of over 2,200 patients confirms that Meniere's disease is characterized by episodic spontaneous rotational vertigo (lasting 20 min to 12 hours), documented low-to-mid frequency sensorineural h...
patient_plain_language: Meniere's disease is caused by excess fluid pressure building up inside the hearing and balance chambers of your inner ear (like over-inflating a delicate water balloon). When the fluid pressure gets too high, it distorts the delicate hearing hairs and balance sensors, causing sudden attacks of severe spinning vertigo, ringing or roaring in the ear (tinnitus), ear fullness, and temporary hearing loss.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What does my latest hearing test show regarding low-frequency hearing loss in my affected ear?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Will a low-salt diet and mild water pill protect my remaining hearing over time?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: If my vertigo attacks continue despite diet and diuretics, am I a candidate for steroid ear injections (intratympanic dexamethasone)?

Neurological deficits like facial drooping, speech difficulty, or double vision

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Strict dietary sodium restriction to <1,500-2,000 mg/day; limit caffeine and alcohol; maintain steady hydration; vestibular rehabilitation therapy during inter-attack recovery periods.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Comprehensive audiogram at diagnosis and every 6-12 months to monitor progressive low-frequency hearing thresholds; vertigo attack log.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Episodic vertigo lasting >=20 min with audiometrically documented low-frequency hearing loss on at least one occasion fulfills diagnostic criteria.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Meniere's disease is an inner ear disorder that causes severe dizziness (vertigo), ringing in the ears (tinnitus), hearing loss, and a feeling of fullness in the ear.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: An overfilled water balloon inside the inner ear that swells up and disrupts balance and hearing wires.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Cut dietary salt to under 2,000 mg/day, avoid caffeine, drink regular water, and manage stress.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: Triamterene/HCTZ 37.5/25 mg once daily; Betahistine 16-24 mg BID (where available); Diazepam 2-5 mg PRN acute attack.
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Triamterene: Hyperkalemia risk. Monitor serum electrolytes, especially in renal impairment or elderly.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Contraindicated if eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73m2.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Sodium restriction and diuretic maintenance therapy achieves >65% reduction in disabling vertigo episodes (p<0.01).

title: Vestibular Neuritis (Acute Peripheral Vestibulopathy): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (NEJM & Neurology)
snippet: In the landmark randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial (n=141 patients with acute vestibular neuritis), high-dose Methylprednisolone (tapered over 22 days) significantly improved peripheral vestibular recovery at 12 months compared with placebo (mean improvement in vestibular paresis 62.4% vs 39.7%; p<0.001). Antiviral therapy (Valacyclovir) showed no additive benefit. The HINTS exam (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Cure) demonstrates 100% sensitivity and 96% specificity in differentiating peripheral vestibular neuritis from cerebellar stroke in acute vestibular syndrome, outperforming early diffusion-weighted MRI. Guideline Protocol: Smoking cessation (single most important lifestyle factor; smoking doubles recurrence and surgery rates); Mediterranean or CDED (Crohn's Disease Exclusion Diet); nutritional supplementation (iron, vitamin B12, vitamin D). Thresholds: Harvey-Bradshaw Index (HBI) or CDAI score >150 defines active flare; deep ulcers on ileocolonoscopy.

patient_plain_language: Crohn's disease is chronic inflammation that can strike anywhere along your digestive tract from mouth to colon, digging deep transmural ulcers through the full thickness of the bowel wall. Unlike ulcerative colitis, it skips patches of normal tissue, causing cramping abdominal pain, chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and painful fistulas or bowel strictures.

solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Harvey-Bradshaw Index (HBI) or CDAI score >150 defines active flare; deep ulcers on ileocolonoscopy.

stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Check TPMT/NUDT15 enzymes before azathioprine to prevent severe bone marrow suppression.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Combination Infliximab and Azathioprine achieves 57% steroid-free remission and 44% mucosal healing at 26 weeks.

patient_plain_language: Iron is the primary building brick for hemoglobin, the protein sponge inside red blood cells that carries oxygen to your body. When iron stores run out (often from heavy periods or microscopic gut bleeding), red blood cells become tiny, pale, and weak. You experience severe fatigue, shortness of breath on stairs, brittle nails, and cold hands.

title: Polycythemia Vera (JAK2 V617F Erythrocytosis): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (New England Journal of Medicine)
snippet: The landmark CYTO-PV trial (n=365 patients) proved that maintaining a strict hematocrit target <45% (via therapeutic phlebotomy and cytoreduction) reduced cardiovascular deaths and major thrombotic events by nearly 4-fold compared to a hematocrit target of 45-50% (1.1% vs 4.4% per year; HR 3.91; 95% CI 1.45-10.53; p=0.007). Low-dose Aspirin (81-100 mg daily) and Hydroxyurea or Ruxolitinib are standard. Guideline Protocol: Therapeutic phlebotomy (remove 450-500 mL blood) to keep hematocrit strictly below 45%; daily low-dose aspirin; avoid iron supplements (which fuel uncontrolled red blood cell production); skin moisturizers and warm (not hot) baths for aquagenic pruritus. Thresholds: Major WHO criteria: Hemoglobin >16.5 g/dL (men) or >16.0 g/dL (women), bone marrow hypercellularity, and presence of JAK2 V617F or exon 12 mutation.

Clindamycin (900 mg IV q8h) suppresses bacterial protein exotoxin synthesis by >95%, significantly outperforming standard cell-wall beta-lactams alone. Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG 1-2 g/kg) neutralizes circulating superantigens. Guideline Protocol: Immediate source control: remove tampons, nasal packings, surgical wound packings; inspect all surgical incisions (even benign-appearing wounds can harbor TSST-1 producers); aggressive crystalloid resuscitation (often requires 6-10 L in 24h). Thresholds: Five mandatory criteria: fever >38.9 C, diffuse macular erythroderma ('sunburn rash'), hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg), multisystem involvement (>=3 organ systems), and late desquamation (1-2 weeks on palms/soles).

patient_plain_language: Toxic shock syndrome is an overwhelming immune reaction to a toxin produced by common Staph bacteria (often associated with high-absorbency tampons or wound packings). The toxin supercharges your immune cells, causing a sudden high fever, widespread sunburn-like skin rash, vomiting, and a dangerous drop in blood pressure.

solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Continuous arterial line BP and cardiac telemetry; serial liver and renal profiles; full body skin inspection for desquamation.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Five mandatory criteria: fever >38.9 C, diffuse macular erythroderma ('sunburn rash'), hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg), multisystem involvement (>=3 organ systems), and late desquamation (1-2 weeks on palms/soles).

stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Clindamycin is bacteriostatic; combine with bactericidal agent (vancomycin or cefazolin).
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Intensive ICU fluid resuscitation for massive capillary leak

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Adding Clindamycin to neutralize superantigen synthesis reduces toxic shock mortality from 30% to under 8%.

title: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome & Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (SJS/TEN): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (British Journal of Dermatology)
snippet: IMMEDIATE CESSATION OF ALL INCITING MEDICATIONS (allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, sulfonamides, nevirapine, NSAIDs) and transfer to an accredited Burn ICU slashes mortality by 60%. Cyclosporine (3-5 mg/kg/day) or Etanercept (50 mg SC single dose) halts Fas-FasL mediated keratinocyte apoptosis, reducing epidermal detachment and mortality (p=0.01). Guideline Protocol: Transfer immediately to a specialized Burn Intensive Care Unit; strict reverse isolation (wound care identical to major second-degree thermal burns); daily amniotic membrane ophthalmology care to prevent blinding symblepharon scarring; avoid skin debridement (keep detached epidermis as biological dressing). Thresholds: SJS: <10% BSA detachment; SJS/TEN overlap: 10-30% BSA; TEN: >30% BSA detachment with hemorrhagic mucosal involvement (eyes, mouth, genitalia).

title: Acute Compartment Syndrome (Traumatic Limb Ischemia): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons)

It causes sudden, severe calf pain, swelling, and redness that looks and feels exactly like a dangerous blood clot (DVT). An ultrasound quickly proves the vein is open and the fluid is outside the vein.

title: Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension (CTEPH): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (New England Journal of Medicine)
snippet: CTEPH is the ONLY potentially curable form of pulmonary hypertension. PULMONARY ENDARTERECTOMY (PEA / open surgical removal of fibrotic clots) performed at an expert center cures hypertension and restores near-normal hemodynamics in >75% of patients. In inoperable CTEPH or residual post-PEA hypertension, soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator Riociguat (CHEST-1 trial, n=261) improves 6-minute walk distance (+46 meters; p<0.001) and pulmonary vascular resistance. Guideline Protocol: Lifelong therapeutic anticoagulation (unfractionated heparin, LMWH, or warfarin; target INR 2.5-3.5); multidisciplinary evaluation at an expert CTEPH surgical center; balloon pulmonary angioplasty (BPA) for distal disease. Thresholds: Mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) >20 mmHg with PAWP <=15 mmHg and PVR >2 Wood units, in the presence of mismatched perfusion defects on V/Q scan after >=3 months anticoagulation.

Instead, they transform into tough, fibrotic yellow scars that permanently block your lung arteries, forcing your right heart to pump against crushing pressure. Unlike other forms of high lung pressure, this condition can be completely cured by expert surgeons who carefully peel the old scars out of the lung arteries.

snippet: Autoantibodies against the M-type Phospholipase A2 Receptor (Anti-PLA2R; present in 70-80%) deposit subepithelially, forming the classic 'spike-and-dome' appearance on silver stain. Guideline Protocol: Supportive therapy for 6 months (maximal tolerated ACEi/ARB or SGLT2i, statin for severe dyslipidemia, blood pressure <120/80 mmHg, dietary sodium <2 g/day); prophylactic anticoagulation for serum albumin <2.0-2.5 g/dL (high risk of renal vein thrombosis). Thresholds: Nephrotic syndrome with positive circulating Anti-PLA2R antibodies (titer >14 RU/mL), or renal biopsy showing subepithelial IgG4 and C3 immune deposits with basement membrane spikes.

patient_plain_language: An autoimmune condition where your immune system makes specific antibodies (Anti-PLA2R) that attack the outer wall of your kidney filters. The antibodies form thick clumps and spikes, causing massive amounts of protein to spill into your urine. Measuring these antibodies in a simple blood test tracks your disease, and targeted antibody-clearing infusions (Rituximab) cure the inflammation without harsh chemotherapy.

doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Am I on maximal blood pressure protection (ACE inhibitor or ARB) and cholesterol-lowering pills?

Rapid weight gain with severe shortness of breath and anasarca

solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Serial Anti-PLA2R antibody titers (titer reduction precedes clinical proteinuria reduction by months; immunological remission predicts clinical remission); uPCR and serum albumin every 3 months.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Nephrotic syndrome with positive circulating Anti-PLA2R antibodies (titer >14 RU/mL), or renal biopsy showing subepithelial IgG4 and C3 immune deposits with basement membrane spikes.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Membranous nephropathy is an autoimmune kidney disease where antibodies create clumps in kidney filters, leaking protein.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: Stray leaves and gum clogging the drain grates of a gutter, forcing rainwater to overflow down the walls.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Eat a low-salt diet, take your protective kidney blood pressure pills, and attend regular Rituximab infusions.

Cyclophosphamide oral/IV (Ponticelli Regimen for high risk)

stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: High risk of deep vein and renal vein thrombosis when albumin <2.5 g/dL; consider prophylactic anticoagulation.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Pre-medicate rituximab with methylprednisolone, acetaminophen, and diphenhydramine.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Rituximab achieves superior durable complete/partial remission at 24 months compared to cyclosporine (60% vs 20%; p<0.001).

title: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS - APOL1 Podocytopathy): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Kidney International)
snippet: FSGS is characterized by sclerosis affecting segments of some (focal) glomeruli, driven by podocyte injury (APOL1 high-risk variants G1/G2 in individuals of African ancestry, circulating permeability factors, or genetic slit-diaphragm mutations). Primary FSGS with nephrotic syndrome requires high-dose corticosteroids (Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for minimum 16 weeks) or Calcineurin Inhibitors (Tacrolimus/Cyclosporine). Genetic or secondary FSGS (hyperfiltration from obesity, solitary kidney) DOES NOT RESPOND TO IMMUNOSUPPRESSION. Guideline Protocol: Differentiate primary vs secondary/adaptive FSGS (secondary FSGS shows glomerulomegaly, sub-nephrotic proteinuria, absence of severe hypoalbuminemia, and does NOT benefit from steroids); rigorous blood pressure control (<120/80 mmHg); weight reduction; sodium restriction (<2 g/day). Thresholds: Focal segmental consolidation of the glomerular tuft with obliteration of capillary lumina and podocyte detachment on renal biopsy.
key_takeaway: FSGS is characterized by sclerosis affecting segments of some (focal) glomeruli, driven by podocyte injury (APOL1 high-risk variants G1/G2 in individuals of African ancestry, circulating permeability factors, or genetic ...
patient_plain_language: Scar tissue forms in scattered patches (focal) and in small segments of your kidney filters. Because the damaged filter walls cannot seal, protein leaks into your urine and healthy kidney tissue slowly gets replaced by scars. It is crucial to determine whether your FSGS is autoimmune (which needs steroid pills) or caused by kidney strain and high blood pressure (which needs blood pressure pills and weight loss, not steroids).

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Did my kidney biopsy and clinical tests confirm primary autoimmune FSGS rather than secondary hyperfiltration?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Have I been tested for APOL1 genetic risk variants or podocyte genetic mutations?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Am I taking an ACE inhibitor, ARB, or SGLT2 inhibitor to protect my remaining kidney filters from pressure overload?

red_flags: Rapid rise in serum creatinine with declining urine output (accelerated chronic kidney disease progression)
Severe uncontrollable swelling in the legs and abdomen despite high-dose water pills

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Differentiate primary vs secondary/adaptive FSGS (secondary FSGS shows glomerulomegaly, sub-nephrotic proteinuria, absence of severe hypoalbuminemia, and does NOT benefit from steroids); rigorous blood pressure control (<120/80 mmHg); weight reduction; sodium restriction (<2 g/day).
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Serial uPCR and serum creatinine every 4-8 weeks; genetic testing for APOL1 and podocyte structural genes (NPHS1, NPHS2, INF2) if steroid-resistant.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Focal segmental consolidation of the glomerular tuft with obliteration of capillary lumina and podocyte detachment on renal biopsy.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: FSGS is patchy scarring in kidney filters that causes protein leakage and gradual decline in kidney function.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: Patches of rust and calcification welding some of the fine valves shut on a hydraulic pump system.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Restrict salt, keep blood pressure strictly under control, take your kidney protective medications, and avoid smoking.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day (max 80 mg) for minimum 16 weeks; or Tacrolimus 0.05-0.1 mg/kg/day divided BID.
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Do NOT use immunosuppression for secondary/adaptive FSGS (causes pure toxicity without benefit).
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Tacrolimus trough monitoring (5-8 ng/mL); adjust for worsening renal function.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Prolonged corticosteroid therapy achieves complete or partial proteinuria remission in 50-60% of primary FSGS.

title: IgA Nephropathy (Berger's Disease - Synpharyngitic Hematuria): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (JAMA & Lancet)
snippet: IgA Nephropathy is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide, caused by galactose-deficient IgA1 (Gd-IgA1) forming mesangial immune complexes. Classic presentation is 'synpharyngitic hematuria' (gross red/cola-colored urine developing CONCURRENTLY within 24-48 hours of an upper respiratory infection). Maximal optimized supportive care (ACEi/ARB, SGLT2i Dapagliflozin, and endothelin blocker) is foundational; targeted-release oral budesonide (Nefecon) or reduced-dose oral methylprednisolone with antibiotic prophylaxis (TESTING trial, n=503) cuts 5-year renal failure risk by >40%. Guideline Protocol: Maximal tolerated supportive therapy (ACEi or ARB titrated to maximum dose, SGLT2 inhibitor, strict BP <120/80 mmHg, dietary sodium <2,000 mg/day, smoking cessation, healthy lifestyle) for at least 3 months prior to immunosuppression. Thresholds: Dominant or codominant mesangial deposition of IgA on immunofluorescence of renal biopsy.

patient_plain_language: The most common kidney filter disease in the world. Your body makes an unusual form of an antibody called IgA that gets trapped in the central tissue (mesangium) of your kidney filters. The hallmark sign is noticing painless dark, cola-colored urine during the exact same 1 to 2 days that you catch a sore throat or cold. Taking blood pressure pills (ACE inhibitors and SGLT2 inhibitors) shields your kidney filters from pressure damage.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What was my Oxford MEST-C pathology score on kidney biopsy (are there active crescents or permanent scars)?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Am I taking both an ACE inhibitor/ARB and an SGLT2 inhibitor (like Dapagliflozin) to reduce kidney protein spillage below 0.5 grams?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Am I a candidate for targeted-release gut budesonide capsules (Nefecon) to stop the abnormal IgA antibodies at their source?

red_flags: Sudden appearance of dark cola-colored or bloody urine during a feverish sore throat or flu
Rapidly doubling creatinine indicating rare crescentic rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Maximal tolerated supportive therapy (ACEi or ARB titrated to maximum dose, SGLT2 inhibitor, strict BP <120/80 mmHg, dietary sodium <2,000 mg/day, smoking cessation, healthy lifestyle) for at least 3 months prior to immunosuppression.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (target uPCR <0.5-0.75 g/g or <0.5 g/day); eGFR slope tracking; Oxford MEST-C histological classification score.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Dominant or codominant mesangial deposition of IgA on immunofluorescence of renal biopsy.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: IgA nephropathy is antibody clumps settling in kidney filters, often causing cola-colored urine during a cold.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: Fine coffee grounds getting trapped between the mesh screen and drainage plate of a French press.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Drink plenty of water, eat a low-salt diet, take your kidney-protective blood pressure medicine daily, and never smoke.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: Nefecon 16 mg once daily in the morning 1 hour before breakfast x 9 months; Dapagliflozin 10 mg daily.
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: High-dose systemic steroids carry significant infection risks (Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis required); Nefecon reduces systemic exposure.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Dose adjust all medications based on baseline eGFR.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Oral methylprednisolone significantly reduces eGFR decline and kidney failure in high-risk IgA nephropathy (p<0.001).

title: Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN - Latent Subepithelial Humps): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Pediatric Nephrology)
snippet: PSGN occurs after Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus infection (pharyngitis 1-3 weeks prior, or impetigo 3-6 weeks prior). Classic nephritic triad: gross hematuria ('tea-colored' urine), periorbital edema, and hypertension. Hallmark laboratory findings: PROFOUNDLY DEPRESSED SERUM COMPLEMENT C3 with normal C4, and elevated anti-streptolysin O (ASO) or anti-DNase B titers. Management is ENTIRELY SUPPORTIVE (fluid and salt restriction, loop diuretics for volume overload). Over 95% of children and 75% of adults recover completely without immunosuppression. Guideline Protocol: Strict sodium (<1.5-2.0 g/day) and fluid restriction during acute oliguric phase; loop diuretics for edema and hypertension; antibiotic therapy (oral penicillin or amoxicillin) ONLY to eradicate any residual streptococcal carriage and prevent spread to close contacts (does NOT alter the course of glomerulonephritis). Thresholds: Evidence of preceding streptococcal infection (elevated ASO or anti-DNase B), low C3 complement, acute nephritic syndrome, and resolution within 6-8 weeks.
key_takeaway: PSGN occurs after Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus infection (pharyngitis 1-3 weeks prior, or impetigo 3-6 weeks prior). Classic nephritic triad: gross hematuria ('tea-colored' urine), periorbital edema, and hyperten...
patient_plain_language: An immune reaction in your kidneys that strikes 1 to 3 weeks AFTER a strep throat infection (or 3 to 6 weeks after a strep skin sore). It is NOT an active kidney infection; rather, your body's leftover immune complexes deposit in the kidneys, causing tea-colored urine, puffy eyes, and high blood pressure. In over 95% of people, the condition heals completely on its own with temporary salt restriction and water pills.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Did blood tests confirm low complement C3 and elevated anti-streptococcal antibodies (ASO or Anti-DNase B)?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Why are steroid pills NOT needed, and how will water pills and salt restriction protect my kidneys while they heal?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: When will we re-check my complement C3 level to confirm it has returned to normal within 6 to 8 weeks?

red_flags: Sudden severe headache, visual changes, or seizures caused by acute hypertensive encephalopathy
Severe breathlessness and inability to lie flat from acute pulmonary edema

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: Strict sodium (<1.5-2.0 g/day) and fluid restriction during acute oliguric phase; loop diuretics for edema and hypertension; antibiotic therapy (oral penicillin or amoxicillin) ONLY to eradicate any residual streptococcal carriage and prevent spread to close contacts (does NOT alter the course of glomerulonephritis).
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Blood pressure checks every 4-6 hours during acute phase; serum complement C3 (MUST normalize within 6-8 weeks; persistence beyond 8 weeks mandates renal biopsy to rule out C3 Glomerulopathy or Membranoproliferative GN); serum creatinine.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Evidence of preceding streptococcal infection (elevated ASO or anti-DNase B), low C3 complement, acute nephritic syndrome, and resolution within 6-8 weeks.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: PSGN is a temporary immune inflammation of kidney filters that develops weeks after a strep infection.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: Dust and debris blowing into an outdoor pool after a severe storm, clouding the water until the pump filter cleans it.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Restrict dietary salt and fluids during swelling, take prescribed water pills, and attend follow-up lab checks.

approved_drugs: Furosemide oral/IV (for volume overload and hypertension)
stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: Furosemide 1-2 mg/kg/dose (or 20-40 mg IV in adults) titrated for diuresis; Amoxicillin 500 mg TID x 10 days.
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Corticosteroids and immunosuppressants have NO proven role in PSGN and are contraindicated.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Monitor potassium closely during brisk diuretic therapy.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Supportive therapy yields complete renal recovery in >95% of pediatric and >75% of adult PSGN patients.

disease: Lupus Nephritis (ISN/RPS Class IV Diffuse Proliferative)
title: Lupus Nephritis (ISN/RPS Class IV Diffuse Proliferative): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (New England Journal of Medicine)
keywords: lupus nephritis (isn/rps class iv diffuse proliferative)
snippet: Class IV proliferative lupus nephritis carries the highest risk of end-stage renal disease. The landmark BLISS-LN trial (n=448) proved that adding B-cell activating factor inhibitor BELIMUMAB (10 mg/kg IV monthly) to standard induction therapy (Mycophenolate Mofetil + Glucocorticoids) achieved significantly higher Primary Efficacy Renal Response (43% vs 32%; p=0.031) and reduced renal-related death by 49%. Alternative induction is the Euro-Lupus IV Cyclophosphamide protocol. Guideline Protocol: MANDATORY HYDROXYCHLOROQUINE FOR ALL PATIENTS (reduces renal damage accrual, prevents flares, and improves survival; target blood level >750 ng/mL); pregnancy planning (teratogenic drugs must be stopped 6 months prior under stable remission); sun protection. Thresholds: ISN/RPS Class IV criteria: Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis involving >=50% of glomeruli with subendothelial immune deposits ('wire-loop' lesions).
key_takeaway: Class IV proliferative lupus nephritis carries the highest risk of end-stage renal disease. The landmark BLISS-LN trial (n=448) proved that adding B-cell activating factor inhibitor BELIMUMAB (10 mg/kg IV monthly) to sta...
patient_plain_language: Lupus (SLE) causes your immune system to attack and severely inflame your kidney filters, causing protein and blood to leak into your urine. Diffuse proliferative (Class IV) is the most aggressive form, requiring strong immune-calming medicines. Combining Mycophenolate pills with monthly Belimumab biologic infusions calms the attack and preserves your kidneys without harsh old-school chemotherapy.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What exact class of lupus nephritis was diagnosed on my kidney biopsy (Class III, IV, or V)?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Am I taking daily Hydroxychloroquine (Plaquenil) to protect my kidneys and prevent future lupus flares?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Are we using the newer Belimumab biologic addition to help reach a safe target protein level below 0.5 grams?

red_flags: Sudden jump in blood pressure accompanied by rapidly decreasing urine and swollen legs
New-onset confusion, severe headaches, or seizures indicating lupus cerebritis

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: MANDATORY HYDROXYCHLOROQUINE FOR ALL PATIENTS (reduces renal damage accrual, prevents flares, and improves survival; target blood level >750 ng/mL); pregnancy planning (teratogenic drugs must be stopped 6 months prior under stable remission); sun protection.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Serial uPCR (target <0.5 g/g by 12 months); serum anti-dsDNA antibodies and complement C3/C4 monthly during induction; annual ophthalmology exam for hydroxychloroquine retinopathy.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: ISN/RPS Class IV criteria: Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis involving >=50% of glomeruli with subendothelial immune deposits ('wire-loop' lesions).

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Lupus nephritis is autoimmune inflammation of the kidney filters caused by Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: A home security alarm system that goes haywire and sprays fire retardant foam over all the delicate computer servers.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Take your medications daily without missing doses, protect yourself from direct sun exposure, and track your urine protein.

approved_drugs: Pulse Methylprednisolone IV then oral taper
stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: Belimumab 10 mg/kg IV at weeks 0, 2, 4, then every 4 weeks; Mycophenolate 1 g BID titrated to 1.5 g BID.
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Mycophenolate is a potent teratogen (Black Box Warning for pregnancy loss and congenital malformations).
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Hydroxychloroquine max dose 5 mg/kg actual body weight to prevent retinal toxicity.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Adding Belimumab to standard therapy significantly increases 2-year renal response and halves renal events in lupus nephritis.

disease: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD - Tolvaptan GDMT)
title: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD - Tolvaptan GDMT): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (New England Journal of Medicine)
keywords: autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (adpkd - tolvaptan gdmt)
snippet: ADPKD (PKD1 on chromosome 16 in 78%, PKD2 on chromosome 4 in 15%) causes progressive development of thousands of fluid-filled cysts, destroying renal parenchyma and causing ESRD by age 55-60. The pivotal TEMPO 3:4 (n=1,445) and REPRISE (n=1,370) phase 3 trials proved that selective Vasopressin V2 Receptor Antagonist TOLVAPTAN slowed kidney volume expansion by 49% and reduced annual eGFR decline by 1.0-1.27 mL/min/1.73m2/year. Guideline Protocol: High fluid intake (minimum 3.0-4.0 L/day evenly spaced, including waking at night to drink, to suppress endogenous vasopressin secretion); dietary sodium restriction (<2,000 mg/day); dietary protein moderation (0.8 g/kg/day); strict blood pressure target (<110/75 mmHg in young patients via HALT-PKD trial). Thresholds: Mayo Imaging Classification 1C-1E with documented annual eGFR loss >=2.5-3.0 mL/min/1.73m2.
key_takeaway: ADPKD (PKD1 on chromosome 16 in 78%, PKD2 on chromosome 4 in 15%) causes progressive development of thousands of fluid-filled cysts, destroying renal parenchyma and causing ESRD by age 55-60. The pivotal TEMPO 3:4 (n=1,4...
patient_plain_language: A genetic condition where thousands of fluid-filled blisters (cysts) slowly grow inside both of your kidneys over decades. The expanding cysts crush and replace healthy kidney tissue, making the kidneys enlarge to the size of footballs. Drinking large amounts of water (3 to 4 liters a day) and taking a targeted pill called Tolvaptan blocks the hormone that feeds cyst growth.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: What is my Mayo Imaging Classification category (Class 1C, 1D, or 1E) based on my kidney MRI volume?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Am I eligible for Tolvaptan (Jynarque) to slow down cyst growth and delay dialysis by years?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Have I been screened with a brain MRA scan for silent cerebral berry aneurysms, especially if a family member had an aneurysm?

red_flags: Sudden severe 'thunderclap' headache with neck stiffness (Ruptured Intracranial Berry Aneurysm)
Severe flank pain with high fever and chills indicating infected kidney cyst

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: High fluid intake (minimum 3.0-4.0 L/day evenly spaced, including waking at night to drink, to suppress endogenous vasopressin secretion); dietary sodium restriction (<2,000 mg/day); dietary protein moderation (0.8 g/kg/day); strict blood pressure target (<110/75 mmHg in young patients via HALT-PKD trial).
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Total Kidney Volume (TKV) measured by MRI using Mayo Imaging Classification (Classes 1C, 1D, 1E represent rapidly progressive disease eligible for Tolvaptan); monthly liver function tests for first 18 months on Tolvaptan.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Mayo Imaging Classification 1C-1E with documented annual eGFR loss >=2.5-3.0 mL/min/1.73m2.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: ADPKD is a genetic disorder causing thousands of growing fluid cysts in both kidneys.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: A cluster of balloons gradually inflating inside a small cardboard box until the box bursts open.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Drink 3 to 4 liters of water every day, strictly avoid smoking, keep your blood pressure low, and take Tolvaptan.

stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: Tolvaptan split-dose: 45/15 mg daily, titrated to 60/30 mg, then max 90/30 mg (morning dose upon waking, second dose 8 hours later).
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: BLACK BOX WARNING: Tolvaptan can cause severe, potentially fatal drug-induced liver injury; requires strict monthly LFT monitoring for 18 months.
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Thirst and polyuria (5-7 L/day) are expected pharmacodynamic effects; maintain brisk hydration.

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Tolvaptan slows total kidney volume growth by 49% and significantly decelerates kidney function decline in ADPKD.

disease: Distal Renal Tubular Acidosis (Type 1 dRTA - Alkaline Urine pH >5.5)
title: Distal Renal Tubular Acidosis (Type 1 dRTA - Alkaline Urine pH >5.5): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Kidney International & CJASN)
keywords: distal renal tubular acidosis (type 1 drta - alkaline urine ph >5.5)
snippet: Type 1 dRTA is impaired alpha-intercalated cell H+-ATPase / H+/K+-ATPase excretion in the collecting duct, preventing normal urine acidification. Diagnostic hallmark: NORMAL ANION GAP METABOLIC ACIDOSIS WITH INAPPROPRIATELY ALKALINE URINE (URINE pH >5.5) IN THE PRESENCE OF SYSTEMIC ACIDOSIS. Chronic buffering leads to severe hypercalciuria, bilateral nephrocalcinosis, recurrent calcium phosphate kidney stones, and severe hypokalemia. ORAL POTASSIUM CITRATE or sodium bicarbonate completely corrects acidosis and prevents stone recurrence. Guideline Protocol: High fluid intake (>2.5-3.0 L/day); lifelong oral alkali replacement therapy (target normal serum bicarbonate 22-24 mEq/L and normal 24h urine calcium); dietary sodium restriction (<2 g/day to reduce urinary calcium excretion); screen for underlying autoimmune Sjögren's syndrome or rheumatoid arthritis. Thresholds: Systemic metabolic acidosis (serum HCO3 <20 mEq/L) with normal serum anion gap, positive urine net charge (Urine Na + K - Cl > 0), and urine pH persistently >5.5.
key_takeaway: Type 1 dRTA is impaired alpha-intercalated cell H+-ATPase / H+/K+-ATPase excretion in the collecting duct, preventing normal urine acidification. Diagnostic hallmark: NORMAL ANION GAP METABOLIC ACIDOSIS WITH INAPPROPRIAT...
patient_plain_language: The tiny microscopic pumps in the collecting tubes of your kidneys cannot pump acid out into your urine. Because acid builds up in your blood, your bones dissolve to release calcium to buffer the acid. This calcium pours into your urine, causing recurrent kidney stones and calcified kidneys (nephrocalcinosis). Taking daily potassium citrate alkalizing powder neutralizes the acid and completely stops stones from forming.

doctor_consultation_checklist.parameter_question: Is my urine pH persistently above 5.5 even when my blood tests show metabolic acidosis?
doctor_consultation_checklist.safety_question: Did a kidney ultrasound show calcium deposits (nephrocalcinosis) or calcium phosphate stones?
doctor_consultation_checklist.action_threshold_question: Am I taking sufficient Potassium Citrate liquid or tablets to keep my blood bicarbonate level at 22 to 24?

red_flags: Severe generalized muscle weakness, cramps, or paralysis caused by profound hypokalemia (<2.5 mEq/L)
Recurrent agonizing flank pain from obstructing calcium phosphate kidney stones

solution_protocol.non_pharmacological_targets: High fluid intake (>2.5-3.0 L/day); lifelong oral alkali replacement therapy (target normal serum bicarbonate 22-24 mEq/L and normal 24h urine calcium); dietary sodium restriction (<2 g/day to reduce urinary calcium excretion); screen for underlying autoimmune Sjögren's syndrome or rheumatoid arthritis.
solution_protocol.monitoring_cadence: Serum electrolytes (bicarbonate, potassium) every 3-6 months; 24-hour urine collection (measuring pH, calcium, citrate, and creatinine); renal ultrasound tracking nephrocalcinosis.
solution_protocol.clinical_thresholds: Systemic metabolic acidosis (serum HCO3 <20 mEq/L) with normal serum anion gap, positive urine net charge (Urine Na + K - Cl > 0), and urine pH persistently >5.5.

stack_1_medlineplus.layman_summary: Type 1 dRTA is the inability of kidneys to excrete acid into urine, causing blood acidity, low potassium, and kidney stones.
stack_1_medlineplus.plain_analogy: A chemical factory chimney whose exhaust vent is jammed closed, forcing acid fumes back into the production floor.
stack_1_medlineplus.lifestyle_action: Drink plenty of water, take your prescribed potassium citrate alkali powder daily, and limit dietary salt.

approved_drugs: Potassium Citrate oral (Urocit-K - First Line Alkali)
stack_2_openfda.dosing_gdmt: Potassium Citrate 30-60 mEq/day divided TID with meals (target urine citrate >450 mg/day and serum HCO3 22-24).
stack_2_openfda.black_box_warning: Avoid sodium bicarbonate monotherapy if hypokalemic (sodium load accelerates distal potassium wasting).
stack_2_openfda.organ_clearance_cutoffs: Monitor potassium and bicarbonate closely; avoid potassium citrate in severe renal failure (eGFR <20).

stack_3_pubmed_cebm.endpoints: Alkali therapy with potassium citrate normalizes bone mineral density and eliminates kidney stone recurrence in dRTA.

disease: Proximal Renal Tubular Acidosis (Type 2 pRTA - Fanconi Syndrome)
title: Proximal Renal Tubular Acidosis (Type 2 pRTA - Fanconi Syndrome): Evidence & Clinical Guidelines (Kidney International)
keywords: proximal renal tubular acidosis (type 2 prta - fanconi syndrome)
snippet: Type 2 pRTA is defective proximal tubule bicarbonate reabsorption (Na+/HCO3- cotransporter NBCe1). Usually part of generalized proximal tubule dysfunction (FANCONI SYNDROME: glucosuria with normal blood sugar, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria, and hypouricemia). Unlike Type 1, the distal collecting duct functions normally: when serum bicarbonate drops below tubular threshold, URINE CAN BE FULLY ACIDIFIED (URINE pH <5.5). Massive alkali doses (10-20 mEq/kg/day) plus potassium and phosphate are required; nephrocalcinosis is RARE. Guideline Protocol: Massive oral alkali therapy; oral neutral phosphate supplementation and active vitamin D (Calcitriol) to treat hypophosphatemic rickets / osteomalacia; identify and remove causative drugs (Tenofovir disoproxil, ifosfamide, platinum agents, expired tetracyclines) or evaluate for multiple myeloma (light chain cast nephropathy). Thresholds: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with Fanconi syndrome features (glucosuria, aminoaciduria, hypophosphatemia) and ability to acidify urine to pH <5.5 during severe acidemia.

Often, they also spill sugar (even though your blood sugar is normal), phosphate, and amino acids—a condition called Fanconi syndrome. Losing phosphate weakens your bones (rickets or osteomalacia). Taking high doses of bicarbonate plus phosphate and vitamin D restores healthy bones.

snippet: Type 4 RTA is the MOST COMMON RTA, caused by aldosterone deficiency or collecting duct resistance (hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism in diabetic nephropathy, or drug-induced by ACEi, ARB, spironolactone, trimethoprim, heparin, NSAIDs). patient_plain_language: The most common kidney tubular acid condition, frequently occurring in individuals with diabetes or mild kidney disease. Your adrenal glands make too little aldosterone hormone, or your kidney tubes ignore it. Water pills (diuretics) or a tiny hormone replacement pill (Fludrocortisone) lowers potassium and restores balance.
